summary: Started chunkdown with a splitter that walks the remark syntax tree and emits chunks at block boundaries instead of cutting raw text by characters.
body:
Set up the repository today with TypeScript, unified, remark-parse and Vitest. The first design question was whether to split the raw string or the tree. I chose the tree, because splitting raw text broke fenced code blocks and lists in the first spike.

The splitter parses with remark-parse and walks the root's children. Each top-level node is stringified back using the original source offsets (position.start.offset and position.end.offset), so the output keeps the author's exact formatting and not a normalized version. Nodes are accumulated into a chunk until the next node would push it past the limit, then the chunk is closed.

The first version has one rule: a node is never cut if it fits alone in a chunk. A node larger than the limit is passed through whole for now and flagged with a TODO. I know that is wrong for long paragraphs and will fix it when the size limit work starts.

I added src/split.ts, src/index.ts and a first test file with five small inline documents. All five pass. Checked that joining the chunks with a blank line gives back the input for documents without odd spacing. Spacing between blocks is not preserved exactly yet, which is a known gap.

Next: a real size limit with a fallback for oversized nodes, then tests with documents taken from real projects.

summary: Added the maxChars limit and a fallback that splits oversized paragraphs at sentence ends, so no chunk exceeds the limit unless a single unbreakable word does.
body:
Worked on the oversized-node TODO from two days ago. The splitter now takes an options object with maxChars, default 1000. When a node fits, nothing changes. When a paragraph is too large, it is split at sentence boundaries using a simple regex on period, question mark or exclamation mark followed by whitespace.

If a single sentence is still too long, the fallback cuts at the last whitespace before the limit. Only a token with no whitespace at all, such as a long URL, can exceed maxChars, and I decided that is acceptable and documented it in a code comment.

Headings got a rule of their own: a heading is never left as the last block of a chunk. If the next block does not fit, the heading moves to the new chunk with it. This took a few lines and removed the most ugly outputs in my sample documents.

The tests now check that every chunk is at most maxChars on a 40 KB sample file. One failure showed up: inline code containing a period was split in the middle. I fixed it by splitting on the text nodes only, and the test passes. Lists and code blocks still pass through whole when too large.

summary: Large lists are now split between items, and a list that continues into the next chunk keeps its numbering through the start attribute.
body:
Today's topic was oversized lists. Before this, a list larger than maxChars went through as one chunk, which broke the limit for changelog-style documents.

The splitter now treats a list as a container: it walks the listItem children and groups them like top-level nodes. For ordered lists the continuation chunk needs the right numbers, so I read list.start and add the number of items already emitted, then render the marker explicitly. Without that, the second chunk began again at 1.

Nested lists were the hard part. A list item containing a sublist that is too large is split recursively, and the parent item's first line is not repeated. I considered repeating it for context and decided against it for now because it changes the text. It may become an option later.

Loose and tight lists differ in spacing between items. I keep the original separator by slicing the source between items. A test with a tight list of 200 items and a loose list of 80 items passes with maxChars 500.

One bug: task list items lost their checkbox because I rebuilt the marker from scratch. I now reuse the original source text up to the content start. The test with checkboxes passes. Still open: block quotes that are too large.

summary: Block quotes over the limit are now split by their inner blocks with the quote marker re-added on every line of each chunk.
body:
Finished the last container type of the first version. A block quote larger than maxChars is split by its children, like a list. The difficulty was that stringifying children from source offsets loses the leading > characters.

I solved it by taking the child text and prefixing each line with "> " again. Empty lines get ">" without a trailing space. This keeps the output valid Markdown, and the parser reads each chunk back as a block quote.

I added a round-trip test: parse each chunk, check the root has one blockquote child. It passes on three samples. A nested quote of depth three also passes.

I also noticed the default of 1000 characters is a guess. Real documents will tell me more, so the next step is collecting real Markdown files for tests.

summary: Collected eight real Markdown documents as fixtures and the splitter failed three of them: html blocks, setext headings and a footnote section needed fixes.
body:
Spent the morning building tests/fixtures with eight real documents: two READMEs, a long changelog, a blog post, API docs, a tutorial with many code blocks, a contributing guide and a page full of raw HTML. Each fixture is run at three limits, 300, 1000 and 4000 characters, and the checks are that no chunk is empty, none exceeds the limit (unless one word does), and the text content is preserved.

Three failures came out. First, setext headings (underlined with === or ---) were treated as paragraphs by my heading-keeps-next-block rule because I checked the source text and not the node type. I now check node.type and it works.

Second, raw HTML blocks that are larger than the limit had no fallback at all. I split them at blank lines inside the html value, and if there is none, at line breaks. It is not smart, but it keeps the size limit.

Third, the footnote definitions at the end of a document were each emitted as tiny chunks, 40 to 80 characters. That is the chunk-too-small problem, and it will probably get worse. I added a merge pass: when a chunk is under 25 percent of maxChars and the next one fits with it, they are joined. This reduced the chunk count of the blog post from 31 to 24.

All eight fixtures pass at all three limits now. The merge pass does shuffle some heading boundaries, so I want to look at that again.

summary: The merge pass was joining chunks across unrelated sections, so it now merges only inside the same top-level heading and stops at a heading of equal or higher level.
body:
Looked at the merge pass from this morning. In the changelog fixture, the end of one version section got glued to the heading of the next version, which is bad for retrieval because the chunk mixes two topics.

The merge rule now needs the next chunk to start with a heading of a deeper level than the current section, or not to start with a heading at all. A chunk that begins with a heading of the same or a higher level is never merged backwards.

I had to track the section level while walking, so each chunk now carries a small internal record with firstHeadingLevel. This is not exposed yet.

The changelog gives 52 chunks instead of 44, but each one covers one version. I think that is the better trade. All eight fixtures still pass. I wrote a snapshot test for the changelog so changes to this behavior show up in review.

summary: Wrote the README with usage examples, ran every example as a test, and found two examples in the draft that printed different output than claimed.
body:
Today was documentation. The README has an install section, a quick start, an options table and four examples: plain text docs, a document with code, a list-heavy document and a custom limit.

To keep the examples honest, I put each one in tests/readme.test.ts and run them with Vitest. The test compares the actual output to the text I paste in the README. This caught two mistakes. In the quick start, I had written that the sample splits into three chunks, but it gives two. In the list example, I showed the list split after item 3, while the real split happens after item 4 because of the separator length.

I corrected both in the README, not in the code, since the code behavior was correct. I also added a section called How chunks are formed with a short explanation of the rules: blocks are never cut when they fit, headings stay with the next block, small chunks are merged inside a section.

The options table lists maxChars and the merge threshold. I named the second option minRatio with default 0.25, and moved it out of a hardcoded constant. A test checks that minRatio 0 turns the merge off.

I also checked the package.json fields: name, version 0.1.0, main, types, files, license MIT. The build is not set up yet and I use tsdown for it next. Open for the release: a changeset, a CI workflow and an npm dry run.

summary: Set up tsdown, the GitHub Actions workflow and changesets, and published the first version 0.1.0 to npm after a dry run showed test files in the package.
body:
The release day. First I added tsdown with an ESM and CJS output and a generated .d.ts. The build runs in about 400 ms. I checked the output with a small script that imports both formats and splits a string.

The npm pack dry run listed the tests directory and the fixtures, about 300 KB, which nobody needs. The files field in package.json only had dist at first, but an .npmignore I created earlier was confusing things. I removed the .npmignore and kept the files whitelist. The package is now 14 KB packed.

The GitHub Actions workflow runs install, typecheck, test and build on Node 18, 20 and 22. The first run failed on Node 18 because a fixture test used Array.prototype.toSorted, which does not exist there. I replaced it with a copy and sort, and the run turned green.

Changesets is configured with a minor changeset that describes the first release. I ran the version command, which created the changelog entry, then published with npm publish --access public. The package page shows up and a fresh project installed it without trouble.

I tagged the commit v0.1.0 and wrote a short note in the repository's releases page. Next steps are tables, which the fixtures showed to be a weak point, and code blocks that are too large.

summary: Checked early feedback and found that GFM tables are not parsed at all because remark-gfm was never added, so tables were treated as paragraphs and cut mid-row.
body:
After the release, a first look at what a table does with the splitter. I tried a document with a 60-row table and the output cut rows in the middle of a line.

The cause was simple: remark-gfm was not in the processor, so the table was a plain paragraph and my sentence splitter worked on it. The same problem also affected task lists and strikethrough, which only worked by accident.

I added remark-gfm to the dependencies and to the unified pipeline. The tables now arrive as table nodes, with tableRow and tableCell children. At this point they are passed through whole, as lists were at the start, so large tables still break the limit but never in the middle of a row.

All earlier tests still pass. The footnote fixture changed slightly, since remark-gfm parses footnotes, and I updated its snapshot after checking the diff by hand. I opened a note for myself for the table splitting by rows with a repeated header, which is the main topic of the next days. A patch release 0.1.1 with the gfm fix is queued as a changeset.

summary: Released 0.1.1 with the remark-gfm fix and added a regression test with a table so the parser setup cannot lose it again.
body:
Wrote the regression test first: a document with a table, a task list and a strikethrough, checking the node types after parsing. It failed on the old code and passes now.

The patch changeset says that GFM syntax is now parsed. I ran the version command and the CI workflow. All three Node versions passed. Then I published 0.1.1.

I checked in a clean folder that npm install chunkdown gives 0.1.1 and that the table example from the test splits without breaking a row. It does.

The table splitter by rows is next. I plan to repeat the header row at the top of every continuation chunk, and I need to decide how to count the length of the header against the limit.

summary: Designed table splitting on paper: rows are grouped under the limit, the header and delimiter row repeat in each chunk, and a header larger than the limit is an error case.
body:
Spent a short session on the design before writing code. A table chunk is header row plus delimiter row plus a group of body rows. The header cost is subtracted from the budget for each chunk, so the effective room for rows is maxChars minus header length.

Edge cases I wrote down: a table with a header longer than half the limit, a single row longer than the remaining room, and column alignment markers in the delimiter row. The alignment must be copied exactly from the source.

For a row that is too long alone, I plan to emit it as it is, over the limit, and document it. For a huge header I plan to skip the repetition and warn. I will write the tests for these four cases before the implementation.

summary: Implemented row-wise table splitting with a repeated header; a 60-row table now yields six chunks that each parse as a valid table.
body:
Wrote the tests from the design notes, then the code in src/table.ts. The function takes the table node and the source, slices the header and the delimiter row from the original text, and then adds rows while the running length stays under the budget.

Each emitted chunk is checked by parsing it again with the same pipeline and asserting that it contains exactly one table node. That caught an off-by-one: my first version dropped the newline after the last row, so a following paragraph glued itself to the table.

With maxChars 600 the 60-row sample gives six chunks of ten rows each, all with the header. Alignment markers like :---: are kept since I copy the delimiter row verbatim.

The header-too-large case emits the table without repetition and does nothing else for now; the warning mechanism needs an options hook I do not have yet. Cell content with a pipe inside inline code still works because I rely on the node positions, not on splitting at |.

summary: Added the onWarning option and used it for the oversized table header and the single row that exceeds the limit, which both used to pass silently.
body:
Added an onWarning callback to the options. It receives an object with a code and a message, for example table-header-too-large or row-exceeds-limit. By default nothing is printed so a library user is not surprised by console output.

The two table cases now call it. I wrote tests that pass a spy and check the codes. The same hook will serve for oversized code lines later.

I documented the option in the README table of options. All tests pass.

summary: Large fenced code blocks are now split on line boundaries with the fence and language repeated, so each chunk is valid code block Markdown.
body:
Evening session on code blocks. Before this a fenced block larger than maxChars was passed through whole, which broke the limit on tutorials with long listings.

The new function reads the fence info, the language and the meta string, from the code node, then splits the value on line breaks. Every chunk gets an opening fence with the same info string and a closing fence. The budget subtracts the length of both fences.

A subtle issue is the fence length. If the code itself contains three backticks, the original block used four. I take the fence from the source text instead of assuming three, and a test with a nested example confirms it.

Indented code blocks have no fence. I split them the same way but keep the four spaces of indentation on every line. The test with an indented block passes.

A single line longer than the limit is emitted whole, and onWarning gets code-line-exceeds-limit. Minified code in one fixture triggered it once, as expected.

I also thought about splitting at blank lines inside code, as that often keeps functions together. I tried a first version that prefers blank lines within the last 30 percent of the budget. On the tutorial fixture it keeps most functions in one chunk, which is better for retrieval. I kept it behind a default-on behavior and added two tests. The snapshot for the tutorial changed, and I reviewed the diff by hand.

summary: Introduced a length function option so the limit can be measured in tokens, with a default character counter and a test using a fake word-based counter.
body:
Started the token counter. Instead of a maxTokens option, I made the limit generic: options.length is a function from string to number, and maxSize is the limit in that unit. The default is the string length, so existing users see no change. maxChars stays as an alias for now.

All the places that compared string lengths now call the function: the node accumulation, the table budget, the code fence budget and the merge pass. I found seven of them with a grep for .length. Two were in the sentence splitter and were easy to miss.

The test uses a fake counter that counts words. With maxSize 50 words, every chunk of the blog post fixture is at most 50 words. A second test checks that the default behaves the same as before on the eight fixtures.

One concern is speed, since a real tokenizer may be slow and the splitter calls the function many times on growing strings. I will measure that with a real tokenizer in the next step.

summary: Plugged a real tokenizer into the length option and measured it: calling it on every growing candidate made splitting 12 times slower, so counts are now cached per node.
body:
Used a GPT-style tokenizer package as a test in a script outside the library, since the library itself must not depend on one. The script splits the API docs fixture with maxSize 256 tokens.

The result was correct but slow: 1.9 seconds against 160 ms with the character counter. A profile showed that the accumulation loop recounted the whole candidate chunk each time a node was added, which is quadratic in the chunk size.

The fix is to count each node once and keep a running sum, plus the separator cost. That is an approximation, because tokens of joined text can differ slightly from the sum of the parts. To keep the limit hard, I do a final exact check on a closed chunk, and if it is over, the last node moves to the next chunk.

After the change the same run takes 310 ms, and the exact check moved the last node in 3 of 41 chunks. Tests pass with the fake counter and with the real one in the script.

I will describe this approximation in the docs so a user knows why a chunk can be a little under the limit.

summary: Published the tokenizer option as 0.2.0 with docs for tiktoken-style and word-count examples, and fixed a cached-count bug found while writing the example.
body:
The goal today was to ship the pluggable counter. I wrote two docs examples: one with a tiktoken-compatible encoder and one with a simple word counter. Both are run as tests in the README test file, the encoder example with a stub so the test suite does not need the package.

While running the word counter example I found a bug. The per-node cache I added yesterday used the node's start offset as the key, and the table splitter creates synthetic nodes for row groups with the same offsets as the original table. A group got the count of the whole table and a chunk came out too small. I changed the key to the pair of offsets plus the text length, and the test with a table and a token counter now passes.

I renamed the option properly: maxSize and length are the documented names, and maxChars remains as a deprecated alias that logs nothing but is marked in the type definitions with a JSDoc deprecated tag.

The changeset is minor. The CI run was green on all three Node versions. I published 0.2.0 and checked the type definitions in a fresh project, where the length option shows its signature correctly.

To do next: a CLI, since several people may want to try the splitter without writing code.

summary: Built the first CLI: it reads a file or stdin, takes flags for size and format, and prints chunks as JSON or separated by a marker line.
body:
Started the command line tool today. I used node's util.parseArgs, which avoids another dependency. Flags: --max-size, --format (json or text), --separator, and --help. A file path is a positional argument, and a dash or no argument reads from stdin.

The JSON format prints an array of objects with index, text and length. The text format prints chunks separated by a line with three dashes and the chunk number, and the separator flag changes that line.

The bin entry in package.json points to the built dist/cli.js with a shebang. tsdown needed a second entry point for it. I checked that the shebang survives the build and that the executable bit is set after npm install; npm handles that for bin files.

Tests run the CLI as a child process with fixtures and compare the JSON. Three cases: file input, stdin input and an invalid flag. The invalid flag test exposed an ugly stack trace for an unknown option. I now catch the parseArgs error and print one line plus the usage text, with exit code 2.

I also found that a missing file printed the raw ENOENT error. It now prints Cannot read file: name and exits with 1.

The tokens flag is not here yet. It needs a way to choose a tokenizer, and the decision is whether to load a module by name. I will think about that for the next session.

summary: Added a --tokenizer flag to the CLI that loads a module by path or name exporting a count function, with a clear error when the export is missing.
body:
Decided to let the CLI load a user module for the tokenizer. The flag takes a path or a package name; the module must export a function named count, or a default function, taking a string and returning a number.

The loading uses dynamic import. Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory, not the CLI location, which was a bug in the first try: ./count.js was looked up inside dist and failed. I resolve it with path.resolve and a file URL now.

If the module has no usable export, the CLI prints Tokenizer module must export a count function and exits with 2. A test covers it with a small fixture module. Another test uses a word counting module and checks the chunks at --max-size 40.

The flag is documented in the CLI section of the README with a short example. I did not add a built-in tokenizer, to keep the package without heavy dependencies.

One more detail: --max-size with a non-number, such as abc, now fails with a clear message and not NaN behavior, which before made every node its own chunk.

summary: Reworked the docs into a small site structure with a guide, an options reference and a recipes page, and tested every code sample.
body:
The README had grown too long, so I split the docs. A docs folder now has guide.md, options.md and recipes.md, and the README is shorter with links.

The options reference lists maxSize, length, minRatio, onWarning and the deprecated maxChars, each with type, default and a short example. I generated the signatures from the type definitions by hand and checked them against src/types.ts, since a mismatch would be worse than no docs.

The recipes page has four cases: chunks for an embedding model with a 512-token limit, keeping a heading path as metadata, handling large tables, and using the CLI in a shell pipeline. The heading path recipe is a bit long, and it made me think that the library could return the path itself. I added it as an idea to the issue list for later.

A script extracts the TypeScript code blocks from the docs folder and compiles them with tsc in no-emit mode. It found one sample that used a wrong option name, minimumRatio, from an early draft. The script runs in CI now as a docs check step.

I also fixed a few places in the README that still said maxChars. The wording is consistent with maxSize everywhere else.

summary: Added heading path metadata: splitting can return objects with the text and the list of headings above each chunk, which the recipe had needed by hand.
body:
Followed up on the idea from the docs session. A new function, splitWithMeta, returns an array of objects with text, length and headings, an array of the heading texts from the top level down to the section where the chunk starts.

The heading stack is kept during the walk: when a heading of level n arrives, the stack is cut to the entries with a level below n, and the new one is pushed. A chunk takes a copy of the stack at its start. The heading text comes from the node's children, flattened to plain text, so emphasis and inline code do not leave markup in the path.

The existing split function keeps returning plain strings and now calls the same core, then maps to the text. I checked that the eight fixtures give the same strings as before.

A test with nested headings, h1 to h3 and then back to h2, checks the stacks. Another test covers a document with text before the first heading, where the path is empty.

I rewrote the recipe to use the new function, and the docs check passes. A minor changeset describes the addition.

summary: Profiled the CLI on a 4 MB Markdown file: the time went into repeated parsing of chunks for validation, so the check now only runs when a debug flag is set.
body:
Tried the CLI on a big concatenated file of 4 MB. It took 14 seconds, more than I would expect from a parser that runs in linear time.

A profile with node --cpu-prof showed 60 percent of the time in the unified processor, called from a function that re-parses each chunk to verify that it is valid Markdown with the same node count. I had added that check as a safety net during the table work and left it on.

I moved the check behind an internal validate option, which the tests turn on and the default turns off. The same file now takes 5.1 seconds. That is still slower than I want, and the profile shows string concatenation in the accumulation loop, plus slicing the source for every node twice.

I fixed the double slicing by keeping the slice in the node record. This brought it to 3.8 seconds. The rest is mostly the remark parse itself, about 2.9 seconds, which I cannot change without leaving the parser.

All tests pass with validate on. I wrote the numbers in the notes file so I can compare later when the real performance work starts.

summary: Released 0.3.0 with tables, code block splitting, the length option, the CLI and heading metadata, after cleaning up the changelog and checking the package in a fresh project.
body:
This was the release day for everything of the last weeks. I reviewed the pending changesets first: there were six, and two said nearly the same thing about the length option. I merged them into one text so the changelog is readable.

The version command produced 0.3.0 and the changelog sections. I read the generated file and fixed one entry that mentioned an internal function name.

Before publishing I ran the whole checklist. Typecheck, tests with validate on, the docs check, the build and an npm pack. The tarball is 22 KB and has dist, the README and the license, nothing else.

I installed the tarball in a fresh folder and ran three things: the library from an ESM script, the library from a CJS script, and the CLI on a sample file with --format json. All three worked. The CLI printed the help text with the right version number, which I take from package.json at build time.

CI ran green on Node 18, 20 and 22. I published 0.3.0 and created the git tag and the release note, which lists the main additions and the deprecation of maxChars.

Open items for the coming weeks: wait for first user reports, watch for chunks that come out too small on real documents, and plan the performance work for large files with the numbers from the CLI profile.

summary: Wrote a changelog check and a smoke test that installs the packed tarball in a temp project, after 0.3.0 users reported a missing types path.
body:
Two issues came in after 0.3.0, and one said TypeScript could not find the types when importing from a Node ESM project. I reproduced it by running npm pack and installing the tarball in a fresh folder. The exports map pointed at a .d.ts file that tsdown had emitted under a different name for the ESM build.

I fixed the exports map in package.json so the import and require conditions each list their own types file. Then I added scripts/smoke.mjs, which packs the library, installs it into a temp directory and runs a tiny tsc compile plus a require and an import call.

The smoke test runs in CI after the build step now. It failed on the old exports map and passes on the new one, which is what I wanted to see. I also checked with the arethetypeswrong tool and it reported no problems after the change.

Not done yet: the CLI bin path is not covered by the smoke test. I will add that next, because a broken shebang would only show up after a release. A patch release 0.3.1 is queued with a changeset describing the types fix.

summary: Users saw tiny trailing chunks after tables and code blocks, so the splitter now merges a small tail chunk back into its predecessor when the result still fits the limit.
body:
An issue reported chunks of only a few characters, often a single closing line or a short paragraph after a large table. I reproduced it with the document attached to the issue. The table split produced chunks that were nearly full, and the paragraph after it became its own chunk because the merge pass did not look at chunks made by the table splitter.

The cause was that the merge pass worked on the list of top-level blocks, while table and code splitting happened afterwards. So pieces created late never took part in merging. I moved the merge to run after all splitting, over the final chunk list.

A new rule is that a table chunk is never merged with a following paragraph if that would put a partial table before text, since the repeated header would look odd. Only plain text chunks merge with plain text chunks. Code chunks keep their own fences and stay apart.

I added a minSize option, default zero, so the behaviour is opt-in for people who like small chunks. With minSize set to 200 the sample document went from 41 chunks to 33, and none was under 200 characters except the last one.

Tests cover the table-then-paragraph case, the code-then-paragraph case and the last chunk of a document. I replied on the issue with the option name and asked the reporter to try the branch build. The docs reference page has the new option and an example.

summary: Replied to an issue asking why a heading is alone in a chunk: headings now stay attached to the first block that follows them.
body:
The reporter showed a chunk that contained only a heading line. This happened when the heading was followed by a block larger than the remaining space. The splitter closed the chunk and started the next block fresh, leaving the heading orphaned.

I added a keep-with-next rule for headings in the chunk builder. If the current chunk ends with a heading, it is moved into the next chunk before that chunk starts. A test with a heading before a big list now passes.

One edge case remains: a heading followed by a table whose header alone is near the limit. The heading goes along and may push the first chunk over, which triggers the existing warning. I noted that in the issue.

summary: Links that break at chunk borders: reference-style links lose their definitions when the definition lands in another chunk, so definitions are now copied into each chunk that uses them.
body:
A user showed that a chunk containing [text][ref] was useless on its own because the [ref]: url line sat at the end of the document. Inline links were fine, since they live inside one paragraph. Reference links and footnotes were the problem.

First I looked at what the syntax tree gives: remark produces linkReference nodes with an identifier and a definition node elsewhere. I wrote a pass that collects all definitions before splitting and stores them in a map by identifier.

After splitting, each chunk is parsed for linkReference and imageReference nodes, and the needed definitions are appended at the end of that chunk. The appended text counts toward the size limit, so the pass runs before the final size check. That was the tricky part: adding definitions can push a chunk over the limit. I reserve space by computing the definitions needed for each block while the chunk is being built, not afterwards.

That made the builder slower, because it now asks for each block's references. I cached the reference list per node in the same way as the token counts, and the timing on the 4 MB file went from 1.9 seconds to 2.0.

Footnotes are handled the same way: a footnoteDefinition is copied next to its reference. A footnote that is itself long is the known problem, and it triggers onWarning if the definition alone exceeds the limit.

Tests: four new cases, including two references to the same definition in one chunk, which must appear only once. An option, copyDefinitions, defaults to true. I left the old behaviour available with false for people who postprocess chunks themselves.

Still open: links whose text was split across a sentence-boundary fallback. I have not seen one in real documents yet, so I did not touch it.

summary: Fixed an inline link split in the middle by the sentence fallback: the splitter now treats a link's text as unbreakable and only cuts at sentence ends outside links.
body:
Following yesterday's reference work, I went looking for the case I had left open and found one in a documentation fixture. A long paragraph contained a link whose text had a period in it, like [v1.2. notes](url). The sentence splitter cut after the period and produced two chunks with broken link syntax.

The sentence fallback worked on the raw paragraph string. I changed it to work on the paragraph's inline nodes, so it only considers sentence ends in text nodes, never inside link, image or inline code nodes.

The splitter then rebuilds text from node positions in the original source, so formatting stays byte-identical. I checked this with a test that joins all chunks and compares to the input, ignoring whitespace between blocks.

The fixture now passes. I also ran the fuzz-like test that I keep with random inline mixes and 500 cases passed.

A link longer than the limit still cannot be split, and it goes out as an oversized chunk with a warning.

summary: Added a benchmark script with three generated large files, which shows splitting time is quadratic in the number of blocks of one section.
body:
People wrote that large files were slow, so before changing anything I wanted numbers. I added bench/run.ts that generates three files: 1 MB of many short sections, 1 MB of one huge section with 20,000 paragraphs, and a 5 MB mixed file.

Results on my laptop: the short sections file took 0.8 seconds, the mixed file 4.1 seconds, and the huge section file 31 seconds. The last one is the outlier and grows quadratically; at 10,000 paragraphs it took 8 seconds.

A quick profile pointed to the merge pass, which re-joins and re-measures the text of the whole current chunk after each added block. In a huge section that is the same chunk list scanned over and over.

I have not fixed it yet. The plan is to keep a running length per chunk and add block lengths incrementally, and then compare the benchmark. The script is committed so the numbers can be repeated.

summary: Made the chunk builder track a running length instead of re-measuring text, and the one-huge-section benchmark dropped from 31 seconds to 1.4 seconds.
body:
I followed the profile from the earlier benchmark session. The builder called the length function on the joined candidate chunk for every block, which is quadratic when one chunk is built from thousands of blocks.

The new approach keeps a running length per chunk: length of the chunk so far plus length of the next block plus the separator. For the default character counter that is exact. For a token counter it is not exact, because tokens at a join may merge differently.

To keep correctness I used the sum as a quick upper-bound check. If the sum is clearly below the limit, the block is added. If the sum is within a small margin of the limit, the real joined text is measured once. Only then is the decision made. The margin is 2 percent by default, and I made it an internal constant.

I wrote a property test that builds chunks from random documents with a word-based counter and a character counter, and checks that no chunk exceeds the limit. 1,000 runs passed. I also checked the output against the previous version on the eight fixtures, and chunks were identical for seven. The eighth differed by one block position, and it turned out the old version was too conservative, so the new result is fine.

Benchmarks now: huge section 1.4 s, mixed 5 MB file 1.1 s, short sections 0.5 s. Memory on the mixed file fell from about 480 MB to 310 MB.

I added the benchmark numbers to the contributing notes so future changes can be compared. Next I want to look at parse time itself, which is now the larger part.

summary: Parse time dominates large files now, so the splitter reuses a single processor instance and skips position data for nodes it does not need, saving about a third of the time.
body:
After the builder fix, a profile of the 5 MB file showed about 70 percent of the time in remark parsing and the mdast conversion. I looked at what the library does around it.

First finding: the processor was created again for every call of split(). Creating a unified pipeline with remark-gfm is not free, since it builds extension lists. I moved it to a lazily created module-level instance keyed by the options that change parsing. Calling split() on many small documents became 25 percent faster.

Second finding: after parsing I walked the tree once to attach lengths and once for references and once for headings. I merged those into a single walk with a visitor that fills all three caches. That removed two traversals of roughly 400,000 nodes.

Third: I tried removing position data from the tree, but the splitter needs positions to slice the original source. So that stays. I only avoid stringifying nodes, and slice by offsets instead. The one place that still stringified was the table splitter, and it uses source offsets for rows now.

The result on the 5 MB file went from 1.1 s to 0.72 s. A 50 KB document went from 14 ms to 9 ms.

One risk: the cached processor is shared state. The processor is frozen after setup, and parse is pure, so I think it is safe, and a test runs 50 concurrent calls with different options to check that.

I did not touch streaming input. A user asked for it in an issue, and it would need a different parser approach, so I wrote a note in the issue instead of promising anything.

summary: Answered the streaming question in the issue: chunkdown needs the full tree, but a split-by-top-level-section helper could give bounded memory.
body:
The reporter processes files of several hundred MB and wanted to feed a stream. I explained that the splitter needs the whole syntax tree, because reference definitions and footnotes can come at the end of a file.

A possible compromise is to cut the file at top-level headings with a cheap line scanner that respects fenced code, and then call split() on each section. Definitions would be collected in a first pass over the file.

I sketched this in the issue with about twenty lines of code. I marked it as a recipe candidate, not a feature, until someone confirms it works for them.

summary: Planned the 1.0 API: a single split() function with an options object, named result objects, and removal of the three positional signatures that grew over the 0.x releases.
body:
I spent the session writing down what a clean major version should look like, since issues keep asking for things the current API makes awkward. The current API has split(text, maxChars), split(text, options) and splitWithMeta(text, options). They return different shapes depending on flags.

Proposal: one function split(markdown, options) that always returns an array of chunk objects with text, headingPath, index, and length. A helper chunkTexts() returns plain strings for people who only want those. The old heading metadata flag disappears because objects are always returned.

Options get grouped: limit: { size, unit or measure }, tables: { repeatHeader }, code: { repeatFence }, links: { copyDefinitions }, and onWarning stays on top. The old maxChars and length options become limit.size and limit.measure.

I listed breaking changes in a document for the migration guide: removed positional signature, return shape, renamed options, and the Node minimum raised to 18. I counted usages in the README and docs to see how many samples need rewriting: 23 code samples.

The question was whether to keep deprecated aliases. I decided to ship a 0.4 release first that warns when old forms are used, so users see messages before 1.0 breaks them. That gives people a path.

I also wrote the TypeScript types first, in src/types.ts, without implementation, to check they read well. Chunk is an interface with readonly fields. Options is a plain interface, no classes.

Next step: implement the new shape behind the old function names, then add the deprecation warnings.

summary: Implemented the new options shape and chunk objects internally, with a normalizeOptions function that maps every old option name to the new one.
body:
Starting from the morning plan, I wrote src/options.ts. normalizeOptions takes either the old flat options or the new grouped ones and returns one internal structure. The rest of the code reads only the internal one.

The mapping: maxChars becomes limit.size with measure set to characters, length becomes limit.measure, withMeta is ignored because objects are always built. When both old and new names are present, the new one wins and a warning goes to onWarning.

The core now always builds Chunk objects with text, headingPath, index and length. The older functions are thin wrappers: split with the old signature maps the objects to strings or to the old meta shape, depending on the flag.

I ran the whole test suite unchanged against the wrappers, and 212 of 214 tests passed. Two failed since they compared the exact object shape of the old metadata, which now has an extra length field. I updated those two tests deliberately and noted it for the changelog.

Then I added tests for normalizeOptions: 14 cases, covering conflicts, defaults and unknown option names. Unknown names now throw a TypeError with the name in the message, which catches typos such as maxChar.

The length field of each chunk is computed by the same cached counter, so no additional counting is needed. The benchmark shows no change.

Tomorrow: deprecation warnings for old forms and the 0.4 release notes.

summary: Added one-time deprecation warnings for the old call forms and released 0.4.0 so users get messages before the 1.0 break.
body:
The warnings go through a small helper that prints each message only once per process, using console.warn unless onWarning is given. Each message names the old form and shows the new one, for example: split(text, 500) is deprecated, use split(text, { limit: { size: 500 } }).

I covered four deprecated forms with tests, and checked that a message appears once even after 100 calls. There is an environment variable CHUNKDOWN_NO_DEPRECATION to silence them for CI logs, because one user said they run many tests.

I wrote the migration guide page with before and after samples for all 23 README and docs examples. The samples are run as tests, as before.

The changeset describes 0.4.0 as a minor release: new grouped options, chunk objects through a new function, and deprecations. I ran the smoke test on the packed tarball and it passed, including the bin path I had added earlier. Published 0.4.0.

I will watch the issue tracker for a week before starting on 1.0 itself.

summary: Front matter support, step one: a YAML block at the top was being parsed as a thematic break plus a heading, and now it is detected and kept out of chunk text.
body:
An issue showed a blog post whose first chunk contained '---', a few key lines and a heading made from the last key, because the closing --- turned the lines above it into a setext heading. That looked wrong in retrieval results.

I added remark-frontmatter to the parser setup, with yaml and toml types. The tree now has a yaml or toml node as its first child. The splitter previously did not know that type and fell into the generic block path, so it was emitted as a chunk by itself.

For now I made the splitter skip the node and store its raw text on a separate variable. split() returns the chunks as before, and the front matter is available through a new function extractFrontMatter(markdown), which returns { data: string, type, body }. I did not parse the YAML, to avoid a dependency. Users can parse it with whichever library they use.

Tests: yaml front matter, toml front matter with +++, a document with a --- thematic break in the middle that must not be taken as front matter, and an unclosed block that must be treated as ordinary content. All four passed after I made the detection require the block to start on the first line.

Open questions are whether front matter should be repeated or summarized in each chunk as metadata, which several people have asked for. I will think about that tomorrow and decide on the option.

I also checked that heading paths do not get polluted by a title key inside the YAML. They do not, since the node is not a heading.

summary: Front matter step two: a frontMatter option with three modes, skip, first-chunk and metadata, and a parsed data field when the user passes a parse function.
body:
I decided how front matter reaches the output. Three modes: skip drops it from chunks, first keeps it as the start of the first chunk, and metadata attaches the raw text to every Chunk object in a frontMatter field. Default is skip, because that was the least surprising for retrieval.

For the metadata mode I added an optional parseFrontMatter function in the options, so someone can pass js-yaml's load and get an object instead of a string. Errors thrown by the function go to onWarning and the field then holds the raw string.

The first mode raised a size question: front matter counts toward the limit of the first chunk. If it is larger than the limit, it becomes its own chunk with a warning. I reused the oversized-block path for that.

The metadata mode costs nothing for the limit, since it is not in the text. But I realized that people may be surprised that chunk.length does not include it. The docs now say so explicitly.

I wrote 11 tests across the three modes plus parse errors. One bug surfaced: in first mode the heading path of the first chunk was empty when the front matter came before the first heading, and that is correct, but the index offsets were off by one because I counted the node as a block. Fixed by treating it as a prefix.

The CLI got --front-matter with the three values, and with metadata the JSON output includes the field. I tested it by piping a file in.

The docs options reference and a recipe, 'Using front matter as metadata with js-yaml', were written, and the recipe code was run in a test.

I also added the front matter cases to the benchmark generator, to be sure that detection does not slow down a big file. Nothing measurable changed.

This feature will be part of 1.0, so I added a line to the changelog draft.

summary: Checked the issue tracker a week after 0.4.0: two reports of deprecation noise in test output, both solved by the silencing variable.
body:
Two people wrote that the deprecation messages filled their test logs. Both had a wrapper calling split in many places with the old form.

I pointed them to CHUNKDOWN_NO_DEPRECATION and to the migration guide. One of them replied that the migration took them ten minutes.

No bug reports on the new options. I decided to start the 1.0 work next.

summary: Started the 1.0 branch of work in main: removed the old positional signatures and flat option names and rewrote the tests and docs that used them.
body:
Since there are no branches in this project, I did this on main in small commits and did not release in between. First I removed the positional forms split(text, number) and splitWithMeta. The wrappers and the deprecation helper are gone, which deleted about 180 lines.

Then normalizeOptions lost the old names. Passing maxChars now throws a TypeError with a message that points to limit.size and to the migration guide URL. I thought it was kinder to throw clearly than to ignore a name.

The tests that used the old forms were rewritten. 41 tests needed changes, mostly mechanical. I did them with a codemod script written with jscodeshift for the repeated patterns and by hand for the rest.

The README examples and docs samples moved to the new forms. The test that runs all samples caught three that I had missed, because they still used the flat option names.

The CLI flags stayed the same, since they were already clean. Only --max-chars got an alias --size, and the old one stays for now, which is the one place where I kept compatibility.

I changed the minimum Node version to 18 in package.json engines and in the CI matrix. I dropped the Node 16 job, and the workflow runs on 18, 20 and 22.

Type checks pass. The full suite has 206 tests, all passing. The bundle size went from 41 KB to 37 KB.

Still to do: update the changeset to a major bump, read the migration guide once more against the final API, and run the smoke test on the tarball.

I also noticed that the Chunk type exports a mutable array for headingPath. I changed it to readonly string[] so users cannot modify shared data held in a cache.

summary: Released 1.0.0 after checking the migration guide against the final API, running the tarball smoke test, and trying the package in two sample projects.
body:
This morning I read the migration guide line by line against the code. Two things were wrong: the guide said the default for copyDefinitions was false, and it is true, and a before/after sample used the removed splitWithMeta name on the wrong side. Both fixed.

The smoke test passed on the packed tarball, including the types check for the ESM and CommonJS builds and the bin path. Then I installed the tarball into two sample projects: a small Express server in CommonJS and a Vite app using ESM and TypeScript with strict mode. Both compiled and produced the same chunks for a sample document.

I ran the benchmark one more time to record the 1.0 numbers: short sections 0.5 s, mixed 5 MB 0.7 s, huge section 1.4 s. They are in the contributing notes.

The changeset was set to major. The generated changelog entry was too long, so I rewrote it into five groups: API, options, front matter, links and performance. Each has a one-line summary and a link to the section in the migration guide.

I published 1.0.0 with the latest tag. Then I checked that npm install chunkdown in an empty directory gives 1.0.0, and that the README on the npm page renders the tables properly.

After that I opened a pinned issue titled 'Upgrading to 1.0' with the three most common changes, so people with questions have one place to ask. I also moved the old 0.x docs to a folder named v0 in the docs site, with a banner link.

What remains: watch for upgrade problems this week, and see whether the CLI needs a config file, since two people asked.

One small thing found while publishing: the repository field in package.json lacked the directory-free URL form, and npm warned about it. I corrected it in the same release commit.

summary: Fixed an upgrade bug in 1.0.1: a custom length function that returned a float broke the cache comparison and produced chunks one item too long.
body:
A user upgrading to 1.0 reported chunks that were slightly above the limit with their own length function. It returned a float, since it estimated tokens as characters divided by four.

The running length code from the performance work compares a sum with the limit minus a margin, and I had used integer math in one place with Math.floor on the margin. With floats the sum drifted, and the final check passed for a value of 500.2 against a limit of 500 because the check used a rounded value.

I removed the rounding and compare the raw numbers. I also made the length wrapper reject NaN, negative values and Infinity with a clear error that names the function result, since one more person had returned undefined by mistake.

A regression test uses the estimating function with 300 random documents and checks that every chunk length is less than or equal to the limit. It failed before the fix on 11 of them.

Released 1.0.1 with a patch changeset and replied on the issue.

summary: Added a config file option to the CLI after two requests: chunkdown.config.json is read from the working directory, and flags override it.
body:
Two people wanted to avoid long command lines in scripts. I added support for a chunkdown.config.json file, found in the current directory or passed with --config.

The file holds the same grouped options as the library, minus the functions. A tokenizer is given as a module path, as with the existing --tokenizer flag, and resolved relative to the config file, which was a choice I had to think about. Relative to the working directory would break when the config is passed from elsewhere.

Precedence is defaults, then config file, then flags. I implemented it by building the options object in three layers and merging with a small deep merge helper, since the options are nested.

Validation reuses normalizeOptions, so a typo in the file gives the same TypeError, and the CLI prints it with the file path. I added the line number of the key when possible, but JSON.parse does not give positions for keys, so only the key name is shown.

Tests: config only, flags override config, bad key, missing file with --config (error) and missing default file (no error). All five pass. I documented it on the CLI page with an example file.

A question for later is whether to support a key in package.json. I did not add it, to avoid another lookup rule.

summary: Reviewed an outside pull request that adds a Windows line ending fix and asked for a test with a table, since CRLF broke row detection there.
body:
The PR normalizes CRLF to LF at the start of split(). The idea is right, and it fixes a reported bug in which a code fence repeated with a stray carriage return.

I ran the branch locally and found that the offsets in chunk positions no longer match the original text, because the text was changed before parsing. I asked the author to keep a mapping or to document that offsets refer to the normalized text.

I also asked for a test with a CRLF table, since the table splitter slices rows by offsets.

summary: Merged the CRLF pull request after the author added table tests and a note that offsets refer to normalized text, then added one more case for a lone CR.
body:
The author updated the PR the same day. The new tests include a CRLF table split into three chunks and a fenced block with CRLF inside a list item. I pulled the branch and ran the suite, with 214 tests passing.

The docs now state that chunk text always uses LF and that offsets, when exposed, refer to the normalized text. I think that is acceptable, since chunk objects do not expose offsets at the moment.

I added a case for a lone CR, as in old Mac files, which the regex in the PR did not cover. I changed the pattern to handle CRLF and lone CR in one replace.

Merged with a squash and thanked the author in the PR. A changeset for a patch release was added. Release 1.0.2 is planned with the next fix.

summary: Investigated deeply nested lists splitting into chunks that lose their parent item context, and designed an ancestors option that repeats parent item text as a prefix.
body:
An issue showed a nested list of four levels where the second chunk started at a level-3 item. On its own that chunk read as a list with no meaning, since the parent items were in the previous chunk.

First I reproduced it with a fixture from the issue: 120 items, limit 400 characters. The current logic splits between items at any depth, and keeps numbering through the start attribute only at the top level.

I considered three ideas. The first was to never split inside an item that has children unless forced, but that creates oversized chunks. The second was to repeat the ancestors' first lines as context. The third was to add headings only in the metadata. I chose the second as an option because it keeps the chunk readable as Markdown.

The implementation: when the list splitter starts a new chunk in the middle of a nested list, it computes the chain of ancestor items and renders only their first paragraph, without the other children. These lines go before the continuing items, with the same indentation as in the source, so the structure is preserved.

The repeated lines count toward the limit. If the ancestors take more than half of the limit, the option is dropped for that chunk and a warning is sent. This prevents a loop where context never leaves room for content.

Ordered lists needed care: an ancestor item keeps its number, not a restart at 1, so I set the number from the original node index.

I added the option lists: { repeatAncestors: boolean }, default false for now, because it changes output and 1.x users should not see surprises. Tests cover three levels, an ordered parent, a task list item with a checkbox, and the half-limit rule.

On the issue fixture, the chunk count went from 9 to 10 and every chunk starts with the context of its parents. The reporter will try a build.

To do: decide whether this should become the default in 2.0, and add a recipe for it.

summary: Released 1.1.0 with the repeatAncestors list option and the CLI config file, after the reporter confirmed the nested list fixture reads well.
body:
The reporter tried the build and confirmed that the chunks are now readable, and asked for one change: the checkbox of a task item should not be repeated in the ancestor line. That made sense, because a repeated checked box looks like extra state. I stripped the marker from ancestor lines and added a test.

Then I prepared the release. The changeset set was a minor bump with three entries: the repeatAncestors option, the config file for the CLI, and the CRLF handling by the outside contributor, credited by name in the changelog.

I ran the smoke test on the tarball, then the full suite on Node 18, 20 and 22 in CI, which all passed. The benchmark showed no change in time for the default settings. With repeatAncestors on, the nested fixture took 3 percent longer.

Published 1.1.0. I installed it in a clean directory and ran the CLI with a config file to see that the new path works from the published package.

I wrote the recipe 'Keeping context in nested lists' and tested the sample. The pinned upgrade issue got a short comment about the new option.

summary: Started on setext headings and HTML blocks: a reporter showed chunks cutting a raw HTML block in the middle, so the splitter now treats an HTML node as unbreakable unless it is over the limit.
body:
An issue came in with a README that contains a long <details> block. The splitter cut it between two tags, and the chunk text ended with an unclosed element. I reproduced it with a 40-line fixture in test/fixtures/html-details.md.

The cause was that remark gives an html node as one literal string, and the block splitter had no rule for it, so it fell through to the sentence fallback. That fallback split on periods inside the markup. I added a rule: an html node is kept whole when it fits the limit.

When it does not fit, the splitter now cuts at blank lines inside the literal, then at line ends. It never cuts inside a tag. I wrote five tests: a small block, an oversized block, a block with a nested comment, an inline html span in a paragraph, and a block with a blank line inside a pre element.

The inline span case turned out to be fine already, since inline html lives inside the paragraph and the sentence fallback does not cut at tags there. Setext headings I only checked, and they already work: the tree is the same as for the hash form. I added one test to pin that down.

The oversized case is the open question. A chunk with half a details block is still unbalanced, and I did not try to repair it. I left a note in the issue that closing tags could be repeated per chunk, like the link definitions, and asked the reporter if that matters for their use. The fix is in main and not released yet.

summary: The reporter of the HTML issue replied that unbalanced tags in oversized blocks do hurt their embeddings, so I built an option that closes and reopens open tags at an html chunk border.
body:
The reply came overnight. They feed chunks to an embedding model and also render them, so a stray closing tag shows up as visible noise. They asked for balanced html in each chunk where possible.

I wrote a small tag scanner in src/html-balance.ts. It reads the literal, keeps a stack of open elements, and ignores void elements such as br, img and hr. It also ignores comments and anything inside a pre element. I did not pull in an html parser, because the scanner only needs open and close names.

When the splitter cuts an oversized html node, it now appends closing tags for the stack to the first part, and prepends the reopened tags with their attributes to the next part. The added text counts toward the size limit, so the builder reserves space before it chooses a cut line. That reservation was the fiddly part, and my first version produced chunks over the limit by about 20 characters.

The feature sits behind balanceHtml, default false, because it changes text the user may expect to be verbatim. The tests cover nesting three deep, an attribute with a quote character, and a stack that is empty at the cut. A fuzz test with random cut points checks that the output of every chunk has a stack that ends empty.

I ran it on the reporter's README: 14 html chunks, all balanced. Docs for the option are still to write.

summary: Wrote docs for balanceHtml and released 1.2.0 with the HTML block handling, after the tarball smoke test caught a missing export for the new option's type.
body:
I started with the docs: a section in the options reference and a short recipe on html in READMEs. The recipe uses the reporter's details block as the example and shows the chunk output before and after.

Then I wrote the changeset as a minor bump with two lines, one for unbreakable html nodes and one for balanceHtml. I ran the changelog check, which passed.

The tarball smoke test failed. It installs the packed package into a temp project and compiles a file that imports the option types. The type HtmlBalanceOptions was declared in src/html-balance.ts but not re-exported from the index, so the compile gave error TS2305. Inside the repo the tests import from the source path, and so they never saw it. I added the export and a line to the smoke test that uses the type, so this kind of miss is covered from now on.

I also searched the other new types for the same problem and found one more, the scanner result type, which is internal on purpose. I marked it as such in a comment.

After the fix the smoke test passed on Node 18 and 20 in CI. I published 1.2.0, checked the npm page, and installed it in a sample project. The sample ran with balanceHtml on and produced the expected chunks.

I commented on the issue with the version and asked the reporter to close it if the README now splits well. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: The reporter confirmed 1.2.0 fixes their README and closed the issue; I also answered a question on whether chunkdown can count tokens of the added closing tags.
body:
The confirmation came this morning with a before and after of their chunk list. All html chunks are balanced and none is over their limit of 512 tokens.

They asked in the same message whether the closing tags added by balanceHtml are counted with their tokenizer. They are. The builder asks the configured length function about the exact text, tags included, before it accepts a cut. I pointed them to the test that checks this with a word-count function, where a reopened tag with attributes adds several words.

I looked at whether the answer deserved a line in the docs. It did, since a user could assume the tags are free. I added one sentence under balanceHtml: added tags count toward the limit, so a very small limit can make an element impossible to balance. In that case the splitter falls back to a plain cut and a debug message is printed.

I checked that fallback with a limit of 30 characters and a tag with a long attribute. It works as written. The issue is closed and the docs change is in main without a release, since it is only prose.

summary: Users reported slow splits on documents with thousands of list items, and profiling showed the ancestor prefix being rebuilt for every item, so it is now cached per parent.
body:
The report came with a 6 MB changelog file made of nested bullet lists. With repeatAncestors on, the split took 48 seconds, and with it off it took 3 seconds. That pointed straight at the feature from 1.1.0.

I ran the benchmark script with a new generated file of 20,000 list items, three levels deep. The CPU profile showed 70 percent of the time in buildAncestorPrefix. For each item it walked up to the root, serialized every parent with remark-stringify, and then measured the result.

The fix has two parts. First, the serialized text of a parent item is now computed once and stored in a WeakMap keyed by the node. Second, the prefix for an item is the joined prefix of its parent plus the parent's own line, so it is built incrementally and not from the root each time.

After the change the generated file takes 3.4 seconds with the option on. That is close to the cost with it off, and the remaining difference is the added text being measured.

I added a test that the output is byte for byte identical to the old implementation on five fixtures. I kept the old function in the test folder as a reference for this comparison. Then I added a benchmark case to the script so a regression shows up in the numbers.

One more thing came up. The prefix of a very deep item can by itself exceed the limit. The code already drops the outermost ancestors until it fits, but I found that this loop re-measured the text each round. I changed it to use the cached lengths, which saved another 0.4 seconds.

I told the reporter to try the main branch with their file. A patch release comes after their answer.

summary: Started on setext headings and HTML blocks: a reporter showed chunks cutting a raw HTML block in the middle, so the splitter now treats an HTML node as unbreakable unless it is over the limit.
body: A user opened an issue with a README that contained a long <details> block, and the chunks cut it in the middle of a nested table. I reproduced it with their file in a new fixture, html-details.md, and saw that the splitter handled html nodes like paragraphs and fell back to the sentence splitter on them. That is wrong, because the text of an html node is markup and has no sentences. The fix was in the block classifier: an html node is now atomic, and it is only cut when it alone is over the limit. In that case it is split at line breaks, and never inside a tag. While there I checked setext headings, the underlined style, because the issue file used them as well. They were parsed correctly by remark and attached to the next block like the others, so no change was needed there, and I added two tests so it stays that way. The lossless check passed on the new fixture and on the eight real documents of the test set. One case is still open: an oversized html block ends up with unbalanced open tags in its chunks. I wrote that down in the issue and asked the reporter whether it matters for their embeddings. Next step is to wait for the answer before designing anything.

summary: Released 1.2.1 with the faster nested list handling and added the 20,000-item list case to the benchmark that runs in CI as a soft check.
body:
I published 1.2.1 and checked the registry page and an install in a sample project.

The benchmark case for the big list is part of the script now. I also wired the script into a GitHub Actions job that runs weekly and on manual start. It does not fail the build. It prints the timings into the job summary so I can compare them by eye.

I chose a soft check because CI machines vary a lot, and a hard limit would fail at random. The job summary has a table with the four generated files and their times. The first run gave 1.3, 3.2, 3.5 and 0.9 seconds, which fits the local numbers.

The issue is closed with a link to the release. Next I plan to look at the open question about tables with merged-looking cells.

summary: Looked into a bug report about table rows that contain pipes inside inline code, and found the row splitter cut them although remark parsed the cell correctly.
body:
The report said that a table row such as | `a|b` | c | became three cells in the chunk output, and the table header repeat then did not match the columns. I reproduced it with a three-row fixture.

First I checked the parser. In GitHub Markdown a pipe inside code in a table cell must be escaped as \|, and without the escape the row really has three cells. So remark was right to give three cells, and the fixture in the report was not valid for a two-column table. The reporter had copied it from a page that renders it differently.

However, a second case in the same report was a real bug: | `a\|b` | c |, with the escape. The parser gives two cells. My row serializer wrote each cell back with the backslash removed, because it used the cell's text value and not the source slice. The output was then a row with three cells.

The fix is to take each cell's source text from the position data. I had turned off position data for some nodes as a speed trick last year, and table cells were among the nodes that had it off. I turned it on for cells only and measured: the large-table benchmark went from 2.1 to 2.2 seconds, which I accepted.

I added tests for an escaped pipe, an escaped pipe inside code, a cell with a trailing backslash, and an empty cell. The trailing backslash case was the hardest: the source slice ends with the backslash and the pipe after it is a separator, and my first regex took the pipe as escaped. I replaced the regex with a small scanner that counts the backslashes before a pipe.

I replied to the reporter with both findings: the first case is not valid table syntax, with a link to the spec section, and the second is fixed in main. I also added a note to the docs about escaping in tables, since two users have now hit it.

The release will go out with whatever else comes up this week.

summary: Reviewed an outside pull request adding a sentence splitter option for Chinese and Japanese text, and asked for tests with mixed scripts before merging.
body:
The author wants the sentence fallback to cut after the characters 。！？ and not only after a period followed by a space. The change is small: a new regex in src/sentences.ts and an option language with the values auto and default.

I checked out the branch locally and ran the tests, which pass. Then I tried it on three texts of my own: a Chinese news paragraph, a Japanese blog post, and an English text with a quoted Japanese phrase. The first two split well. The third cut the English sentence after the Japanese full stop inside quotes, which left a chunk that ended in the middle of a quote.

So my review asks for three things. A test with mixed scripts like the third text. A rule that a closing quote bracket after the full stop stays with the sentence, as in 。」. And the default of auto should only turn on when more than half of the letters in the paragraph are in CJK ranges, so English documents behave as before.

I also noted that the regex runs on every paragraph, and asked for a quick check of the benchmark. I ran it myself: no measurable change on the three generated files, since they are English.

The author is friendly and replied within an hour that they will do all three. I will look again when the update comes.

summary: Merged the CJK sentence splitting pull request after the author added mixed-script tests and closing-bracket handling, then added a case for a full-width period inside a table cell.
body:
The update had all three points. The mixed-script test now passes, closing brackets such as 」 and ） stay with their sentence, and auto mode needs more than half of the letters to be in CJK ranges.

I read the diff again. One thing I changed myself before merging: the detection counted characters with a loop over code points for every paragraph, even in default mode. I made the detection run only when the option is auto, which it is by default, but then it stops after the first 200 letters. That keeps the cost flat for long paragraphs.

I then tested a few edge cases that the pull request did not cover. A full-width period inside a table cell: the table splitter never uses the sentence fallback for cells, so nothing changed, but I added a test so that it stays so. A paragraph in Korean: Hangul is not in the CJK ranges of the detector, and Korean uses the western period, so default mode applies and works well. I added a comment in the code about this.

A third case was text with an emoji right after a full stop. The regex handles it, since it only looks at the characters before the cut. I added it as a test anyway.

I merged with a squash and thanked the author in the pull request. In the changeset I credited them by their GitHub name, as they asked.

The docs got a short section called Languages. It explains auto and default, and says what is not covered, for example Thai, which has no sentence marks. I also added the CJK example to the recipes page.

The next release will include this together with the table pipe fix from last week. I want to run the tarball test and check the changelog first, and I plan that for tonight.

summary: Released 1.3.0 with CJK sentence splitting and the table escaped-pipe fix, and the changelog check flagged a missing credit line that I added before publishing.
body:
I first ran the full test suite and then the changelog check. The check failed because the pull request changeset did not have the format the script wants, which is a bump line and one sentence ending in a period. The author had written two sentences without the final period.

I corrected the text by hand and kept the credit. Then I combined the entries into the release: a minor bump for the language option and a patch for the table fix, which npm treats as one minor release.

The tarball smoke test passed on the first try this time. The new option type is exported, which I checked with the compile step that I had added after 1.2.0.

I published 1.3.0 and installed it in two sample projects, one with ESM and one with CommonJS. Both resolved the types and ran a split with language set to auto on a Japanese sample file. The chunk boundaries were as expected.

Then I posted on the table issue with the version number. The reporter had not answered since the explanation about escaping, so I wrote that I will close it in a week if there is no reply.

I looked at the open issues after the release. There are three: a question about Docusaurus admonitions, a request for a chunk overlap option, and a bug about footnotes. The overlap request has been asked twice, and I want to think about its design before I answer. Footnotes seem the most concrete, so that comes next.

summary: Reproduced the footnote bug: definitions of footnotes are cut off from their references at chunk borders, the same problem links had before reference definitions were copied.
body:
The report has a document with 12 footnotes at the end, which chunkdown puts into the last chunk. A chunk with the reference [^3] has no way to show what the note says.

I wrote a fixture with 5 footnotes and a small limit, and the output shows exactly this. The footnoteDefinition nodes all land in the last chunk or two.

The design is close to what I did for links: copy the definition into each chunk that has a reference to it. The difference is that a footnote definition can hold several paragraphs and even a list. I will count its full length against the limit and, when it does not fit, put a shortened first paragraph in. That still needs a decision, and I will write it up before I start.

summary: Designed footnote handling in a short plan: copy definitions into chunks that reference them, with a size reserve and a truncation rule for long notes.
body:
The plan has four points. First, a pass over the tree collects footnoteReference identifiers per top-level block, the same way the link definition pass does. Second, when a chunk is closed, definitions for its references are appended after the content, separated by a blank line.

Third, the size reserve: the builder must know the definition length before it decides a block fits. I will precompute the length of each definition once and add it when a block with a reference is added to the chunk, counting each identifier only once per chunk.

Fourth, long notes: if a definition alone is over a third of the limit, keep only its first paragraph and add an ellipsis mark. I picked a third by hand, and the option footnoteMaxShare can change it.

I also decided that numbering stays as written. Renumbering would make the chunks consistent in themselves, but the original numbers help a user who searches for the source text.

summary: Implemented footnote copying in the chunk builder: references are collected, definitions are appended to each chunk that uses them, and the size reserve prevents chunks over the limit.
body:
I added src/footnotes.ts with two functions. collectFootnoteRefs walks a block and returns the set of identifiers. buildDefinitionTable maps each identifier to its node and its serialized text and length.

In the builder I extended the running length idea from last year. The builder keeps a set of identifiers already in the chunk. When it adds a block it computes the extra length of definitions not yet in the set, and checks block plus extra against the limit.

The first test run showed a problem: a block with a footnote reference that alone just fits the limit would no longer fit with its definition. The builder then put the block into its own chunk, and it was still too long. I added the rule that a block whose definition cannot fit is allowed to go without the definition, or with a truncated one, using the footnoteMaxShare rule.

Truncation was easy to write. It keeps the first paragraph of the definition and adds an ellipsis. For a note with a list I keep only the first item.

A second problem was a footnote that references another footnote. It is rare, but remark allows it. A loop over the closure of identifiers handles it, and a visited set prevents cycles. I wrote a test with a cycle of two notes, which gave an endless loop at first.

I wrote 11 tests in total. They cover the single reference, two references to the same note in one chunk, in two chunks, an unused definition, which is dropped from every chunk and goes to no chunk, and the cycle.
