The unused definition is a decision I want to check: should a note without a reference be kept somewhere? I think it should not appear, since there is no way to know which chunk it belongs to. I will mention it in the docs.

The benchmark did not change, since the pass is linear. The docs and the release come later.

summary: Wrote the docs for footnote copying and answered the reporter, who tested main on their 12-note document and saw each chunk carry its notes.
body:
The reporter ran the main branch on their document and sent the output. Every chunk with a reference now has its note after the content, and the last chunk has only the notes it references. Chunk sizes are all within their limit of 800 characters.

I wrote the docs section Footnotes with an input and output example and the behavior for long notes. I also added the sentence about unused definitions being dropped.

They asked whether the added notes can be marked in the chunk object so they can strip them before display. That is a good idea and cheap: I will add a field named appended with the type of each appended piece. I opened an issue for myself and linked it. This goes into the next release.

summary: Added an appended field to chunk objects that lists the link definitions, footnotes and ancestor prefixes added to a chunk, so users can strip them for display.
body:
The field is an array of objects with a kind, which is linkDefinition, footnote or ancestorPrefix, and the start and end offsets inside the chunk text. Chunks without added content get an empty array.

The builder already knows where it adds these pieces, so I only had to record the offsets. The ancestor prefix was easy, since it is always at the start. For definitions I record the offsets after the final text is assembled, because the blank line between parts shifts them.

I wrote tests that rebuild the original content by cutting out the appended ranges. They pass for the fixtures with links, footnotes and nested lists. One test failed at first for a chunk with both a prefix and a footnote, since I computed the second range before adding the prefix. I fixed it by computing all offsets in one final step.

The type is exported from the index, and the smoke test uses it. The docs got a short section in the chunk object reference. The release is planned for the next days.

summary: Considered the chunk overlap request and prototyped it, then decided on a block-level overlap option because a character overlap would cut through links and code.
body:
The request has come twice now: users want the last part of one chunk repeated at the start of the next, which is common in retrieval pipelines. I spent the evening on a design.

The first idea was a plain character overlap. I tried it for twenty minutes and dropped it, because it breaks what the library exists for. An overlap of 100 characters cuts through links, code fences and table rows, and then the chunk is not valid Markdown any more.

The second idea is overlap by blocks. The option overlap takes a size in the same unit as the limit, and the builder starts the next chunk with as many whole blocks from the end of the previous chunk as fit within that size. A block that is bigger than the overlap size is never included, so a code block is not repeated.

I prototyped it in the builder. The size accounting is the hard part, as the overlap text counts toward the limit of the new chunk. If the overlap takes 200 of 800 characters, the new content has only 600 left. The builder therefore reserves the overlap length first, and the first block of the new chunk must fit in the rest. If it does not, the overlap is dropped for that chunk.

The prototype passed a basic test on the README of the project: chunks of 500 characters with an overlap of 100 now share one paragraph or list item. The appended field gets a new kind, overlap, so the display stripping works the same way.

Two interactions need care. Heading attachment: a chunk starts with the heading of the first block, and the overlap goes before it, so the heading would not be the first line any more. I decided that the overlap goes first and the heading path metadata stays correct, since it describes the new content. Second, tables: a repeated header row is added to a split table chunk, and an overlap block that is a table row would be strange. I excluded table rows from the overlap.

I wrote 8 tests and the main cases work. Missing: the CLI flag, docs, and the benchmark. I also want a second opinion from the issue authors before I release it, so I posted the design on the issue and asked for feedback.

summary: Considered the chunk overlap request and prototyped it, then chose a block-level overlap option because a character overlap would cut through links and code.
body: An issue asked for overlap between chunks, which many RAG pipelines use so that a fact at a border appears in both chunks. I started with the simple version: copy the last N characters of each chunk to the start of the next one. I tried it on the test documents and it went wrong quickly. The copied text started in the middle of links, inline code and table rows, and in four of the eight documents it produced broken Markdown at the start of a chunk. That is exactly what the whole library tries to prevent. I then tried a second prototype that counts overlap in blocks: the option takes a number of characters as a budget and repeats whole blocks from the end of the previous chunk while they fit in it. This keeps the structure, since a block is a paragraph, a list, a table or a code block. The first results looked good, and the output of the splitter stayed valid Markdown in all eight documents. There are some rules to settle. A block bigger than the overlap budget is not repeated at all. A table is repeated whole or not at all, and it does not get a header on its own. The overlap counts against the size limit, so the chunk builder has to reserve room, as it does for footnotes and link definitions. A chunk that is made only of overlap must never be created. I also thought about the appended field: overlap blocks are not like definitions, because they are real content, but users may want to remove them for display. I decided to list them in the same field with a kind marker. The property tests for the lossless check need a change, because the text now appears twice on purpose. I wrote the first version of the option as overlapBlocks in a local branch of work and left it unfinished. Tests, docs and a reply to the issue come next.

summary: Released 1.4.0 with footnote copying, the appended field and block overlap, after a diff review turned up a docs example whose output did not match the code.
body:
I read the whole diff of the release again this morning. The code was fine, but the overlap docs example had a three-chunk output that I had written by hand. When I ran the example, the second chunk contained one block less than in the docs, because the first block of that chunk had been too big for the remaining room and the overlap was dropped.

The real behavior is correct. The example was wrong. I changed the input to use shorter paragraphs so that the picture shows what I want to show, then ran it and pasted the real output. Since the docs have a test that runs every code sample, I added this sample to that test, which I had forgotten when I wrote it.

The tests and the changelog check passed. The smoke test passed too, with the types for the appended field and the overlap option.

I published 1.4.0 and installed it in the ESM and CommonJS sample projects. I ran the README example with overlap and the output was right.

I commented on three issues: the footnote one, the overlap one, and the admonition question. For the footnote and overlap issues I linked the release and closed them. The reporters of both had tested main already.

The admonition question is still open. Docusaurus uses :::note blocks, which remark parses as plain paragraphs unless a plugin is present. A user could pass a plugin through the processor option, and I want to test whether the splitter treats the resulting nodes as blocks. That is next.

summary: Tested Docusaurus-style admonitions with remark-directive and found that unknown container nodes were treated as one unbreakable block, even when far over the limit.
body:
I installed remark-directive in a scratch project and passed it through the plugins option. A container directive then arrives as a containerDirective node with children.

The splitter has a list of node types it knows how to split: lists, tables, code, blockquotes and sections. Anything else counts as a leaf and is cut with the sentence fallback only if it is a paragraph. A container directive is none of these, so it was kept whole. A 3,000-character admonition then made a chunk of 3,000 characters with a limit of 800, and no warning.

The fix is general and not only for directives. Any unknown node that has children is now treated like a blockquote: the splitter descends into its children and splits them, and it repeats the opening and closing markers if it knows them. For containerDirective I know the markers, which are the colons and the name, and for other types I do not repeat anything.

I wrote tests with a note, a tip and a nested admonition. In the nested case the outer marker has four colons and the inner has three, and both are repeated correctly.

I also checked that without the plugin nothing changes, since the paragraphs are plain text there. The test for this is in place.

One risk: a plugin could add a node type whose children are not blocks, such as an inline wrapper at block level. In that case descending into the children and joining them again is still lossless, since the splitter joins children with the same separator it found. I added a check that the chunks joined together contain all the text of the original, run on the admonition fixtures.

I have not written the docs yet.

summary: Wrote the docs and a recipe for admonitions and other plugin nodes, and released 1.4.1 after the lossless check also found a bug with an empty directive.
body:
The recipe shows how to pass remark-directive in the plugins option and what the output looks like for a note with a long body. It also explains that nodes from other plugins are split by their children, and that the markers are repeated only for container directives.

While I wrote the sample I tried an empty directive, :::note followed directly by :::. The splitter crashed with a message that read Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'position'). The container had a children array of length zero, and my code took the position of the first child to find where the content starts.

I fixed it by treating a node with no children as a leaf. I added the empty case and one with only a blank line to the tests. The lossless check from yesterday did not run for these, so I extended it to run over every fixture in the folder, and not only the admonition ones. It found nothing else.

The docs sample test picked up the new recipe, and all samples pass. I wrote a patch changeset with two lines. The changelog check and the smoke test passed.

I published 1.4.1 and replied to the admonition issue with a link to the recipe and the version. The user had asked a question and not reported a bug, so I wrote that I would leave it open for a few days for follow-up.

The issue list now has only that one and a request for an ESM-only build. The second is an old topic, and I think a short answer will do: the package already ships both, and the exports map decides which one a tool uses. I plan to check that the map is right for the common bundlers.

summary: Checked the package exports map with four bundlers and Node, found that one resolved the CommonJS types for an ESM import, and fixed it with separate type entries.
body:
The user who asked for an ESM-only build said that their setup had an error about types: they used moduleResolution node16 and got a message that the module is a CommonJS module. I made a scratch project for each case to see.

The cases were Node 20 with plain ESM, Node 20 with CommonJS, Vite, esbuild and TypeScript with node16 resolution. The first four resolved the right files. TypeScript with node16 showed the problem: the exports map had one types entry at the top, pointing to index.d.ts, and TypeScript used the same declaration for both import and require. With a package that has type module off, a d.ts file is treated as CommonJS, and the ESM import then reports the mismatch.

The fix is the usual one: nested conditions, where import has its own types file index.d.mts and require has index.d.cts. tsdown can emit both files, and I turned that on in the config. I changed the exports map and the types and typesVersions fields for older resolvers.

Then I added a case to the smoke test: a small project with node16 resolution that imports the package in an ESM file and a CJS file and compiles both. It failed before the change and passed after. I also ran publint on the packed tarball, which reported no errors, only a suggestion about the files field that I took.

I answered the issue with the explanation. An ESM-only build is not needed, because the dual package works once the types are right. I asked the user to try the main branch, since the fix is in main and not released.

The patch release will wait for their answer. Nothing else is open except the admonition question.

summary: Wrote a plan for a streaming API that yields chunks as the document is parsed, after two users with 50 MB files asked for lower peak memory.
body:
Two users running chunkdown on very large exported wikis reported peak memory of over 1.5 GB. The cause is that the whole syntax tree is built before the first chunk is produced. I measured a 48 MB file and saw the tree take about 1.1 GB of the heap.

I considered three designs. The first is to split the source text at top-level block borders before parsing, and parse each part alone. The second is a custom parser pass, which I rejected because it would drop remark plugin support. The third is a hybrid where we cut the text only at blank lines outside fenced code and parse each part separately.

The hybrid has risks. Reference link definitions and footnote definitions may live far from their references, so a first pass must collect them with a cheap line scan. Setext headings and HTML blocks also need care, because a blank line inside an HTML block does not end it.

I wrote the plan in docs/plans/streaming.md with the API shape: chunkStream(input: AsyncIterable<string>, options) returning an AsyncGenerator of chunks. The existing chunk function stays as it is. Next step is a prototype of the definitions pre-scan and a memory benchmark on the 48 MB file.

summary: Tested streaming memory behaviour on a 50 MB document and found that the tree parse dominates peak memory, so the plan now splits the input into top-level sections before parsing.
body:
Two users with 50 MB files asked for lower peak memory, and I started the day by measuring where it goes. I generated a 50 MB document by concatenating the corpus files and ran the current splitter under node with --max-old-space-size set to different values. Peak resident memory was about 2.1 GB, and the heap snapshot showed that the remark syntax tree with position data accounts for most of it.

The chunk list itself was small by comparison, about 90 MB. This means that yielding chunks early does not help unless the parse is also done in pieces. I first tried a cheap idea: drop the position objects after the splitter has read them. That saved around 12 percent and was not worth the extra code.

The second idea is to cut the source into sections at top-level headings before parsing, parse each section alone, and yield its chunks before reading the next one. I wrote a throwaway script for it and ran it on the same file. Peak memory fell to about 180 MB, and the output was identical to the full parse for 11 of the 12 test documents.

The difference came from a document where a reference definition sits at the end and is used in a section far above. A section-local parse cannot see it. Footnote definitions have the same problem, since the copy logic needs the definition when the reference is met.

I decided on a two-pass design for this. A cheap first pass scans lines for definitions and footnote labels without building a tree, and keeps only those in a map. The second pass parses sections and gets the map as input.

Fenced code blocks need care in the scan, because a line that looks like a heading inside a fence must not start a section. The scanner tracks the fence marker and length. Setext headings are a second problem, as the heading is only known from the underline on the next line, so the section flush has to look one line ahead.

I wrote all this into a plan file in the repo notes, with the API sketch: chunkStream takes a string or an async iterable of strings and returns an async iterable of chunks. Open questions are lists that span a heading level and HTML blocks that contain blank lines. Next step is to implement the line scanner with tests on fences and setext headings, then the async input.

summary: Added the async iterator input and a test suite for chunkStream, and found that a CRLF file made the section flush rule miss blank lines.
body:
chunkStream now accepts a string, an Iterable of strings or an AsyncIterable, such as a Node read stream. Incoming pieces are joined into a line buffer, so a piece that ends in the middle of a line works.

I wrote 14 tests in test/stream.test.ts. They cover input split at every byte offset of a small document, empty input, a document with no blank lines, a fenced block that stays open to the end of the file, and a very long single paragraph. The byte offset test is cheap and found one bug at once: a piece that ended between CR and LF made a lone CR line.

The CRLF case also showed a second problem. The blank line check compared to the empty string, and a line with only a CR is not empty. I normalized line endings in the line reader, in the same way as the CRLF fix of last year's pull request, so offsets still refer to normalized text.

All 14 tests pass now. Left to do are the docs and the CLI flag --stream, which I want to try on stdin.

summary: Added the --stream flag to the CLI and checked that piping a 48 MB file through it writes the first line of output after about 90 ms instead of after the whole parse.
body:
The CLI now has --stream. With it the input is read from a file or from stdin as a stream, and chunks are written as JSON lines, one chunk per line, as soon as they are ready. Without it the output format is unchanged.

I timed it with a 48 MB file. The first output line appeared after about 90 ms, compared to over 11 seconds before any output in normal mode. Total time was about the same, 12.4 seconds against 11.8, because of the pre-scan.

Two things came up. If the flag is combined with --format json, which prints one array, the CLI would have to buffer everything, so it now stops with a clear error message. The config file may also set stream: true, and flags still override it.

I added CLI tests that run the built binary on a fixture and compare the output lines to the non-streaming result. The suite is green on Node 18, 20 and 22 in CI. The docs section for streaming is still missing, and so is a note on the memory limits.

summary: Wrote the streaming docs and a memory table, and released 1.5.0 with chunkStream and the CLI --stream flag.
body:
The new docs page explains when to use chunkStream, how the flush rule works, and what differs from chunk(): sections are parsed on their own, so a remark plugin that needs the whole tree will not see it. I added that warning in bold at the top, since it is the most likely surprise.

The memory table lists three files, 2 MB, 12 MB and 48 MB, with peak heap for both modes. The numbers come from a script in bench/memory.ts that I committed so they can be repeated.

I wrote the changeset as a minor bump and ran the tarball smoke test. It passed on the first try this time, and the new types are exported. Then I published 1.5.0 and checked the npm page.

I also commented on the two issues that asked for it, with a link to the docs and the install version. One reporter had already tried main and confirmed their wiki export now runs in under 200 MB.

summary: Looked at reports of tiny chunks, reproduced them on three user documents, and found the cause is headings left alone at the end of a chunk and short blocks after a code fence.
body:
Three people have now reported chunks that are too small to be useful for retrieval. I asked each for a sample document and reproduced the problem with all three. The first step was to measure it, so I added a script that prints the share of chunks under 10 percent of the limit. On the corpus it came to 9 percent, which is high.

I looked at what those small chunks contain. About half are a heading with nothing else, because the heading fit at the end of one chunk and its paragraph did not. Retrieval then returns a heading that says nothing and a paragraph that has no heading.

A second group is a short paragraph right after a large code block. The code block fills a chunk to the limit, and the paragraph that explains it starts a new chunk and stays small because the next block is a table that does not fit.

The third group is the last chunk of a document, often only one line. That one I want to treat separately, since it has a different fix.

For the headings I considered moving the heading to the next chunk whenever the following block does not fit with it. That is simple and keeps the heading with its body. The cost is that the previous chunk becomes a little smaller, but it was already full enough in all the cases I checked.

For the short paragraphs I would add a minimum size option. A chunk below it tries to take the next block, even if that makes the chunk exceed a soft target, but never the hard limit. I wrote down that the limit stays hard, because users depend on it for their embedding models.

I ran a rough prototype of the heading rule on the three documents and the share of small chunks fell from 9 percent to 5 percent. The rest would be covered by the minimum size. I wrote the findings to the issue and said that I would implement both rules next, with the option named minChunkSize, and asked the reporters to test main when it lands.

summary: Implemented heading binding and a minChunkSize option, which cut the share of chunks under 10 percent of the limit from 9 percent to under 2 percent on the corpus.
body:
In src/merge.ts a heading now sticks to the next block before any size decision. If the heading and its first block do not fit together, the block is split as before and the heading goes with the first part.

I changed the merge rule so paragraphs, lists, quotes and headings can join each other. Code blocks and tables join only when the result stays under the limit, since a half table or half code block is worse than a small chunk.

The new option minChunkSize defaults to 25 percent of maxSize. Setting it to 0 gives the old behaviour for users who want it. I checked a setting of 0 against the old snapshots and they match except for the heading binding, which I consider a fix.

On the corpus, chunks under 10 percent of the limit went from 9 percent to 1.8 percent. The remaining ones are real: a short last section of a document, or a table larger than its neighbours. I updated 11 snapshots and read each diff by hand. One of them showed a heading with a code block that exceeded the limit, so the heading was now a separate chunk, and I added a test for that case.

summary: Replied to the three reporters of small chunks with the fix on main and asked them to confirm on their own documents.
body:
I posted the same short note in the three issues: heading binding and the minChunkSize option are on main, with the config example and the default of 25 percent. I asked each person to run their document and show the smallest chunks.

One answered within an hour that the output was much better, but that they wanted a hard minimum, so tiny chunks are never produced even if a table sits next to them. I said that this conflicts with keeping tables intact and explained the tradeoff. They accepted it, and said they would post-filter.

The second reporter found a chunk of 31 characters at the end of their document. That is the last section and cannot be merged forward, so I told them it merges backward only if it fits. In fact it did not merge backward in my code. I opened a small follow-up for backward merging of the last chunk.

summary: Added backward merging of a short final chunk into the previous chunk when it fits, which fixes the 31-character tail reported in the issue.
body:
The merge pass went only forward, so the last chunk of a document stayed alone even when the previous chunk had room. I added a final step: if the last chunk is below minChunkSize and the sum is within maxSize, the two are joined.

The join keeps the appended field correct. Both chunks may carry link definitions, and the same definition must not be listed twice, so I deduplicate by label. A test covers this with two chunks that both reference one link.

I ran the corpus again. Four documents lost their tiny tail chunk. Nothing else changed. The reporter's file now ends with a chunk of 1,870 characters. I will include this in the next release together with the heading change.

summary: Investigated a report that links split by a chunk border show the wrong text in the appended definitions when the label differs in case, and fixed the lookup.
body:
A user showed a document where [Docs][API] and a definition [api]: https://example.com/api exist. Chunks with the reference had no definition appended, so the link was dead in the output.

CommonMark says labels match case-insensitively, after collapsing whitespace. Our collector keyed definitions by the raw label. remark itself gives both the label and the identifier, and the identifier is already normalized, so the fix was to use the identifier on both sides. I found the same raw-label use in the footnote code from 1.4.0, so footnotes with [^Note] and [^note] were affected as well.

I wrote tests for case differences, for labels with several spaces, and for a label with a Unicode letter, where lowercasing is not the same as case folding. The last one needed a toLowerCase on the identifier from remark, which is not folded for German sharp s, so I used a small helper with a fold for that letter. The tests pass.

The appended field lists definitions with the label as written in the source, not the identifier, so users see their own text. I added a test for it. Then I checked the streaming pre-scan, which has its own regex, and it had the same bug. It now lowercases and collapses whitespace in the same way. I ran the 48 MB file through both modes and the output still matches.

This goes into the next patch or minor release.

summary: Checked the 1.6.0 release candidate against the three small-chunk documents and found one document where the minimum size merged a table into a paragraph and went over the limit by two characters.
body:
Before cutting 1.6.0 I ran the release candidate against the three documents from the small-chunk reports. Two of them looked right: the share of chunks under 10 percent of the limit was below 2 percent in each. The third document failed my limit check, because one chunk was two characters over.

I traced it to the merge step that joins a short chunk with the next block. It compared the length of the two texts but forgot the newline that joins them. A table following a paragraph is the case where the separator is a blank line, so the error was two characters and not one.

I changed the merge to compute the size of the joined text instead of adding two sizes. I also added a property test that generates random block sequences and asserts that no chunk exceeds the limit with the option on. It ran 2,000 cases and found one more case, with a list item ending in a code span, which the same change fixed.

After that I reran the three documents and the full test suite, and all passed. I wrote a short comment on the issue that the fix is in main and that the release follows once the reporters have had a look. The release is planned for tomorrow, if nobody finds another overflow.

summary: Checked the 1.6.0 release on a fresh install and found the docs site still described the old merge rule, then corrected two pages.
body:
After the release I installed chunkdown@1.6.0 into an empty folder and ran the README example. The output matched the docs.

The page on chunk sizes, though, said that headings may stand alone as chunks and that there is no minimum. That is wrong since the change. I rewrote the section to describe heading binding, the minChunkSize default and the tail merge.

The recipe page for retrieval had a screenshot-like output block with a 40-character chunk. I regenerated it with the script that runs the examples, which I should have done before the release. I added the script to the release checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md, as a step before the tarball test.

No user issue came from this. I only noticed it myself.

summary: Answered a user question about how to keep chunk borders on headings of a given level, and decided against a new option for now.
body:
A user asked whether chunks can always start at an h2, so each section of their handbook is one chunk if it fits. Today the splitter packs as many blocks as fit, so a chunk may hold the end of one section and the start of the next.

The merge code already has the information. I tested a quick patch where merging stops at a heading of level less than or equal to a splitLevel value. On their handbook it gave the result they wanted, with the cost of more small chunks for short sections.

I did not merge it. It interacts with minChunkSize, because the two options contradict each other for short sections, and I do not yet know which should win. I wrote that in the issue and offered a workaround: split the Markdown by h2 with a few lines of code using the exported parse helper, then call chunk on each part.

I gave them the snippet and labelled the issue as a possible feature, to see whether others ask.

summary: Two more users asked for section-aligned chunks, so I implemented splitLevel and decided that it overrides minChunkSize.
body:
After two more requests in the same issue I built the option. With splitLevel: 2 a chunk never spans a heading of level 2 or higher in rank, meaning h1 and h2. The binding rule from last week still holds, so a heading stays with its first block.

The conflict with minChunkSize is solved by letting splitLevel win. A short section stays a small chunk, because the user asked for aligned sections explicitly. The docs say so in one sentence and the option table shows the interaction.

I wrote tests with a document of five sections, of which two are shorter than the minimum. They check the borders and the sizes. A third test uses a section larger than the limit, which must still be split inside, and the heading of the section is repeated only if repeatAncestors is on for headings, which is off by default.

I asked whether anyone wants the heading path as a prefix, since that is the next obvious request. One person said yes, so I opened an issue for it, without a plan yet.

summary: Designed a headingPath field for chunks that holds the list of parent headings, as metadata instead of text added to the content.
body:
The user who asked for a heading prefix wanted it in the text for embeddings. Another reader wanted it only as metadata for filters. Adding text to the content changes the size, and we already have the appended field for such additions.

My decision is to do both with one mechanism. Each chunk gets headingPath, an array of strings from the top heading down to the closest one, always present. A separate option, prefixHeadingPath, adds the path as a line of text at the start of the chunk, counted against the size limit and listed in the appended field.

The cases to think about: a chunk that starts before the first heading has an empty path. A setext heading and an ATX heading give the same text. Headings with inline markup, such as links or code, should have the plain text in the path, so I will take the text with mdast-util-to-string. A chunk that spans two sections gets the path of its first block, plus a field lastHeadingPath is not needed, which I decided against.

I wrote this in the issue and asked the two requesters whether the first-block rule is fine for them. Implementation will follow once they answer.

summary: Implemented headingPath and prefixHeadingPath, and a test for a sentence-long heading made the prefix eat 40 percent of the size budget.
body:
The two requesters agreed on the first-block rule. I added a heading stack to the chunk builder in src/builder.ts. It is pushed and popped by depth while the blocks are walked, and each chunk copies the stack at its first block.

The prefix option adds a line like 'Guide > Install > Linux' at the top of the chunk. The separator is configurable. The prefix length is reserved in the size budget just as the footnote reserve is, and it is listed in appended with the kind 'headingPath'.

A test with a real heading of 160 characters under a nested list of three more long headings showed the prefix taking about 40 percent of a 1,000 character limit. I added a rule: if the prefix is more than a quarter of maxSize, it is truncated in the middle of the path and the shortened levels are replaced by an ellipsis, keeping the first and the last level.

Tests: 12 new, all green. I also updated the JSON schema for the CLI config file so the new options validate.

summary: Profiled a report of slow splitting on a 9 MB file full of tiny tables and found the header repeat code cloning the whole table for every row group.
body:
A user said a 9 MB file of API docs takes 31 seconds. It has about 4,000 small tables. I profiled it with node --cpu-prof and opened the result in the browser tools. 68 percent of the time was in one function, cloneTable in src/table.ts.

The function was written when tables were first split. For each group of rows it deep cloned the whole table node, then removed the rows that did not belong. For a table of 20 rows that means 20 times the copying, and for a table of 400 rows much worse. Most of the user's tables were small, but the cost also hits the big ones.

The fix is to build a new table node from the header row and the slice of rows, sharing the cell nodes, since we never mutate them. I checked that no later step mutates cells. The width calculation reads them only, and the serializer too.

After the change the file takes 9.6 seconds, a three times speed up. The profile now shows serializing to Markdown as the top cost, at 41 percent.

I also found that the alignment row was rebuilt for each group. I cache it per table. That gave another 4 percent. I added the file as a generated fixture to the benchmark, which runs in CI as a soft check.

summary: Looked into the serializer cost found in the profile and made it skip stringify for nodes whose source slice is unchanged, saving about half of the remaining time.
body:
After the table fix, the remaining top cost was remark-stringify, called for every chunk. Many chunks contain nodes that we did not touch, and their original text is available through the position offsets.

I changed the builder to use the source slice for any node with a position that was not modified. Modified nodes are those with a repeated table header, a balanced HTML tag or an added prefix. These still go through stringify. The slice keeps the user's own formatting, which some users had asked for anyway, for example their bullet character and their emphasis style.

That is a visible change of output, so I checked the corpus. 14 of 60 documents changed, all in the style of markup only, such as asterisks instead of underscores for emphasis. The text content is the same. I decided to keep this, call it a fix, and put it in the changelog, since keeping source style is what people expect.

Time on the 9 MB file went from 9.6 to 4.7 seconds. I updated the snapshots and read the diffs for the 14 documents.

summary: Reviewed an outside pull request adding a Markdown-to-plain-text output mode, and asked the author to handle tables and code blocks before it can merge.
body:
The pull request adds an option format: 'text', which strips markup from chunks, for users who embed plain text. The idea is good and fits the project, and the author is polite and responsive.

I read the diff and ran it on three documents. The core approach uses mdast-util-to-string on each node. That works for paragraphs and headings. Two problems showed. First, tables come out as the cell texts joined by nothing, so 'NameType' turns up where there should be a row. Second, code blocks lose the language and their line structure collapses to one line.

I wrote a review with these two examples, showing the real output. I suggested that tables be rendered as tab-separated rows, as that keeps the cell borders and is a common format, and that code keep its line breaks and drop only the fence.

I also asked three smaller things. The option should not change the size accounting, so the limit refers to the text that is output. The appended field must stay consistent, and the new tests should use the shared fixtures instead of inline strings. The author answered within the hour that they would work on it this week.

I also noted a question I need to decide myself: whether the text format should apply to the appended definitions. I think links should be shown as their text only, so the definitions are not needed, and I left a comment on this.

summary: Wrote a script that checks that chunks joined together give back the source text, and it caught a lost blank line between a list and a following code block.
body:
We have a lossless check from the admonition work, but it only ran in a test on a few documents. I made a script, scripts/lossless.ts, that runs it on the whole corpus and on any folder I give it, with the settings as arguments. For each file it chunks with overlap off and with every appended part removed, joins the chunks, and compares the result with the source after normalizing line ends.

I ran it with ten combinations of options on the 60 documents, which is 600 runs. 596 passed. Four failed, all with the same pattern: a list directly followed by an indented code block, where the blank line between them is missing in the output.

The cause is in the merge step. When two blocks are joined it adds a blank line, unless the first block ends with a newline already. A list item that holds the code block ends with the closing fence and a newline, so no blank line was added and the next paragraph touched the fence. The result is correct Markdown only by accident in some cases, and in others the fence swallows the next lines.

I changed the join to compute the separator from the source offsets: the gap between the end of the previous block and the start of the next one is copied from the source text when they are neighbours. When they are not, because something was dropped, a blank line is used.

With this, 600 of 600 pass. I added the four documents as small regression fixtures. I also put the script into CI as a job that runs on the smaller corpus, since the full set takes about two minutes.

One more option set, with splitLevel and prefixHeadingPath, is still missing from the matrix, but they add text on purpose, so the check needs to strip the prefix. I will add that tomorrow.

summary: Extended the lossless script to strip heading prefixes, found that the prefix was also missing from the appended field in merged chunks, and fixed that.
body:
To test prefixHeadingPath I made the script remove each prefix, using the appended field. That immediately failed on 23 runs, and the reason was not the script. In a merged chunk, where two chunks were joined, the second chunk's prefix stayed in the middle of the text and the appended field had only the first one.

The merge step should not keep a prefix of the second chunk at all. A merged chunk has the path of its first block, as I wrote in the design. The second chunk's prefix is now dropped when merging, and the size of the merged chunk is computed again afterwards, since removing the prefix frees space.

There was a second case. When the second chunk begins with a heading of a deeper level, dropping its prefix hides the context from a reader, but the heading itself is still in the text, so the information is there. I kept the rule simple.

I ran the matrix again, now with 14 option combinations, 840 runs. 3 failures remain, all with splitLevel and prefixHeadingPath together on a document that starts with text before any heading. The path is empty, so the prefix should be an empty line and not 'undefined'. The code produced a blank line with a separator character. I made an empty path produce no prefix.

After that all 840 pass.

I also fixed the CLI. The flag --prefix-heading-path did not exist, and the config file option was read but never passed along. I added the flag and a test that runs the binary. Then I ran the whole test suite and the benchmark. Both are fine, and the benchmark is within 3 percent of last week.

Left for tomorrow: update the docs for headingPath, splitLevel and the source style change, and prepare the release notes.

summary: Wrote the docs for headingPath, splitLevel and prefixHeadingPath and the note on source formatting, and ran the example script to refresh all outputs.
body:
The options table on the docs site got three new rows, and each has an example with real output from the script that runs the examples. I made sure the script ran before I wrote any text this time, as the release checklist now says.

The page on retrieval got a new recipe: embedding the chunk with its prefix and storing headingPath as metadata for filters. I used a small document about installation with three levels of headings, so the path is easy to read.

The change log note about the source style is the most important one for users. I wrote that output now keeps the original markup for untouched nodes and that this may change emphasis markers and bullet characters compared to 1.6. A short sentence tells people with exact snapshots to expect diffs.

I checked all links on the docs site with the link checker, and one was dead, an anchor that had been renamed. I fixed it.

summary: Merged the plain text output pull request after the author added tab-separated tables and kept code line breaks, then fixed the size accounting myself.
body:
The author pushed the changes: tables are now rows of cells separated by tabs, and code blocks keep their lines without the fence. The tests use the shared fixtures. I ran the lossless script with format 'text' skipped, since it is lossy by design, and the other tests passed.

One thing remained. The size check still measured the Markdown version of a chunk and not the text that is output, so chunks in text mode were smaller than needed, about 6 percent on the corpus. I made the builder measure the converted text when format is text. That needed the conversion to happen before the fit test, and the author's code did it after.

I pushed this to their branch with their permission on the pull request, with an explanation and a test that checks that no chunk in text mode is over the limit. Then I merged it using squash and thanked the author in the changelog, with their name as in the earlier credit lines.

summary: Released 1.7.0 with headingPath, splitLevel, text output, the table speedup and source-style output, after the tarball test and a check of the changelog credits.
body:
The changeset list had seven entries. I read each one and sorted them: three features, two performance changes and two fixes. The credit line for the text output author was present this time, since I added it during the merge.

The tarball smoke test passed, including the new type exports for headingPath. The two sample projects built and ran, one of them as an ESM project and one as CommonJS.

Before publishing I ran the benchmark once more. The 9 MB table file took 4.6 seconds, down from 31 at the report, and the 20,000-item list case was unchanged.

I published 1.7.0 and answered in the issues that asked for splitLevel, the heading prefix and the text format, with the version number. I also closed the slow tables issue with the numbers.

summary: Started the front matter work after two issues asked for YAML at the top of a file to stay out of chunk text, and settled on parsing it into a metadata field.
body:
Two issues came in within a week: one user's chunks began with a `---` block of YAML, and another had the front matter title repeated in every embedding. I read how remark-frontmatter represents the node and checked what the splitter does with it today. It treats the node as a paragraph-like block, so it lands in the first chunk and counts against the size limit.

I considered three options: drop it, keep it in the first chunk only, or lift it into a `frontMatter` field on every chunk. Dropping loses information that users clearly want for filtering. Keeping it in the first chunk is the current behaviour and is the complaint. I chose the field, with the raw text kept so that the lossless check still works.

The plan is a `frontMatter` option with values 'keep', 'strip' and 'metadata', and the default stays 'keep' until the next major. TOML front matter with `+++` also needs a decision, and I will support it through the same plugin config. I wrote the cases into a scratch test file: empty front matter, front matter without a closing fence, and a file that is only front matter.

Nothing is implemented yet. The next step is the parse step, then the size accounting, since stripped front matter must not count toward the limit.

summary: Implemented the frontMatter option with keep, strip and metadata modes, and a file made only of front matter exposed that the splitter returned one empty chunk.
body:
I added remark-frontmatter to the parser setup for both YAML and TOML. The new option `frontMatter` takes 'keep', 'strip' or 'metadata'. In metadata mode the raw text goes into `chunk.frontMatter` on every chunk, and the node is removed from the content.

The first test run showed the case I had listed: a file with only front matter produced one chunk with empty content. I changed it to return an empty array in strip and metadata modes, and to return the single front matter chunk in keep mode. An unclosed `---` is not front matter in remark, so that file is parsed as a thematic break and stays as it was.

Size accounting was the other part. In metadata mode the front matter does not count toward the limit, because it is not in the content. I documented that, since a user with a 2 KB front matter block might be surprised by chunks of the full size.

I added 11 tests and all of the 214 existing tests still pass. Parsing the YAML into an object is left out on purpose, as the library should not pick a YAML parser for its users.

summary: Added a parseFrontMatter hook so users bring their own YAML parser, and the lossless script found that strip mode dropped the blank line after the closing fence.
body:
The raw text field was not enough for two of the people in the issue thread. They wanted an object. Instead of bundling a YAML parser I added an option `parseFrontMatter: (raw, format) => unknown`, which fills `chunk.meta`. The library calls it once per document and shares the result between chunks.

I wrote tests with js-yaml and with a function that throws. A throwing parser is caught, and the chunk gets `meta: undefined` and a warning through the existing `onWarn` callback. I chose not to fail the whole split because of a bad title line in a single file.

Then I ran the lossless script with strip mode on the corpus. It reported a diff on 6 documents: the blank line after the closing `---` was gone, so the first chunk joined to the rest without the separator. The cause was that I removed the node and also its trailing gap in the source slice. I fixed the slice logic so that only the node range is removed and the following whitespace is kept, then the script was clean on all 83 documents.

I also tested a Windows file with CRLF and a byte order mark in front of the opening fence. The BOM broke detection, because the fence has to be at offset 0. I now strip a leading BOM before parsing and put it back when the mode is 'keep'.

The CLI got a `--front-matter` flag with the three values. I updated the help text and a CLI test that checks the output of each mode.

What is left is the docs page and a changeset. I left the default at 'keep' and put a note in the changeset about changing it in 2.0.

summary: Wrote the front matter docs page and a changeset, and fixed a README example whose output still showed the title inside the first chunk.
body:
I wrote the docs page for front matter with one section per mode and a short recipe for js-yaml. The example script regenerates all outputs, and after running it the README example for strip mode differed: the old text still showed the title in the first chunk. I fixed it from the script output instead of by hand.

The changeset is a minor bump. It lists `frontMatter`, `parseFrontMatter`, the BOM handling and the CLI flag. I also added the note about the future default.

One reporter asked whether TOML is covered. It is, and I added a test with a `+++` block and the same three modes. I replied on the issue with the version that will have it.

summary: Released 1.8.0 with front matter support after the tarball test caught a missing type export for the new option interface.
body:
Before publishing I ran the tarball test that installs the packed file in a clean project under Node and two bundlers. The TypeScript check failed in the ESM project: `FrontMatterMode` was not exported from the index, so users could not name the type of the option. I added the export and a type test that imports it.

After that the test passed in all three setups. I ran the full test suite again, 225 tests, and the lossless script on the corpus, both clean. The changelog credits the two reporters of the issues.

The release workflow published 1.8.0 and I checked the page on npm and installed it in a fresh folder. The CLI printed the new flag in `--help`. I then commented on both issues with the version and closed them.

One thing I noticed while reading the workflow log: the build step takes 41 seconds, mostly from the declaration files. Not a problem yet, so I only noted it.

summary: Looked at an issue about links broken at a chunk border in reference-style images and found the appended definitions only covered links, not images.
body:
A user reported that images written as `![alt][logo]` lose their definition when the chunk border falls between the image and the `[logo]: ...` line. I reproduced it with a small document and a limit of 200 characters. The appended field was empty for that chunk.

The collector looked for `linkReference` nodes only. Remark uses `imageReference` for images, so those were never collected. I extended the collector to both node types and shared the label normalization, which is the same case-insensitive lookup fixed earlier.

I added three tests: an image reference, a mixed chunk with a link and an image sharing one definition, and a missing definition, which should add nothing. All passed. The lossless script was clean as well.

I replied to the reporter and will put the fix into the next patch release.

summary: Answered a question on whether chunkdown can count tokens with a Hugging Face tokenizer and wrote the short adapter example into the docs.
body:
A user asked how to use a tokenizer from transformers.js for the size limit. The pluggable counter takes a function from string to number, so it works without library changes. I wrote a six-line adapter and tested it with a small model.

The first attempt was slow, because the tokenizer was called for every block. I added a note to cache the counts with a Map keyed by the text, which cut the time on a 2 MB file from 14 s to 3 s in my test. I put the example and the cache note on the tokenizer docs page and replied on the issue.

summary: Started the 2.0 API plan by listing every option and return field and marking which names are inconsistent between the splitter, the stream and the CLI.
body:
The new major version was planned a while ago, so I made the list of what the API looks like now. There are 19 options. Some names do not match: `maxSize` in the splitter and `--limit` in the CLI, `appended` as a field but `appendDefinitions` as an option, and `minChunkSize` next to `splitLevel`.

I wrote each name in a table with the proposed new name and the reason. The big ones are a single `size` object with `max`, `min` and `unit`, a `headings` group for splitLevel and the path options, and `frontMatter` becoming an object with `mode` and `parse`.

I also listed what should stay: the chunk fields `content`, `headingPath` and `meta`. The default for front matter changes to 'metadata'.

The table sits in `docs/rfc-2.md` and I will go through it again before touching any code. Open question: whether to keep the old option names for one more version with a warning. That costs code, but users with a few hundred installs will notice a break.

summary: Decided to accept the old option names in 2.0 with a deprecation warning, after counting how many lines the mapping layer needs.
body:
I prototyped the mapping layer for old option names in a scratch file. It is a single function that takes the old shape and returns the new one, and it calls `onWarn` once per name. It came to 38 lines including types.

That is small enough, so the decision is to keep it for the whole 2.x line and remove it in 3.0. I wrote this into the RFC. The warning text names the old option and the new one, for example `maxSize is deprecated, use size.max`.

A conflict case needs a rule: when both old and new are given, the new one wins and a warning says so. I added that to the RFC with a test list.

Next is the type design for the new options object.

summary: Implemented the new grouped options object for 2.0 and a migration layer, and a type test showed that a union of old and new shapes gave poor error messages.
body:
I started the code with the new `Options` type: `size` with `max`, `min` and `unit`, `headings` with `splitLevel`, `path` and `prefix`, and `frontMatter` with `mode` and `parse`. The internal splitter now only reads this shape.

The migration layer sits in front. My first version typed the public function as accepting `Options | LegacyOptions`. A type test that passes a wrong value for `size.max` produced a long message mentioning both shapes, and it was not readable. I changed it to overloads, one for each shape, and the error for a wrong new-style call now only mentions the new type.

The layer converts all 19 old names. Each conversion has a test: old name in, new object out, one warning. There is also a test for a mix of old and new names, and a test where the old option is `undefined`, which must not warn.

I had to touch about 40 existing tests that use the old names. I left most of them on the old names on purpose so they check the layer, and moved only the core tests to the new shape. That keeps both paths covered.

The defaults are written once in a `defaults.ts` file. The front matter default is now 'metadata', and the existing front matter tests that depended on 'keep' now pass the mode explicitly.

The suite is at 261 tests and all pass. The CLI is not yet changed and still uses the old names through the layer, which works but warns. That is the next job.

summary: Renamed the CLI flags for 2.0, kept the old flags as aliases, and found that a boolean flag with a value of false was parsed as the string.
body:
I changed the CLI to the new vocabulary: `--size`, `--min-size`, `--unit`, `--split-level`, `--heading-path` and so on. The old flags stay as aliases and print a warning to stderr, so scripts that pipe stdout are not affected.

While writing the alias tests I found a bug that was already there. `--prefix-heading-path=false` was read as the string 'false', which is truthy, so the prefix was turned on. The flag parser treated every `=value` as text. I fixed it by declaring the boolean flags in the parser config and added tests for `=false`, `=true`, `--no-` form and the bare flag.

The help text is generated from a table of flags, and I changed the table to include the aliases in parentheses. A snapshot test of the help output was updated, and I checked the diff by reading it, not only accepting the snapshot.

I also made the CLI read a `chunkdown.config.json` file when it exists in the current folder. Flags override the file. A few users had asked for this in issues about long command lines. It reuses the new options shape, so the file format is the same as the API object.

Tests for the config file: a missing file, invalid JSON with an error message that gives the file name and the position, and an unknown key, which warns and continues. Unknown keys are a likely typo, so the warning lists the closest valid name.

All 279 tests pass. The docs are not yet updated.

summary: Changed the chunk return type for 2.0 so metadata sits under one meta object, and a user-facing codemod idea was dropped as too costly for the benefit.
body:
The chunk shape in 1.x has top-level `headingPath`, `appended`, `frontMatter` and, for streams, `index`. For 2.0 I moved the optional ones under `meta` and kept `content`, `start` and `end` at the top. The reasoning is that adding a field later should never be a possible clash with a name users put on their own objects.

I updated the splitter, the stream, the text output and the CLI JSON output. A compatibility getter was my first idea, but defining properties on every chunk had a cost: on the 9 MB test file the split time rose by about 6 percent. I dropped the getters. The break is documented instead, since it is a major version.

I also thought about a codemod that rewrites `chunk.headingPath` to `chunk.meta.headingPath`. I looked at jscodeshift and the amount of work for what is maybe ten lines in a user's project. I decided against it and will write the three renames as a table in the migration guide.

Types: `Chunk<M = {}>` is generic over the metadata the user's parse function returns, so `chunk.meta.frontMatter.data` is typed. I tested this with a type test that uses a user-defined interface.

The lossless script needed a small change, since it read `chunk.appended`. It now reads from `meta`. It is clean on the corpus.

Tests are at 285 and green. The next piece is the migration guide.

summary: Wrote the 2.0 migration guide from the RFC table and checked every snippet by running it against the new build, which fixed three wrong names.
body:
I wrote `docs/migrating-to-2.md` with sections for options, the chunk shape, the CLI and removed things. Each rename has a before and after snippet.

To avoid errors like the earlier docs example that did not match the code, I extracted every code block of the guide and ran them against the built package with a small script. Three failed. One used `size.maximum` instead of `size.max`, one had the old `appended` field in an after snippet, and one was missing an import. I fixed all three in the guide.

The guide ends with a short list for library authors who wrap chunkdown. It tells them to read `meta` and not the top-level fields, and says the legacy option layer will warn once per name per process, not once per call.

I also added a deprecation count to the layer. A test calls the splitter 100 times with the old name and expects exactly one warning. It passed on the first run, which I took as suspicious, so I temporarily broke the dedupe and saw the test fail.

The README is next. Its examples still use the old names, and the example script that makes the outputs must be run again after I change it.

summary: Updated the README and docs site to the 2.0 API, regenerated all example outputs, and found the streaming memory table had been measured with the old options.
body:
I went through the README and all pages of the docs and changed every example to the new options. The example script that prints outputs now uses the same objects, and I ran it to refresh each output block. That took most of the evening because there are 37 blocks.

While doing the streaming page I noticed that the memory table was measured with settings which no longer exist in the same form. The numbers themselves are still valid, because the parse path did not change, but I wanted to be sure. I reran the 50 MB test with the new build: peak memory was 212 MB against 205 MB in the table. The difference is within noise from my machine, so I kept the table and wrote down the new run command next to it.

The API reference page is generated from the types with a script. After the rename it listed `Options` twice, because the legacy type was exported by the same module. I moved the legacy type to a separate file and marked it as deprecated in the doc comment, and the reference now shows it in its own section.

I searched for the old names in the docs folder to be sure nothing remained. Two hits were intended, in the migration guide, and one in a recipe for admonitions, which I fixed.

A link check of the built site with a small script found two dead anchors after the heading renames. I fixed both anchors.

Two things remain before a release candidate: the changeset for the major bump and a test of the packed file in the usual setups.

summary: Published 2.0.0-rc.1 under the next tag and asked the four people who requested the API cleanup to try it.
body:
The changeset is in pre mode for the major version. The tarball test passed in Node and the bundlers, including the type entries for ESM and CommonJS from the exports fix.

I published `2.0.0-rc.1` with the `next` tag, so `npm install chunkdown` still gives 1.8.x. I checked this with `npm view chunkdown dist-tags`, which listed both.

I wrote a comment on the open API issues with the install command and a link to the migration guide, and asked for feedback within two weeks. I also pinned a short note in the discussions.

summary: Triaged the first feedback on the release candidate: one real bug in the legacy layer, one request for a size callback, and one typing complaint to reproduce.
body:
Three replies came in. The first reporter said that passing `maxSize: undefined` together with `size: { max: 500 }` produced a warning about a conflict. By my own rule an undefined old option should not count, and the test I wrote covered only the case without the new option. The conflict check looked at key presence, not at the value. I fixed it to ignore undefined values and added the mixed test.

The second reporter asked for a `size` that can be a function, so that the limit depends on the heading path, for example smaller chunks in a changelog section. I thought about it. It is easy to implement, but it makes the result harder to reason about, and the merge rules assume one limit for a document. I wrote that on the issue and asked for the concrete case. I am leaning towards a no, with the workaround of splitting the document by section and calling the library per part.

The third reporter wrote that `Chunk<M>` gave an error in their project: `Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'Record<string, unknown>'`. I tried to reproduce it with their code. The cause was a `parse` function with the return type `unknown`, and my generic default constraint required an object. I changed the constraint to accept unknown, and the reporter's snippet now compiles. A type test with an unknown return value was added.

I ran the whole suite, 291 tests, and the type tests under TypeScript 5.4 and 5.7, since the reporter used the older one. The older one found nothing more.

The fixes go into rc.2. I will wait a few days for more feedback before cutting it.

summary: Looked into the claim that 2.0 is slower on small files and measured a 12 percent startup cost caused by building the legacy layer on every call.
body:
One of the reporters said that splitting many small files in a loop was slower than with 1.8. I wrote a benchmark of 20000 files of about 1 KB each and ran both versions on the same machine. Version 1.8 took 4.1 s and the candidate took 4.6 s, about 12 percent more.

I profiled it. The top cost was not the splitting but the options handling: for each call the code built the defaults object, ran the legacy conversion with its 19 checks and created the parser pipeline again. The unified processor was built per call, which was already true in 1.x, but the extra part grew the cost.

I made three changes. The processor is cached by the parser-related options in a small Map. The legacy conversion exits at once when no old key is present, using a precomputed Set of the old names. The defaults object is frozen and spread only when something differs.

After that the benchmark gave 3.6 s, which is faster than 1.8 because of the processor cache. I did not expect that, so I ran each version three times: the range was 3.5 to 3.7 s against 4.0 to 4.2 s.

One risk is the cache holding on to a user's plugin objects. The key is made from the plugin list by identity, and I limited the Map to 16 entries with the oldest removed first. A test checks that the 17th configuration removes the first.

All tests pass. I noted the numbers in the issue and in the changeset.

summary: Released 2.0.0-rc.2 with the legacy layer fix, the Chunk generic fix and the processor cache, and noted that nobody has yet tested the CLI aliases.
body:
I cut rc.2 from main after the suite and the lossless script were clean. The tarball test passed in all setups.

The changelog lists the three fixes, the speedup from the cache and the numbers of the small file benchmark. I published with the `next` tag again and answered the three reporters with the version.

Feedback so far covers the options and the types, but nobody has mentioned the CLI aliases or the config file. Those are the parts with the most new code. I wrote a short test script that runs 30 old-style command lines from the issues against the new CLI and checks that output matches 1.8 byte for byte. Twenty-nine matched. One differed because the warning text is now on stderr and my script merged both streams, so that was the script's mistake, and I fixed it.

I will keep the candidate open for another week.

summary: Answered the size callback request with a decision against it and wrote a recipe for splitting by section and calling chunkdown for each part.
body:
The reporter gave the real case: a changelog with long release sections and a docs set with short pages, in one corpus, where they want 300 characters for the first and 1200 for the second. That is two inputs with two settings, and not one document with a varying limit.

I decided against the callback. A single limit keeps the merge rules, the minimum size and the overlap predictable, and users can already call the splitter with different options per file. I wrote that on the issue in a few sentences.

For the cases where one file really has both parts, I wrote a recipe with `splitLevel` to get the sections as chunks first, then a second call on any chunk above a threshold with a smaller limit. I ran the recipe on a sample changelog and checked that joined output equals the source. It does, and the recipe is on the docs page for advanced use.

The reporter replied that this works for them and thanked me.

summary: Finished the candidate period with a last check of the migration guide against two real user projects and fixed a missing note about the Node version.
body:
Two of the users who tried the candidate sent their project links. I cloned both and followed my own migration guide step by step. The first project migrated in about ten minutes, with the three renames of chunk fields. The second used a wrapper function that read `chunk.appended` in four places, and the guide led them to `meta` without trouble.

One snag came up in the second project. It ran on Node 16 and failed with a syntax error from the build output. Version 2.0 targets Node 18 and later, which the changeset said, but the migration guide did not. I added a requirements section to the guide and to the README, and set `engines` in package.json so that npm warns at install time.

I also tested the packed file on Node 18, 20 and 22 in CI. I extended the matrix of the workflow, since it only had 20 before. All three passed.

The lossless script was clean on the corpus, with one new document added from the second project: a changelog with nested lists of depth 6.

No more issues have come in about the candidate. I plan the final release in the next few days.

summary: Released 2.0.0 stable after the final tarball test and a check that the latest tag points to it, and closed the API cleanup issues.
body:
I left pre mode and ran the version command, which merged the two candidate changelogs into one entry for 2.0.0. I read the result and shortened the list of fixes that only existed between candidates.

The full suite of 296 tests, the type tests and the tarball test all passed. The release workflow published the package. `npm view chunkdown dist-tags` showed `latest` at 2.0.0, and a fresh install in an empty folder gave the new version with the CLI printing the new flags.

I closed the four API issues with a link to the migration guide and the release notes. The deprecated 1.x line gets no more features, but I put a note in the README that security and crash fixes for 1.8 will be done on request.

summary: Handled the first week after 2.0.0: fixed a crash on a document of only a thematic break, a wrong deprecation message and a docs link, and planned the next topic.
body:
Three reports came in after the release. The first was a crash with `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'position')` on a file that contained only `---`. With front matter in metadata mode the parser sees a thematic break, and my code assumed the first node was a front matter node when the text started with the fence. I reproduced it with a one-line file. The fix checks the node type, not the text, and the file now gives one chunk with the rule. I added tests for `---`, `***` and `---\n---`, which is an empty front matter block and returns no chunks.

The second report was a wrong deprecation message. The warning for `minChunkSize` said to use `size.minimum`, while the real name is `size.min`. It was in the mapping table, and my tests checked that a warning appears but not its text. I fixed the text and changed the tests to compare the message with the migration guide table, so they cannot differ again. Two other messages were checked this way and are correct.

The third was a dead link in the README to the old docs page for `splitLevel`, which moved when I renamed anchors. I fixed it and checked every link in the README with the link script, which I had run only on the docs site before.

I released 2.0.1 with the three fixes. The tarball test was clean, and I answered the reporters.

Looking at the open issues, two ask for better handling of HTML blocks inside Markdown, which are currently one unbreakable block. That looks like the same problem as the earlier plugin nodes, and the next entry will be a test of how large HTML blocks behave. I wrote a short list of sample documents to collect for that, among them a README with a big centered HTML table and a page with embedded details elements.

summary: Planned the work after 2.0.0: collected open issues and feedback into a short list and ranked them, putting chunks that are too small after a merge pass at the top.
body:
After the first week of 2.0.0 I sat down with the issue tracker and my own notes and wrote one list of what is open. There were seven items: small trailing chunks, a request for overlap between chunks, a question about splitting HTML blocks inside Markdown, a CLI aliases test nobody has done, a docs search problem, a typing request for the stream API, and a note about the lockfile in the repo.

I ranked them by how many users each touches. Small trailing chunks came first because three separate issues over the last months describe it, and the 2.0 release did not change the behavior. Overlap came second, but it needs a design decision, so it gets a plan and not code yet.

I reproduced the small chunk problem with a real document, the README of a large project, at a limit of 800 characters. Of 142 chunks, 19 were under 100 characters. Most of them were a heading followed by a long table or a code block that did not fit, so the heading stood alone.

The cause is that the splitter closes a chunk when the next node does not fit, and never looks back. A heading alone is a valid chunk by the rules, but it is useless for retrieval.

I wrote down two options. The first is to keep headings with the next node (a rule that a heading may not be the last node in a chunk). The second is a general merge pass with a minimum size. I think both are needed, because a heading rule alone does not fix short paragraphs between two code blocks.

I did not write code today. I added the list to a pinned issue so the people who reported it can see the order, and I plan to start with the heading rule tomorrow because it is small and testable.

I also noted that the CLI alias test is still open and should be done before the next minor release, since it is the only part of 2.0 with no user feedback.

summary: Added a failing test set for the heading-stays-with-next-node rule, built from three real documents that produce lone heading chunks, before touching the splitter.
body:
Tonight I wrote only tests. I took the three documents from the issues and the README sample and saved them as fixtures under test/fixtures/lone-heading.

For each one the test splits at 800 characters and asserts that no chunk ends with a heading node. All four fail now, with 19, 7, 11 and 4 offending chunks.

I also added a test for the edge case where the heading is followed by a node larger than the limit. There the node has to be split anyway, and the heading should go with the first piece. This is the case I expect to be hardest.

A second edge case is a heading directly followed by a deeper heading. Two headings in a row cannot both stay with a next node that fits, so the test only requires that the last heading of a chunk is never the final node unless the document ends there.

I left the tests failing on purpose and committed them with a skip marker, so the main branch still passes in CI. Tomorrow I remove the marker when the rule is in.

summary: Implemented the rule that a heading cannot end a chunk; the four fixtures pass, but a heading followed by an oversized table needed a special path.
body:
The change is in the splitter packing loop. Before closing a chunk, it checks whether the last node is a heading, and if so moves that node to the next chunk.

That made three of the four fixtures pass. The fourth failed because the heading was followed by a table larger than the limit. Moving the heading to the next chunk put it with a table that is then split by rows, and the header repeat code placed the heading in an odd spot.

I changed it so the heading is counted as part of the first piece of the split node. The size budget for the table split now starts reduced by the heading length, so the first row group still fits.

There was one more problem. A heading longer than the limit, which exists in a test of mine with a 300-character heading and a limit of 200, made the loop move it forever. I added a guard: if a chunk would become empty by moving the heading, the heading stays.

All tests pass, 214 of them, and I removed the skip marker. On the README sample the count of chunks under 100 characters dropped from 19 to 8.

The remaining 8 are mostly short paragraphs between code blocks, which is what the merge pass is for. I will do that next.

summary: Wrote the minimum size merge pass behind a new minSize option and found it must not merge across a heading of a higher level, or sections get mixed.
body:
I added a minSize option under the size options group of 2.0, default 0 so nothing changes for current users. After the main split, a pass walks the chunks and merges a chunk smaller than minSize into its neighbor if the result still fits the limit.

First version merged into the previous chunk. On the README sample this produced chunks where the tail of one section was joined with the start of the next, for example a short note under an h3 glued to the following h2 section. That is bad for retrieval because the heading path of the merged chunk is wrong.

The rule now is that a merge is allowed only if the second chunk starts with no heading, or with a heading of a deeper level than the first chunk's last section. Otherwise the small chunk is tried against the next chunk instead, and if neither works it stays small.

At minSize 200 and limit 800 the sample went from 8 small chunks to 2. Both remaining ones are single-line sections at the end of the file with nothing to merge into, which I think is acceptable.

The merge pass also had to update the headingPath and the size fields of the merged chunk. I forgot the offsets first, and the lossless script flagged a mismatch at once. That script is paying for itself again.

Tests added: 9 for merge cases. Docs and a changeset are still to do.

summary: Documented minSize and the heading rule, added a changeset for a minor release, and noted the option does not apply to the token limit mode yet.
body:
I wrote a docs section on minSize with the README sample before and after, using real output from the example script. The heading rule is described as always on, with a note in the changelog since it changes the chunk borders for existing users.

While writing the docs I noticed minSize is read in characters even when the user counts tokens. I tested with the token counter and minSize 50 and got merges at 50 characters, which is wrong. I fixed it to use the same counter as the limit, and added a test with a fake tokenizer that counts each word as one token.

The changeset is marked minor. I thought about whether the heading rule is a breaking change and decided no, because the limit is still respected and the join of chunks is still the source text. I will say it clearly in the release notes anyway.

Not done: a flag to turn the heading rule off. Nobody asked for it, so I leave it out.

summary: Looked into the request for overlap between chunks, tried a prototype that repeats the last sentences, and found it breaks the lossless check by design.
body:
The overlap request comes from a user who wants the end of a chunk repeated at the start of the next one, as many RAG setups do. I wanted to see what it costs.

The prototype copies the last N characters of the previous chunk, cut at a sentence border, into a new field. I first tried putting it in the chunk text, but then the lossless script fails, since joined chunks no longer equal the source. That check is a main promise of the library, so I dropped that approach.

The second prototype keeps the text unchanged and adds a field meta.overlapBefore with the repeated part. The user can then join it with the text at index time or not. The lossless script passes because it ignores meta.
