The sentence border cut was the difficult part. A simple split on a period failed on abbreviations such as 'e.g.' and on decimals. I used Intl.Segmenter, which exists in Node 18 and later, and got correct borders on my test paragraphs, including one in German and one with a URL.

Code blocks and tables are a question. Repeating half a table row is useless. I made the overlap take whole nodes only when the previous chunk ends in a table or code block, and nothing if the last node is larger than the overlap size.

Size accounting: the overlap does not count against the limit, since it is in meta. I think that is right but it could surprise people, so it needs a clear sentence in the docs.

It works on the samples. I am not sure about the name. I have overlapBefore in the prototype but the user asked for just overlap. I will answer in the issue with the design and ask if the separate field is fine for them.

summary: Answered the overlap issue with the meta.overlapBefore design and the reason the chunk text stays exactly the source, and the reporter agreed.
body:
I posted the design in the issue: an option overlap with a size in the same unit as the limit, the repeated text in meta.overlapBefore, chunk text unchanged. I explained that joined chunks give the source back and that this is tested on every release.

The reporter answered within two hours and was fine with it, since they build the index text themselves anyway. They asked for an overlapAfter too, to avoid reading the next chunk. I said no for now: it is the same data as the next chunk's start, and two fields invite confusion.

I cleaned the prototype and added tests, 11 in all, for sentence borders, code block ends, a table end and the case of a first chunk, which has no overlap. The first chunk gets an empty string, not undefined, so the type is simpler.

The option goes into 2.1 together with minSize. I still need the docs and a check of the streaming API, which builds chunks one at a time and has to keep the tail of the previous one.

summary: Made the streaming splitter produce overlapBefore by keeping the tail of the previous chunk, and a test showed it differed from the non-streaming result on one case.
body:
The stream keeps only the current chunk in memory, so I added a small buffer with the last overlap-size characters of the previous chunk and cut it at a sentence border when the next chunk starts.

I compared the stream and the normal splitter on 30 fixtures. 29 were equal. The one that differed had a previous chunk shorter than the overlap size, where the normal splitter took text from the chunk before it too, and the stream could not.

I decided the normal splitter is the one to change: overlap comes only from the directly previous chunk. That is easier to explain, and it matches the memory promise of the stream. After the change all 30 fixtures are equal, and I added the short chunk case as a permanent test.

summary: Finished the docs for minSize and overlap with output samples, and ran the CLI with the new flags, which exposed that --min-size was missing from the help text.
body:
I wrote the docs page section with two real examples and the note that overlap is not counted in the size limit. The example script regenerated the outputs.

The CLI got --min-size and --overlap flags through the same mapping used for the other options. Running chunkdown --help showed no entry for --min-size, because the help text is a hand-kept list. I added both and a test that compares the help text with the flags the parser knows, so it cannot drift again.

I also tried the old alias style with the flag values, since nobody has tested aliases yet, and it worked for the three I tried. That is not a full test, so it is still open.

summary: Tested every CLI alias from 2.0 against its new flag with a table-driven test and found two aliases that silently ignored their value.
body:
Since no user has tested the CLI aliases, I wrote a table-driven test that has every old flag, its new flag, a sample value and the expected option in the resulting config. There are 17 pairs.

Fifteen passed. Two failed: --max-chars and --keep-fm. With --max-chars 500 the config still had the default limit, and --keep-fm gave no front matter mode at all.

The cause for the first one was a typo in the alias map, where the target was sizeLimit and not size.max. The second was an alias to a boolean flag, while the new option is an enum, keep or strip or metadata. The alias now maps --keep-fm to --front-matter keep.

Both would have given no error, which is the bad part: users would just get different chunks. I added a warning that prints once when an alias is used, with the new name, the same as the option layer does.

I also checked what happens when both the old and the new flag are given. The new one wins now, and a warning says so. Before that, the later one in the command line won, which was undefined behavior by accident.

The table test runs in CI now. I wrote a changeset for a patch fix and plan to include it in 2.1 so that the notes mention it.

One more detail: --help does not list the aliases, on purpose. I left that.

Next is the release of 2.1 with minSize, overlap, the heading rule and these fixes.

summary: Ran the tarball test for 2.1.0 and found that the new overlap types were not exported from the package index, then fixed it before release.
body:
The release flow has a step where I pack the tarball, install it in a clean folder and import every public name. Today it failed for ChunkOverlap, the type of meta.overlapBefore's option.

The type was defined in a file that the index did not re-export. Inside the repo, tests import from the source files, so nothing noticed. It is the same kind of miss as the front matter option interface in 1.8.0.

I fixed the export, and then added a check to the tarball test that compares the list of exported names of the built d.ts with a list in the repo, so a new public type must be added to both places on purpose.

I ran the full tests again, 249 now, and the build with tsdown for both ESM and CJS. The CJS build requires the file once in a small script and it worked.

The changelog from the changesets reads well, apart from one line that said the heading rule 'may' change borders. It does change them, so I changed the wording to say it plainly.

I did not publish yet, I will do it after a last look at the docs site build.

summary: Released 2.1.0 after fixing the missing overlap type exports, then checked the changelog and the npm page and noted two follow-ups for the next patch.
body:
The 2.1.0 release went out in the evening, after the tarball test from the earlier session had caught the missing overlap types. I rebuilt with tsdown and packed the tarball again, then installed it into a clean temp project. A small script imported ChunkMeta, OverlapOptions and the stream types from the package root, and all of them resolved under both ESM and CJS. The type check with strict mode passed on the consumer side too.

The changeset run produced the version bump and the changelog entry for minSize, overlapBefore and the heading rule. I read the generated changelog twice. One line said the heading rule was a fix, but it changes output for existing users, so I moved it under the minor changes and added a sentence that chunk counts may go down on documents with lone headings. The credits for the reporters of the lone heading issues were added by hand because the changeset tool did not pick them up.

After publishing I checked that the latest tag pointed to 2.1.0 and that the npm page showed the new README with the minSize section. I also ran the CLI from the published package with npx, using --min-size and --overlap, and both worked on the sample document. The GitHub release notes were copied from the changelog.

Two things stayed open. minSize still does not apply in token limit mode, which is noted in the docs but should be fixed. The streaming splitter also differs from the non-streaming one in one overlap case, and I have a test marked as known difference for it. I wrote both into the plan list as the first items for a 2.1.1 patch, and answered the two reporters who were waiting for the release.

summary: Reproduced the question about HTML blocks inside Markdown and found that large HTML nodes are never split, so a chunk can exceed the limit by far.
body:
The user asked what happens to a big block of raw HTML in a Markdown file. I tried a file with a 6000-character div containing a table and several paragraphs, with a limit of 1000.

The result was one chunk of 6000 characters. The parser gives a single html node, and the splitter treats a node it cannot split as indivisible. For code blocks there is a line-based fallback, but HTML has none.

There is a warning option for oversized chunks, and it did report it, but only if the user turns it on. I think the default should be to warn once per document.

A real fix needs an HTML parser. rehype is available in the unified family, but adding a dependency for a rare case is not good for a small library. A middle way is to split the html node on blank lines and at line breaks, like code, which works for most hand-written HTML.

I wrote the three options in the issue and said I lean to the line fallback.

summary: Implemented the line-based fallback for oversized html nodes, splitting at blank lines first and then single lines, and kept the tags balanced warning as a note only.
body:
The splitter now treats an html node over the limit like a code block: it splits at blank lines, and where a piece is still too large, at single lines. A single line longer than the limit stays as it is.

On my 6000-character div the result is 7 chunks of at most 1000 characters. Joined together they give the source, and the lossless script confirms it.

The drawback is clear: a split can fall inside a tag pair, so one chunk has an opening div and the next the closing one. I considered closing and reopening tags, but that would change the text and break the lossless promise. I left it and wrote it into the docs as a known limit.

I added a warning when an html node was split, off by default, with the name htmlSplit in the warnings list. The oversized chunk warning is on by default now, once per document, as I decided yesterday.

Tests: 6 new, including a comment block and an html node inside a list item, which has to keep its indent. The indent case failed first, because the pieces lost the list indentation, and I fixed it by taking the slice from the source with the original column.

summary: Handled the stream API typing request by making the async iterator generic over the meta type, and fixed a wrong overload that hid the chunk fields.
body:
The request: the result of splitStream should be typed as AsyncIterable of Chunk, and users with a custom parseFrontMatter want their own type in chunk.meta.frontMatter.

I reproduced it in a small project. The stream function had an overload that returned AsyncIterable<unknown> when the options were given as a variable and not as a literal. That is why they saw no fields. I removed the overload and replaced it with one signature and a generic.

The generic is Chunk<M>, with the parser's return type inferred from the parseFrontMatter option. If no hook is given, M is Record<string, unknown>.

I added type tests with expectTypeOf for four cases: a literal option, an option stored in a variable, a hook returning a custom interface, and no hook. All four pass.

The same inference now applies to split(), where it was already right, so I only added the test. A changeset for a patch is written. I replied to the reporter with a snippet to test the next version.

summary: Investigated the docs search that returns no results for option names with dots, and traced it to the tokenizer of the search plugin splitting on the dot.
body:
A user wrote that searching for size.max in the docs gives nothing. I tried it and also saw empty results, while searching for max found too many pages.

The docs site uses a static search index built at deploy time. I opened the index file and found that size.max was stored as two words, size and max, and the query was split the same way but matched as a phrase with a gap rule that failed on the dot.

I looked at three fixes. One is to change the plugin's tokenizer config to keep dots inside words. Second is to add the dotted names as extra keywords in the front matter of the option pages. Third is to switch plugins, which I do not want to do for one problem.

The tokenizer config worked locally for size.max, but it broke searches such as 'config.json' less obviously: a search for config no longer found pages with config.json. I would need to index both forms.

So I went with a mix: the plugin keeps its default, and I added a hidden keywords line to each option page with the full dotted names, generated from the option schema by the docs build script. That way the list cannot go out of date.

I built the site and checked 12 dotted names. All 12 gave the right page as the first result. One name, meta.overlapBefore, found its page only second, behind the front matter page, since that page mentions meta many times. I accepted that.

I also noticed that the generated keywords showed up in the page text on the mobile view, because the line was in a visible element. I changed it to a meta tag that the plugin reads, and checked the page again.

The docs site is deployed, and I answered the user with a link and a thanks.

summary: Tracked the docs search failure on option names with dots to the search plugin tokenizer splitting on the dot, and chose a custom tokenizer config over renaming anything.
body:
A user reported that searching the docs for front matter or for an option such as segmenterLocale worked, but a grouped name like size.min returned nothing. I reproduced it on the local docs build and looked at the search index file. The index contained size and min as separate tokens and no token with the dot. The plugin's default tokenizer splits on every non-word character, so the query was split the same way and then required both words in one field, which failed on the option tables.

I tried a query-side fix first, joining the parts with a phrase match, but the plugin did not support that. Then I changed the tokenizer config so the dot is kept inside a word when letters are on both sides, and rebuilt the index. Searching size.min now finds the options page as the first result, and plain min still finds it too, because I added a second split token. The index grew by about four percent, which is fine. I added a short check to the docs build that searches for three dotted names and fails if one has no result.

summary: Looked into a report of wrong chunks for documents with Windows line endings and found that offsets were computed on text with the carriage returns removed.
body:
A user sent a file with CRLF line endings and said the chunks had text that did not match the source offsets, and that the lossless check they wrote failed.

I reproduced it with a small file converted by unix2dos. The parser normalizes nothing, but my source style code, added in 1.7.0, split the source into lines with a regex on a plain newline and trimmed trailing whitespace, which removed the carriage return from the end of each line. The offsets after that were off by one per line.

The effect grows with the file. At line 100 the slice started 100 characters too early, and the first chunk looked right, which is why my tests, with LF only fixtures, never found it.

I fixed it in two steps. First, the line split now uses a regex for CRLF, CR and LF and keeps the separator. Second, the trim touches only spaces and tabs.

Then I made all test fixtures run in both forms: a helper converts each fixture to CRLF and checks that the chunks, converted back to LF, equal the LF result. That gave 3 more failures in other places, all in the table code, which joined rows with a newline. They use the original separator now.

The lossless script now has a CRLF mode too. All 41 fixtures pass in both modes.

One question stays open: should the chunk text keep CRLF? I think yes, since the promise is that joined chunks equal the source. I wrote that in the docs.

A patch release 2.1.1 is next. I replied to the reporter with the cause and asked for the file to test the fix.

summary: Found that offsets for documents with Windows line endings were computed on text with carriage returns removed, so slices were shifted by one character per line.
body:
A user sent a document with CRLF line endings where chunks started a few characters too late and sometimes cut a word. I reproduced it with a small file and a loop that compared each chunk to the source slice at its reported offset. The first chunk matched, and each later one was shifted by the number of lines before it. That is the signature of an offset calculation made on text without the carriage returns.

The cause was in the input step. The splitter normalized line endings to LF before parsing, which is fine for the syntax tree, but the offsets in the chunk meta were then reported against the normalized text. The source slice used by the lossless check was taken from the original text, so the two disagreed. The lossless script had passed so far because all its fixtures use LF.

I considered normalizing and keeping a map from normalized to original positions. That is more code and a new place for bugs. The simpler fix was to stop normalizing and let the parser handle CRLF, since remark already reads it correctly, and to fix the two places in our own code that searched for a plain newline character. One of them was the code that finds blank lines in the html fallback. I added CRLF copies of five fixtures to the test set, and the lossless script now runs every fixture in both line ending styles. All pass, and the text of each chunk keeps its original CRLF. Lone carriage returns from old Mac files were not tested, and I left a note in the issue.

summary: Measured how chunkdown behaves on a 40 MB generated file after a user asked about limits, and found the parse step dominates memory, not the splitter.
body:
A user asked if there is a size beyond which chunkdown should not be used. I generated a 40 MB Markdown file from the docs repeated with changed headings and measured with the normal splitter and the stream.

The normal splitter took 6.1 seconds and a peak of 1.9 GB of memory. The stream took 5.4 seconds and 1.6 GB. That is not the saving I expected from a stream, and my README table says the stream uses a fraction of the memory.

The README table was measured on a 9 MB file, where the difference was larger. So I looked at where the memory goes. A heap snapshot showed the syntax tree of the whole file, with position data on every node. The stream still parses the entire document before it yields the first chunk.

This is the truth about the design: the stream is streaming in output only, not in input. For true low memory the input has to be cut into pieces before parsing, for example at top-level headings, which is what the recipe from the size callback issue does by hand.

I tested a cut at blank lines outside of code fences as a prototype. On the 40 MB file the peak went down to 210 MB and the time to 4.2 seconds. The risk is that cutting at a blank line may split a list or a table, or a fenced block with blank lines inside, so the cut must know about fences. Reference definitions at the end of the file also point to links in earlier parts.

The prototype handles fences but not references, so the output differs from the normal one on 3 of my 30 fixtures. I will not ship it as it is.

For now I corrected the README, which said the stream saves memory in general. It now says that the output is streamed and the input is parsed whole, with the numbers above, and points to the section recipe for very large files.

summary: Wrote the regression tests and a changeset for the CRLF offset fix and checked that the 40 MB file run was not slower after dropping the normalization step.
body:
Late in the evening I finished the CRLF work from earlier in the day. The test set now has a helper that converts any fixture to CRLF and runs the same assertions, so new fixtures get both styles without extra work. I also added a case with mixed endings in one file, which the parser accepts and the offsets handle correctly.

Because the normalization step was removed, I ran the 40 MB generated file again to see if timing or memory changed. The time went down by about three percent and memory was the same within noise, which fits the earlier finding that parsing dominates. I wrote a patch changeset that says offsets are now correct for CRLF input, and credited the reporter. The release is planned together with the next patch, and the issue got a comment with the fix and the one remaining case of lone carriage returns.

summary: Checked a pull request that adds a Japanese sentence segmenter option for overlap and asked for tests and for use of Intl.Segmenter with a locale instead of a custom regex.
body:
The pull request is from a new contributor. It adds a regex for the Japanese full stop and question marks, used when the overlap is cut at a sentence border.

The idea is good, since Japanese text has no spaces and my first version cut it at arbitrary places. But Intl.Segmenter already handles it with a locale, and I do not want to keep regexes for each script.

I asked them to add a locale option passed to Intl.Segmenter, with a test for Japanese and one for Chinese, and said I would merge it then. I also thanked them for the sample text, which is useful as a fixture.

summary: Merged the locale pull request after changes and found that the default locale made overlap results depend on the machine, so the default is now fixed to undefined-locale rules.
body:
The author updated the pull request the same morning: a segmenterLocale option, two tests, and the docs line. The code was clean.

When I ran the test suite on my machine and in CI, one test differed. The test for an English paragraph with 'e.g.' passed locally and failed in CI. The reason was that Intl.Segmenter was created without a locale, which takes the system default, and CI has a different default than my laptop.

This is a real problem for a library that people use for indexing. The same document should give the same chunks on any machine. I checked what the segmenter gives for 'und', the undetermined locale, and it gave the same results as English for my samples.

So the default is now 'und' explicitly. A user who wants Japanese rules gives segmenterLocale: 'ja'.

I also found the same issue in my own earlier code for the overlap. It created the segmenter without a locale, so every 2.1 user has system-dependent overlap. For English text the difference is tiny, and I could find a difference on only one of my fixtures, but it is a bug.

I wrote a test that sets different default locales through the environment variable LANG for a child process and compares the output. It uses a small script, since Node reads the locale when it starts.

I then merged the pull request into main and put the fix on top as a second commit, with the author credited in the changeset. I wrote a comment in the pull request that explains why I changed their default and thanked them.

A patch release, 2.1.2, will have the locale option and the fix. I will say in the notes that overlap borders may change for users whose system language was not English.

summary: Released 2.1.2 with segmenterLocale and the deterministic default, after the tarball test and a check of the credits in the changelog.
body:
I ran the complete test suite, which is 268 tests, then the tarball test with the exported name check. All passed.

The changelog lists the new option with the contributor's name and a link to the pull request. The second entry describes the default locale fix, and I wrote it as a fix, not as a feature, with the note that overlap borders may change for some users.

I published it through CI, then checked the latest tag and installed the package in a clean folder. I ran the Japanese example from the pull request and got sentence borders at the full stops, as expected.

The LANG test runs on both Linux in CI and my Mac. It uses three locales, en_US, de_DE and ja_JP, and the three outputs are equal.

I added the contributor to the thanks section of the README, since this was their first merged pull request, and I invited them to look at the other open issues if they like.

After the release I looked at the issue list again. The HTML, typing, search, lockfile, CRLF and overlap topics are closed. What remains is the input-side streaming issue and a few questions.

I decided to give the input-side streaming a proper design next, since it is the only thing that made a claim in the README false until I corrected it, and two users asked about it.

summary: Started the design of input-side streaming and found that a cut at top-level nodes needs a first scan for reference definitions, which costs one cheap pass over the text.
body:
I wrote down the problem first: parse the document in parts so that memory stays low, but give the same chunks as a whole-document parse.

Three things can depend on the whole document. Reference definitions, which can be anywhere and are used by links in any part. Footnote definitions, the same. And the list numbering and tight or loose state of a list, which stays within one list if I never cut inside a list.

A first scan could find the safe cut points. I tried a line scanner that tracks fence state, and at the same time collects lines that look like definitions with a regex. On the 40 MB file this scan took 0.3 seconds and little memory, since it keeps only the definition lines.

The parts are then parsed with the collected definitions prepended, so that links resolve, but the prepended text is removed from the output positions. This is the part I like least, since it means a fake prefix, but remark has an option to pass definitions as extra data in the tree and I want to see if that avoids it.

I tried the quick version with the prefix on 10 fixtures that have references. Eight were equal to the normal result. Two differed in the appended definitions field of chunks, which lists the definitions used in a chunk. In the part-wise run, the field also listed definitions from other parts that were not used in that chunk.

The cause is that I take the list of used definitions from the part's tree, and the prepended text is in every part. I need to filter by the links that really occur in the chunk text, which the normal code already does, but it ran before the prefix was added in my prototype.

Nothing is ready to ship. Tomorrow I try the tree data approach, and if it also fails I will limit the first version to documents without reference definitions, and fall back to the whole parse when the scan finds some.

summary: Built the first-scan pass for input-side streaming: it collects reference definitions in one cheap pass so links resolve when a chunk is cut at a top-level node.
body:
The design from five days ago said a cut at top-level nodes needs the reference definitions known before the first chunk is emitted. I wrote src/stream/scan.ts today. It reads the input line by line, matches definition lines with the same rule remark uses, and stores label, url and title in a Map keyed by the normalized label.

The first version treated every line starting with a bracket as a definition and wrongly caught lines inside fenced code blocks. I added a small state machine that tracks open fences, with both backtick and tilde fences and the rule that the closing fence must be at least as long as the opening one. After that the scan agreed with the full parse on all 31 fixtures.

I also checked indented code. A line indented by four spaces is code and not a definition, unless it continues a paragraph. The paragraph case is a lazy continuation and it cannot hold a definition, so I skip it too. One fixture from a real wiki export covers this and it passes.

Memory was the point of the feature, so I measured. On the 40 MB generated file the scan keeps only the definitions, about 2 MB for the Map in the worst fixture, and the pass takes roughly 0.4 seconds. That is small against the parse cost per segment.

The open question is what to do when a definition appears twice with the same label. Markdown says the first one wins, so the Map keeps the first and ignores later ones. I wrote a test for it.

Next step is feeding the Map into the per-segment parse so links in later chunks resolve. I have not started that. I also still have to decide how the stream API accepts input, either an async iterable of strings or a Node readable. Chunk boundaries inside the input must not matter for the scan, so I will test it with input fed one character at a time.

summary: Fed the collected reference definitions into the per-segment parse, so reference links in later chunks of a streamed document resolve like in a full parse.
body:
Yesterday's scan produces a Map of definitions. Today I made the segment parser use it by appending synthetic definition lines at the end of each segment before parsing. The appended lines are removed from the tree again, so offsets and chunk text are unchanged.

First I tried to inject the definitions as tree nodes after the parse, but remark resolves references during parsing, so that did not work. The appended text approach is crude but it works and costs little. To keep the cost low, I append only the definitions whose label appears in the segment, found with a cheap regex over the segment for bracketed labels.

The test compares the streamed result and the normal result on the whole fixture set. 30 of 31 are identical. The failing one has a link reference whose label contains an escaped bracket, and my label regex missed it. I fixed the regex to allow backslash escapes and the fixture passes.

I also ran the one-character-at-a-time input test I planned. The scan result is the same as with a single string, so the boundaries do not matter.

Left for next time: the input type of the stream function, and what happens with a definition that sits after the last reference when the segment is already emitted. Since the scan runs first, this works, but the docs must say that the first pass needs the whole input to be readable twice or buffered. That is a real limit and I want to be honest about it in the README.

summary: Decided the input-side stream takes an async iterable of strings and spills to a temp file for the second pass, instead of requiring a seekable source.
body:
The two-pass design needs the input twice. I looked at three options: require a function that returns a fresh stream, buffer everything in memory, or spill to a temp file during the first pass. Buffering defeats the purpose of the feature, and a factory function is awkward for people who pipe from stdin.

I chose the spill. The first pass writes the text to a file in os.tmpdir() while scanning, and the second pass reads it back. The file is removed in a finally block, also when the consumer stops iterating early. I added a test for the early stop and for an error thrown in the middle.

An option, tmpDir, lets users change the location. If the source is already a file path, the temp copy is skipped and the file is read twice. The API decision is written into the docs draft, and the implementation comes next.

summary: Implemented streamChunks for input streams with the temp file spill, and found that multi-byte characters split across reads corrupted offsets until a decoder was kept.
body:
I implemented the input-side stream today using the design from the last entry. The function takes an async iterable of strings or buffers, writes to the temp file during the scan, then reads the file back in segments cut at top-level nodes.

The first test with a real Japanese document failed. Chunks contained the replacement character at some borders. The cause was that I converted each buffer to a string separately, so a three-byte character cut by a read boundary was broken. The fix is one StringDecoder kept for the whole input, which holds back incomplete bytes until the next read.

After that came the offsets. They are counted in UTF-16 units to match the existing slices of the non-streaming API. I count them while decoding, not from the file size in bytes. A test with emoji, which take two units, checks that slice(source, start, end) returns the chunk text exactly.

I then compared against the normal splitter on all fixtures. 31 of 31 give identical chunks and identical meta, with one exception that I accepted: the overlapBefore tail at the very first chunk is empty in both, so that is not a difference after all.

Peak memory on the 40 MB file went from about 1.1 GB to about 180 MB, with a segment size of 1 MB. Time went up by about 15 percent because of the file round trip. That is a fair price and I will state both numbers in the docs.

Still open: a single top-level node bigger than the segment size, such as a giant table. The segment grows to hold it. I wrote down that this is a known limit and did not try to solve it today. Next is the CLI, which should read stdin through this function.

summary: Wired the CLI to read stdin through the new streaming function, so piping a large file no longer loads it whole into memory.
body:
The CLI used to read all of stdin into a string and then call split. I changed it to pass process.stdin to streamChunks and write each chunk as one JSON line as soon as it is ready.

The output format for the default mode is a JSON array, which needs a closing bracket at the end. I kept the array but write the commas as chunks arrive, so the output starts early and is still valid JSON at the end. If the run fails halfway, the array stays unclosed, which I think is acceptable because the exit code is nonzero.

I tested with a 40 MB file piped in. Memory stayed under 200 MB and the first chunk appeared after about half a second. The table-driven alias test still passes.

One small find: --format ndjson was already in the help text but ignored when reading a file path. I fixed that at the same time.

summary: Wrote the tests and docs for input streaming, including the limit for oversized top-level nodes, and prepared a changeset for a minor release.
body:
Most of today went into the tests that I had postponed. I added a suite for streamChunks with these cases: input fed one character at a time, input with multi-byte characters across reads, early stop by the consumer, an error from the source, an empty input and an input with only definitions.

The empty input case revealed a bug. With no text the scan produced no file, and the cleanup tried to delete a path that did not exist, which threw ENOENT. I made the delete tolerant of a missing file and added the test.

The docs page now has a section called streaming input. It shows an example reading from fs.createReadStream and one from a fetch response body. It lists the numbers I measured: 180 MB peak against 1.1 GB, and 15 percent more time. It also states the limit that one very large top-level node is held in memory whole.

I added a changeset marked minor, since this is a new function and no breaking change. The README feature list got one line.

One point I could not settle: the name of the tmpDir option. A user might expect it to be a cache directory. I kept tmpDir because it says what it is.

Tomorrow I plan the tarball test and look at the type exports, because the last release missed some.

summary: Reviewed the first full run of input streaming on a 1.2 GB generated file and found the temp file spill was fine but the first-scan pass held every reference definition in memory.
body:
After the CLI change of the last entry I wanted to know how input streaming behaves far beyond the 40 MB case from earlier. I generated a 1.2 GB Markdown file from the fixtures, repeated with changed headings, and piped it through the CLI on the laptop. Peak memory stayed around 180 MB for the segment parser, which is what the design promised.

The temp file spill worked as planned. The first pass wrote about 1.2 GB to the temp directory and the second pass read it back in 64 KB reads, and the temp file was deleted on success. I also killed the process halfway with a signal and found the file left behind, so a cleanup handler now removes it on exit and on SIGINT.

The surprise was the first-scan pass. The generated file had about 900,000 reference definitions, because I had repeated a document that uses many of them, and the map holding them grew to 310 MB. That is the real peak, not the parser. A real document will almost never have that many, but a user with a link-heavy wiki export could hit it.

I considered three options: store only the definitions that are actually used, which needs a second scan to know; store them on disk in a small index; or document a limit. The first one defeats the single cheap pass. The second adds a dependency on a file format for little gain. I chose to keep the map, lowercase the labels once, and store only the URL and the title as one string instead of an object, which cut the map to 140 MB in the same test.

I added a test with 200,000 definitions that checks the chunks are identical to the normal split and that the heap stays under a fixed number. The test takes four seconds, so I put it in the slow group that runs only in CI on the main branch. Still open: write the memory numbers into the streaming docs next to the oversized node limit, and decide whether a warning above a million definitions makes sense.

summary: Checked streaming input with Windows line endings and found the scan and the segment parser agreed on offsets, so no change was needed.
body:
After the CRLF offset bug from earlier I wanted to be sure the new path was safe. I made a fixture with CRLF endings and one with mixed endings, then ran both through streamChunks and through the normal split.

The chunks and offsets are identical in both modes. The scan does not strip carriage returns, since it works on the decoded text and only matches line starts. The definition regex tolerates a trailing carriage return.

I added both fixtures to the suite as permanent tests. One more check: a carriage return alone at a read border, with the newline coming in the next read. The scan treated that correctly because it joins the text before splitting lines. Nothing to fix, so the release can go on.

summary: Released 2.2.0 with input streaming after the tarball test, then answered an issue asking for a browser build and decided the stream function stays Node only.
body:
I ran the release flow: changeset version, a last tarball install in a clean folder, the publish and a check of the latest tag. The npm page shows 2.2.0 and the changelog lists streamChunks, the tmpDir option and the CLI stdin change.

A new issue came in the same afternoon. The reporter uses chunkdown in a browser worker and asked whether streamChunks can work there. It cannot as written, because it uses fs and os for the temp file.

I thought about splitting the function into a core and a Node adapter. The core would take a source that can be read twice, for example a Blob, which browsers can slice. That is a good design, but it is more work than the issue justifies today. The normal split function already works in the browser, as the bundle has no Node imports, and I confirmed this by bundling it with esbuild for the browser target without errors.

My answer in the issue: the normal split is browser safe, the stream function is Node only for now, and a Blob based core is possible later. I asked the reporter about the size of their documents, because if they are under a few MB the normal path is fine and fast.

I added a note to the docs under streaming input saying that it needs Node. I also added an exports condition check to make sure the browser bundle does not pull in the stream module by accident. That check found nothing wrong.

The reporter has not answered yet. I labeled the issue as enhancement and left it open.

summary: Started the work on the Blob based core for streaming after the reporter wrote back with 200 MB documents, and defined the source interface that Node and browser share.
body:
The reporter answered that their documents reach 200 MB, so the normal path is too heavy for a worker. That moves the Blob idea from later to now.

I defined a small interface called RereadableSource with one method, open(), which returns an async iterable of strings. The first pass calls open(), the second pass calls it again. The Node adapter implements it for the temp file spill. A new Blob adapter implements it by slicing the blob and decoding with a TextDecoder in stream mode.

I moved the scan and the segment loop into src/stream/core.ts, which imports nothing from Node. The Node file now only builds the source and calls the core. This was mostly moving code, and the existing 31 fixture comparison still passes after the move, which gave me confidence.

The decoder for the Blob adapter needed care. TextDecoder with the stream option true holds incomplete bytes, like StringDecoder does. I wrote the same multi-byte test for it with a Japanese fixture and slices of 7 bytes, and it passes.

One problem: the Blob slice approach reads the blob twice, which is fine, but a File from an input element can change while reading. That is outside my control, so I will only document it.

I checked bundle size. The browser entry grew by 3.1 KB minified, mostly the core. That is acceptable.

What remains: export a streamBlob function, test it in a real browser environment and write docs. Vitest has a browser mode, but for now I will use the jsdom-free Node Blob, which exists since Node 18 and has the same slice API. A true browser test can come after.

summary: Added streamBlob on top of the shared core and tested it with the Node Blob class, with the same 31 fixtures giving identical chunks as the normal split.
body:
With the interface from earlier this morning, streamBlob was short: it wraps a Blob in the Blob source and calls the core. I exported it from a separate entry point, chunkdown/browser, so that Node users do not need it and the browser bundle does not need fs.

The package exports map got a new condition. I tested that import from chunkdown/browser resolves in Node, in esbuild with the browser platform and in the type checker. The first try failed in the type checker because the types field was missing for the subpath, and I added it.

The fixture comparison runs each document through the normal split, streamChunks and streamBlob. All 31 give identical results in all three. I also ran a 60 MB generated file through streamBlob. Peak memory in Node was 150 MB, similar to the file based path, and it needed no temp file.

One difference: streamBlob has no tmpDir option and no cleanup, because nothing is written. Its options type is therefore smaller, and I made it a separate type rather than a union.

Next: a real browser run. I will write a tiny page and run it with Playwright, which is already in the dev tools for the docs site.

summary: Ran streamBlob in a real browser through Playwright with a 200 MB file and found it works, but the main thread froze, so the docs now recommend a worker.
body:
I wrote a small test page that takes a file from an input and prints the number of chunks and the time. Playwright opened it in Chromium and set the file with a 200 MB generated document.

StreamBlob finished, with 61,000 chunks, in about 38 seconds. Memory in the tab stayed near 400 MB at the peak, which is more than in Node but far below what the normal split would need. The result was correct: the chunk count matches the Node run on the same file.

The page froze during the run, because the work is CPU bound and ran on the main thread. The async iterable yields between reads, but the parse of each segment blocks. This is expected, but it should be written down. I added a docs section with a worker example of about 15 lines, posting chunks back in batches of 500.

I also tried a smaller segment size, 256 KB instead of 1 MB. It reduced the longest block to about 40 ms but made the total time 20 percent longer. I left the default and documented the segmentSize option as a trade.

I did not add the Playwright test to CI, because it needs a browser download and the file is big. A small 5 MB variant runs in the normal Vitest suite on Node instead.

Next is a patch release, and a reply to the issue with the numbers.

summary: Looked through the first issues after 2.3.0 and confirmed that two reports were the same bug: a table inside a list item was cut without its header row repeated.
body:
Three issues had come in since the Blob release, and I read them one after the other before choosing anything. The first asked for a way to skip front matter in the CLI output. That already exists as an option, so I answered with the flag name and a link to the docs page, and the reporter had missed it because the page was listed under a different heading.

The second and third reports looked different but had the same cause. Both described a table inside a list item that was split by rows, and the continuation chunks had no header row. I reproduced it with a small document of one bullet with an indented table of 40 rows and a limit of 300 characters. The first chunk had the header, the later ones started directly with data rows.

The cause was in the table splitter. It finds the header by looking at the parent of the table and expects a root node, but inside a list item the parent is the item, and the check failed quietly and returned the rows without the header. Top-level tables passed every fixture, which is why the tests never saw it. The fix is to take the header from the table node itself and not from its position.

I wrote the failing test first with the document from the reports, then changed the splitter and the test passed. I also added a case with a table inside a blockquote, which had the same problem and was not reported yet. Running all 31 fixtures and the streaming tests gave no other change. One question remains: repeated headers inside a list item should keep the indentation of the item, so the chunk text stays valid Markdown, and I have not checked that yet. I left the issues open with a comment and will close them with the patch release after that check.

summary: Triaged the issue list after 2.3.0 and picked a report about nested lists losing their indentation in chunk text as the next fix, since it breaks the lossless promise.
body:
Three new issues arrived over the last days. One asks for a heading path in the meta, such as Guide > Install > Linux. One reports a typo in the German docs example. The third says that chunk text for nested lists loses indentation when a list is split in the middle.

The third one matters most, because chunk text is supposed to equal the source slice exactly. I reproduced it with the reporter's snippet: a list with three levels, limit 200 characters. The second chunk started with the item text but without its leading spaces, so the nesting looked flat when the chunks were rendered alone.

Looking at the code, the splitter takes the start offset from the position of the first node in the chunk. For a list item, remark gives the position of the content, which begins after the bullet marker, not at the line start. The first chunk is fine because the document start is a line start. Later chunks use the item position directly.

The fix idea is to move the start back to the beginning of the line when the text before it on that line is only whitespace and a list marker. I need to decide if the marker should be part of the chunk. I think yes, because a chunk starting with a bullet is clearer.

I wrote a failing test with the reporter's example first. The heading path request I answered with a short note that it is planned, and I put it on the list after this fix. The typo I fixed directly in the docs.

summary: Fixed the list item start offset so chunks begin at the line start with indentation and marker, and checked the change against all fixtures for side effects.
body:
I implemented the idea from this morning. A helper, lineStartIfOnlyMarker, looks at the source text between the line start and the node start. If it contains only spaces, tabs, a list marker or a blockquote marker, the start moves back to the line start.

The reporter's test passes now. Then I ran the full fixture set and saw two other tests fail. Both had lists inside blockquotes, and the move to the line start pulled in the quote marker at the start of the line, which then appeared twice, once from the previous chunk's end and once at the new start. That was not wrong in the text sense, because the source does have the marker there, but the previous chunk's end offset was also off by the same prefix.

The root cause was that the end offset of the previous chunk was the end of its last node, while the new start went before the next node's content. The gap between them held only markers and whitespace, and the lossless check expects chunks to cover the source with no gaps except between blocks. I decided that the gap now belongs to the next chunk. With that rule the two tests pass again and the concatenation check still holds.

I added three new fixtures: nested ordered lists, a list in a blockquote, and a task list with checkboxes. All pass. A run on the 40 MB file showed no change in speed.

A changeset marked patch is written. The one risk is that users who stored old chunk text will see differences after upgrading, so I will mention that in the changelog.

summary: Released 2.3.1 with the list indentation fix and started the heading path feature by writing down three possible shapes for the meta field.
body:
The release of 2.3.1 went through the usual steps: version, tarball test, publish, check of the latest tag. The changelog line says that chunk text for split lists now keeps its indentation and marker, and warns that stored chunks of older versions may differ. I answered the reporter, who confirmed the fix on their documents.

Then I turned to the heading path request. The user wants to know which headings a chunk sits under, so that a retrieval system can show or embed the path. The data is already available inside the splitter, since the heading rule and minSize use the heading stack.

I wrote down three shapes. One is meta.headings as an array of strings, which is simple. Another is an array of objects with depth, text and offset, which allows links back to the source. The third is a single joined string with a separator, which is the least flexible. I prefer the object array because the cost is small and the string case can be built from it.

There is a question about headings inside the chunk itself. If a chunk contains a heading, should the path include it? I think the path is the context before the chunk starts, so a heading inside the chunk is not in the path. That keeps the field from repeating text that is already in the chunk, but it may surprise some people, so I will give an example in the docs.

I also checked the streaming splitter. It keeps the heading stack across segments already, so the feature should work in both modes. A test comparing both will go in first.

summary: Wrote the failing tests for meta.headings in both the normal and the streaming splitter, using four fixtures with skipped heading levels.
body:
I wrote the tests before the code. Four fixtures cover a normal nested document, a document that jumps from level one to level three, a document that starts with text before any heading, and one with two headings of the same level in a row.

Expected results: a chunk before any heading has an empty array. A skipped level just lists the headings that exist, without filling the gap. A same level heading replaces the previous one on the stack.

I wrote each expectation by hand from the fixture text. The same expectations are used for the streaming splitter through a shared test helper. All tests fail now with undefined, as intended. Implementation is next.

summary: Implemented meta.headings with depth, text and offset, and found that heading text with inline code or links needed plain text extraction rather than the raw source.
body:
The stack already existed, so the implementation was to copy it into the meta when a chunk is closed. I store each entry as depth, text and offset, where offset is the start of the heading line in the source.

The text was my first problem. I took the heading source and got things like the hash marks and link syntax in it. A heading such as ## Using `split()` with [options](#opts) gave the raw markdown. For a path used in retrieval, plain text is better: Using split() with options. I used mdast-util-to-string on the heading node, which does that.

The four fixtures pass in the normal splitter. In the streaming splitter three pass and one fails: the case with text before any heading. In streaming, the stack is initialized as undefined, not an empty array, so the first chunk got no field. I changed the initial value and it passes.

I also checked that the array is a copy for each chunk. At first all chunks shared one array that was mutated later, so earlier chunks showed later headings. A test that holds the first chunk and reads it after splitting the whole document caught it. The fix is a slice at closing time.

The type for Chunk is updated: headings is always present, and the generic meta type stays untouched. Docs and an example remain, as well as a decision on whether the CLI prints the field in its default output. I think it should, since the output is JSON anyway.

summary: Finished docs and CLI output for meta.headings, then measured the cost and found a 3 percent slowdown that comes from copying the stack for every chunk.
body:
I documented the field in the API page with a short example document and the chunks it produces, including the case of a heading inside the chunk that is not in its own path. A second example shows how to build a joined string, headings.map(h => h.text).join(' > '), for people who want that form.

The CLI now prints the field in the JSON output. The text format is unchanged, because it prints only chunk text with separators, and I did not want to change that for people who pipe it.

Then I measured. On a 12 MB document with many small chunks the run went from 2.41 seconds to 2.49 seconds, about 3 percent. A profile showed the stack copy and the to-string call for each heading. The to-string work happens once per heading, but I was calling it once per chunk. I cached the plain text on the stack entry when the heading is pushed.

After the cache the difference is about 1 percent, which is within the noise of repeated runs. I ran each variant five times and compared the medians.

There is one more thing I checked, the interaction with minSize. When two chunks are merged, the merged chunk should have the path of the first one, because the path describes the context at its start. I wrote a test for that and it passed without changes, since the merge keeps the first chunk's meta.

One case is unclear: a merge of chunks across a heading of a lower level. The merged chunk then contains a heading inside, which fits my rule. I added it as a fixture so the behaviour is fixed.

A changeset marked minor is ready. I will do the tarball test tomorrow morning, along with a look at how to answer the German docs issue, whose reporter offered to translate more pages.

summary: Ran the tarball test for 2.4.0 and released it with meta.headings, after checking that the new field appears in the types and in the CLI output of the installed package.
body:
The tarball test this morning installed the pack into a clean project. I wrote a small script that splits a document and prints the headings field, and a type test that reads chunk.headings[0].depth. Both worked on the first try, and the export test from the earlier fix also passed.

The CLI check used the installed bin through npx, with a pipe on stdin. The JSON lines include headings, and the executable bit is still set after the postbuild change.

Then the publish. I looked at the npm page, the latest tag and the changelog. The changelog names the feature and shows a three line example. One thing I corrected before publishing was the line about the stored chunks, which belonged to 2.3.1 and was repeated here by mistake.

The issue author who asked for the path got a comment with the release number and a link to the docs example. I closed the issue after they confirmed it fits their use.

For the German docs offer I wrote a reply that thanks the reporter and asks them to start with one page, the getting started page, as a pull request. I also described where the translation files should go, since the docs site has no locale folder yet and I have not decided on the structure.

That last point I put on the list for the afternoon.

summary: Set up the locale folder structure in the docs site so that translated pages can be contributed, and wrote a short contributing note for translators.
body:
The docs site had no support for more than one language. I looked at what the generator offers and chose its built-in i18n option, with English as the default at the root and German under /de/. Pages without a translation fall back to English, so a partial translation does not produce broken links.

I created docs/de/ with a single placeholder page, so that the folder and the sidebar entry exist. The navigation shows a language switch only when more than one locale has content, which avoids an empty switcher for now.

The search plugin config from the dot tokenizer fix needed a check. The custom tokenizer applies to all locales, so option names with dots are still found under /de/. I tested a search for segmenterLocale and one for minSize on the built site, and both returned results.

I added a section to CONTRIBUTING.md for translations: keep code blocks and option names untranslated, copy the front matter, and open one pull request per page. I did not add a rule about review, because I cannot judge German docs myself and I will rely on the contributor and on a second reader if one shows up.

I posted the structure in the issue so the reporter can begin. Left for later: a CI check that reports pages whose English source changed after the translation.

summary: Started the docs translation effort by testing the locale folder with a first Spanish page, and found that the search index mixed languages until each locale got its own index.
body:
After the locale folder structure from this afternoon, I translated the getting-started page into Spanish as a trial. The page built and showed up under /es/, but the search box returned English hits on the Spanish page and the other way round.

The cause was the search plugin building a single index for the whole site. I switched to one index per locale in the plugin config and added a language field to the tokenizer settings, so the custom tokenizer for option names with dots is still used in each locale.

I also checked the sidebar. Untranslated pages fell back to English without a notice, which would confuse readers. I added a small banner component that shows when a page is a fallback, with a link to the contributing note.

The code samples stay in English on purpose, but comments inside them are translatable. I wrote that rule into the translators' note. Link checking in CI failed for two anchors because Spanish headings produce different slugs, so I added explicit heading ids to the page.

Left for next: a script that lists pages whose English source changed after the translation, so stale pages can be flagged.

summary: Wrote a small script that compares the English source of each docs page with its translation and lists the translations that are out of date.
body:
The script reads the git log for each file under docs/en and for the matching file in each locale folder. If the English file has a newer commit than the translation, the page is listed as stale.

I first tried comparing file modification times, but a fresh checkout in CI sets them all to the same value, so that was useless. The git commit time works in CI as long as the checkout is not shallow, so I set fetch-depth to 0 in the docs workflow.

The output is a plain list, one line per page and locale. For now it only prints a warning and does not fail the build, since the Spanish page is the only translation.

summary: Found that the docs script comparing English pages with translations missed pages whose English source changed only in code samples, so the freshness check now hashes the whole file.
body: The out-of-date script from the translation work compared the heading text and the paragraph count of each English page with its translation. A test run on the Spanish page showed it reported the page as current even though the English page had gained a new option in a code sample. The code blocks were not part of the comparison at all, which was the gap. I changed the script to store a hash of the English source file in a small comment at the top of each translated page. The script now compares that stored hash with the hash of the current English file and lists every page where they differ. The first run listed 14 pages, which matched what git history showed as changed since the Spanish page was started. A translator can update the hash after reviewing a change, so a typo fix in English does not force a full rewrite. I also added a flag --ignore-whitespace so that reformatting alone does not count as a change. What is left is to run the script in CI as a warning, not a failure, so contributors are not blocked.

summary: Investigated a report of duplicate text at chunk borders with overlap and a table split by rows, and found the repeated header row was counted as overlap too.
body:
The issue came with a document where a large table was cut into three chunks and each later chunk started with the header row twice. I reproduced it with the sample file and overlap set to 200.

The table splitter prepends the header to every chunk after the first. The overlap step then took the tail of the previous chunk, which ended with table rows, and glued it in front, and the header was added on top of that. So the order of the two steps was wrong for tables.

I looked at three ways to fix it. One was to disable overlap inside tables, which loses context. Another was to apply overlap first and then add the header only if the chunk does not start with it. The third was to make the overlap aware of rows and take whole rows only.

I chose the third because it also fixes a smaller problem I saw: overlap cut a row in the middle of a cell. Overlap for table chunks now takes the last complete rows that fit in the overlap size, and the header is added once after that.

The size limit has to include the header and the overlap rows. In one fixture this made a chunk three characters too long, so the row selection now subtracts the header length first.

The 31 fixtures still pass, and the reporter's file now gives clean chunks. I did not write the new tests yet; that is next, plus a changeset.

summary: Wrote regression tests and a patch changeset for the table overlap fix, including a case where the header alone is larger than the overlap.
body:
I added four tests in the table suite. The first uses the reporter's document and asserts that each chunk has exactly one header row. The second checks that overlap takes only complete rows. The third covers a table with one very wide row, where no row fits into the overlap and so the overlap is empty.

The fourth test was the awkward one: a header longer than the overlap size. The first version of the fix added the header and then went over maxSize by the header length. I changed the row selection so that it works from the remaining budget, and when the budget is negative it drops the overlap rows completely.

All tests pass and the fixtures give the same output as before except for the table with overlap. The changeset is a patch with a short description that mentions the issue number. I will release it together with the next fix.

summary: Drafted and tested the lossless-mode design for the next major version so users with stored embeddings can reproduce the old chunk boundaries, and found two defaults that must stay frozen.
body: The question from the major version discussion was how someone with stored embeddings can keep the old chunking exactly. I started by writing down which behaviours of the 2.x line change in the planned 3.0 API: the overlap defaults, the table header handling, the sentence level and the heading path. Then I wrote a legacy preset idea, a single option called compat with the value 2, that would pin every default to its 2.6 value. To test it I took the 31 fixtures plus the 3000 page wiki export from the footnote work and split them with the current release to make a golden set of chunk texts and offsets. Then I ran the prototype 3.0 branch of the code in compat mode against that golden set. 29 of the 31 fixtures matched byte for byte on the first run. The two differences came from the default overlap unit, which moved from characters to tokens in the new design, and from the sentence segmenter being used for overlap cuts by default. Both are now pinned by compat mode, and after that all 31 fixtures matched. The wiki export had 212 chunks that differed, and every one traced to the table overlap fix of 2.5.0, which changes output on purpose. That is a decision to document, since a user who wants the exact old chunks of a table with overlap cannot get them. I chose to keep the fix in compat mode and to say so clearly, because the old behaviour duplicated header text and was a bug. The golden set now lives in the repository as a test that runs against compat mode, so a later change cannot break the promise without a failing test. I wrote a draft of the migration page that explains compat, the codemod and the known difference for tables. The reporter with the embeddings was asked to try the prototype on their own corpus. The open point is whether compat should be removed in 4.0 or kept for good, and I left that for the discussion thread.

summary: Implemented the htmlSplit option with a line based splitter that avoids cutting inside an open tag, and covered it with tests on three real pages.
body:
The splitter now walks the lines of an html node and accumulates them until maxSize. Before it cuts, it counts unclosed angle brackets with a small scanner that skips quoted attribute values and comments.

The first version broke on a script block that contained the character '<' in a comparison. I made the scanner treat the content of script and style elements as opaque until the closing tag, and the test passes now.

I added fixtures from three saved pages: a blog post, a documentation page and a forum thread. For each the test checks that the chunks joined together equal the original, which is the lossless promise, and that no chunk is above maxSize unless a single line is longer. For one very long minified line the chunk is oversized and a warning is emitted, as for other oversized atoms.

The streaming splitter shares the same node splitting code, so it got the option for free. I ran the streaming test with the blog post and the chunks are the same as the normal run.

The docs got a section that says what the option does and does not do, with the note about unbalanced tags. The default stays 'none'. Next is the changeset as a minor release.

summary: Released 2.5.0 with the htmlSplit option and the table overlap fix after the tarball test.
body:
The changeset for the minor release combined the htmlSplit feature and the table overlap patch. I ran the version command and checked the generated changelog entry, then reworded the line for the overlap fix so that it names the issue.

The tarball test installed the packed file in an empty project and ran both the ESM and the CJS import. The htmlSplit option appeared in the types, and the CLI accepted the new flag --html-split.

Publishing went through the GitHub Action without trouble. I commented on both issues with the version number and closed them.

summary: Triaged a pull request that adds a Korean docs translation and found the contributor had edited the English source pages by mistake.
body:
The pull request had a good translation of five pages. But the diff also touched docs/en for three files, mostly whitespace changes caused by an editor that reformatted the Markdown tables.

The stale-page script from last week flagged the Korean pages as fresh and the English ones as changed, which made the pull request look odd. I asked the contributor to revert the English files and gave the Prettier setting we use, so that the formatting does not change again.

I also read through the translation with a translation tool as a rough check. Two terms were rendered in different ways on different pages, 'chunk' and 'overlap'. I suggested a small glossary file in the locale folder and offered to add the English terms to it.

The contributor answered within the hour and said they would fix both points. I will merge once the diff is clean.

summary: Added a glossary file mechanism for translators and a CI check that fails when a translated page lacks the heading ids of its English source.
body:
The glossary is a small YAML file in each locale folder that maps the English terms chunk, overlap, token and front matter to the preferred translation. It is only guidance for now, not enforced.

The heading id check is stricter. Anchors in links between pages break when a translated heading produces a different slug, which already happened with the Spanish page. The check reads the headings of the English page and the translation, and fails if the explicit ids differ.

Writing it I found that the Spanish page had one heading without an id that was still working because the slug happened to match. The check flagged it as a false positive, so I allowed a missing id when the English page also has none.

The check runs in the docs workflow after the build and takes under two seconds. I documented both things in the translators' note.

summary: Merged the Korean translation after cleanup and fixed a docs build failure caused by a locale code that the search plugin did not know.
body:
The contributor reverted the English files and the diff was clean, so I merged. The docs build then failed on main with an error from the search plugin: unsupported language 'ko'.

The plugin has a fixed list of languages for stemming. For Korean there is no stemmer, so the config needs to fall back to the plain tokenizer. I added a mapping in the docs config from locale to search language, with 'ko' mapped to the default, and kept the custom tokenizer that handles option names with dots.

After that the build passed. I tested the search in the built site with two Korean words and with the option name maxSize, and all three found the right pages.

The glossary file was missing for Korean, so I created it with the English terms and left the translations for the contributor to fill in. They agreed in the thread.

The sidebar showed the Korean pages in the language menu in the wrong order, because the menu is sorted by code. I made the order explicit in the config: English first, then the others by name.

summary: Answered a question on whether chunkdown can keep footnotes with the paragraph that references them, and wrote down what the current behaviour is.
body:
The user asked about footnotes in documents from a wiki export. I tested with a sample: footnote definitions are separate nodes at the end of the document, so they end up in the last chunk, far from the reference.

That is the same situation as reference links, which are solved only for parsing, not for chunk content. For footnotes the text in the chunk is lost for retrieval purposes because the number alone says nothing.

I replied that it is not supported and opened a feature issue to track an option that appends the needed footnote definitions to the chunk that references them. It would make chunks bigger, so it must count against maxSize.

summary: Prototyped the footnote option that appends referenced footnote definitions to a chunk, and found the size accounting needs a second pass because the footnotes change the chunk length.
body:
The prototype collects footnote definitions in a map during the first parse. For each chunk it finds footnoteReference nodes and appends the matching definitions after the text, separated by a blank line.

The problem is that adding the footnotes can push the chunk over maxSize, and the splitter has already decided where to cut. I tried reserving a fixed budget, which wasted space in documents with few footnotes.

The approach that worked better is to compute the footnote text per node during splitting, so the size of a paragraph includes the footnotes it references. A paragraph with a long footnote then gets cut earlier, which is correct.

The same footnote referenced from two paragraphs in one chunk is only appended once, and I added a test for that. A footnote that is longer than maxSize alone is a case I left open; for now it is truncated with a warning.

The lossless promise changes here: the chunk text is no longer a pure slice of the source. I will mark such chunks in meta with a field so users can tell. That and the streaming version are next.

summary: Added meta.appended for chunks with copied footnotes and made the streaming splitter collect footnote definitions in the first scan pass.
body:
Chunks that contain copied footnote text now have meta.appended set to the list of labels. Chunks without it keep the exact slice property, and the test for joined chunks equal to the source only runs on those.

For streaming the footnote definitions can be anywhere, mostly at the end, so the first scan pass has to collect them like the reference definitions. I extended the scan to match the footnote definition syntax and store the text.

The memory problem from the 1.2 GB run applies here too: the scan holds all definitions in memory. I added a cap of 50 MB of definitions in total, with an error message that names the option to turn the feature off.

On a generated file with 100000 footnotes the scan took 2.1 seconds more than before, which is acceptable. The normal and the streaming splitter gave identical chunks on all footnote fixtures.

Docs are still missing, as is the oversized footnote decision.

summary: Decided that a footnote longer than maxSize is kept whole in its own appended block with a warning, instead of being truncated.
body:
Truncating a footnote silently drops information, which is worse than an oversized chunk. The library already allows oversized atoms with a warning, so footnotes follow that rule now.

The change is small: the truncation code was removed and the size check allows the overrun for a single footnote, then emits the same warning object as for other oversized nodes, with the label of the footnote.

I updated the test that expected truncation. A second test checks that the following chunk is not affected by the oversized one.

The docs paragraph about limits mentions footnotes now. I also asked the issue reporter to try a branch build with their wiki export.

summary: The reporter tested the footnote build on a 3000 page wiki export and found 4 percent of chunks over the limit, which traced to nested footnote references.
body:
The reporter sent the result in the morning: most chunks were right, but 4 percent were above maxSize by a lot. They attached three examples.

All three had a footnote whose text itself contained a reference to another footnote. My code appended the first definition, but the second definition was appended after the size check, so it was not counted at all.

I wrote a failing test with a chain of three footnotes first. Then I changed the collection to be recursive: when a footnote is added, its own references are resolved and added too, with a set to avoid cycles. A footnote that refers to itself, which exists in the export, would otherwise loop forever.

The size now includes the whole chain. For the reporter's examples the chunks went back under the limit, apart from two with a single oversized footnote chain, which are reported as warnings by design.

I also found that the label order in meta.appended depended on insertion order in the set. It is now sorted in the order of first reference in the chunk, which is easier to reason about.

I ran the full fixtures and the streaming comparison again and both are clean. The reporter will try again with the new build tonight.

summary: Confirmed with the reporter that the footnote option works on the full wiki export, wrote the docs and the changeset, and released 2.6.0.
body:
The reporter's second run gave zero chunks over the limit except for the 11 with warnings, and they said retrieval quality on questions that depend on footnotes improved. That was the feedback I wanted before release.

The docs section explains the option name footnotes: 'append', what meta.appended means, and that such chunks are not pure slices of the source. I added a short example with input, the chunks and the meta. I also noted the cap on definitions for streaming.

The CLI got a flag --footnotes with the same values. Its help text is generated from the option list, and I checked the output.

The changeset describes a minor release. While reading the generated changelog I noticed the line for the earlier table fix had the wrong issue number, so I fixed it by hand.

The tarball test ran in a clean project, with ESM and CJS imports and a run of the CLI on a sample with footnotes. All passed.

The release went out from the Action. I closed the feature issue and thanked the reporter. One thing remains: the default is 'none', and I may want to revisit that in a major version.

summary: Looked into a report that footnote definitions were copied twice into chunks when two references sat in the same chunk, and traced it to the lookup that ran per reference instead of per chunk.
body: The reporter with the wiki export sent a small example where a chunk had two references to the same footnote and the appended block contained the definition twice. I reproduced it with a four paragraph document and the footnotes option switched on. The meta.appended field also listed the footnote id twice, so the bug was in the collection step and not in the rendering. The code walked the references in the chunk and pushed the matching definition for each one without checking whether it was already in the list. That also made the size accounting wrong, because the length of the copied text was counted two times and the chunk was split earlier than needed. I replaced the list with a Map keyed by the footnote label, which keeps the order of first reference. The second pass for size accounting now uses the Map, so the length is counted once. The streaming splitter shares the same helper, and its test with the same example passed after the change. On the 3000 page export the number of chunks dropped by 0.6 percent, which fits the wasted space that the duplicates took. No chunk went over maxSize in the run. I added two regression tests, one for the plain case and one where the repeated reference is in a nested footnote. The fix goes into the next patch release together with the open items from the list.

summary: Investigated slow splitting of documents with thousands of very short list items and found that the list splitter recomputed the size of the whole list for each item.
body:
