A user reported that a changelog file with 40000 list items took 38 seconds, while a similar size of paragraphs took under one second. I generated a similar file to reproduce it.

The profile showed most time in the function that measures a node. For a list node it concatenates all the items, and the splitter called it again after each item was added to the current chunk. That makes the work quadratic in the number of items.

The fix keeps a running size for the current chunk and adds the size of each item once. Item sizes are cached on the node in a WeakMap, so that a second measurement is free.

There was one subtlety. The separator between items is a newline for tight lists and a blank line for loose lists, so the running size must add the right separator. I wrote a test that compares the running size with a full measurement for both kinds.

After the change the 40000 item file took 0.9 seconds. Other fixtures were not slower; the large paragraph file went from 0.61 to 0.60 seconds, which is noise.

I looked for the same pattern in the table splitter and found it too, with rows. The table code already tracked a running size, so it was fine.

I also checked nested lists, where the item contains a list. The cache is per node, so the inner list size is reused when the outer item is measured. A deep fixture with six levels gave identical chunks before and after.

The changeset is a patch. I asked the reporter to try the build on their real file.

summary: Prepared the patch release notes for the duplicate footnote fix and checked the packed tarball, which showed the types file for meta.appended was missing one field.
body: I wrote a patch changeset for the footnote duplicate fix with a short description and an example of the input. Before the release I ran the tarball test, which installs the packed package into a clean folder and imports it. The import worked and the CLI printed the expected chunks for the example document. A check of the generated types showed that meta.appended was declared with only the label field, while the code also returns the character length of each block. I added the length field to the type in the source and rebuilt, and the type test now covers it. The docs page for footnotes had the same gap, so I added the field to the table there. I also checked that the changelog entry credits the reporter by name. The release itself waits for the other fix that is still in review.

summary: Reviewed a pull request that adds a 'sentence' split level between paragraph and words, and asked for the segmenter to be shared with the overlap code.
body:
The pull request adds a splitting step for paragraphs that are too big: first by sentence, then by words. Until now an oversized paragraph went to a word split directly, which cut sentences in the middle.

The idea is good and the tests are decent. But the contributor wrote a new regex for sentence ends, while the overlap code already uses Intl.Segmenter with segmenterLocale since 2.1.2. Two definitions of a sentence in one library would give different borders for the same text.

I asked them to reuse the segmenter helper and to respect the locale option. I also asked for a test with the abbreviation 'e.g.' and one with Japanese text, because those are where a regex fails.

A second point was the default. Changing the behaviour for all users is a change of results, so it must wait for a major version or sit behind an option. I suggested sentenceSplit: true as an option for now.

The contributor replied quickly and agreed to both. I also checked that the pull request does not touch the streaming splitter, and it does not need to, since the node splitting is shared.

summary: Merged the sentence split pull request after the contributor reused the shared segmenter, and found one more case where a sentence longer than maxSize fell through to word splitting twice.
body:
The updated pull request used the segmenter helper and had tests for the abbreviation and Japanese cases. Both passed on my machine and in CI.

Before merging I tried it on a few of my own fixtures with sentenceSplit enabled. One long paragraph with a single sentence of 3000 characters was split into words, as expected, but the word splitting ran again on the pieces and produced one extra empty chunk.

The cause was that the sentence level returned the whole sentence as a single piece when it did not fit, and the next level then received a piece that it treated as a new oversized node. I fixed it in a small follow up commit so that a single oversized sentence goes to the word level once.

I added a test for it and merged. The contributor is credited in the changeset. The option is documented with the note that the default stays off.

summary: Released 2.6.1 with the list performance fix and the sentence split option, and wrote a plan for what the next major version should change.
body:
The patch release contains the list size fix. The sentence split option is a feature, so the changeset made it a minor, which gave 2.7.0 instead. I corrected the changeset before running the version command.

The tarball test passed on ESM, CJS and the CLI. In the installed package I tried sentenceSplit on a small sample and it split by sentence as expected.

After the release I went through the issue list and the options that exist because of compatibility. There are three defaults I would change in a new major version: footnotes 'append' instead of 'none', sentenceSplit true, and htmlSplit 'lines'. All three improve chunk quality for most users but change the output.

There is also the question of the options object. It has grown to 24 fields, some of which belong together, like the overlap fields and the table fields. I started a document with a grouped shape, for example overlap: { size, unit, locale }, and a codemod that moves the old fields.

I do not want to rush it. The plan in the document is to collect feedback in a discussion thread for a month, then decide. Users of the library with pinned output, such as those with stored embeddings, need a clear note that chunk borders will change.

I opened the discussion with the three default changes and the grouped options, and asked for objections.

summary: Replied to the first comments on the major version discussion; one user with stored embeddings asked for a way to keep the old chunking exactly.
body:
Two people commented. One agreed with all three defaults. The other maintains a search product with embeddings for 2 million chunks and cannot re-embed on every upgrade.

Their request is reasonable: a compatibility preset, for example preset: 'v2', that restores the old defaults and the old option behaviour. That is cheap to build, since it is only a set of default values, and it can be tested by running the v2 fixtures against the new code.

I answered that I will add it, and that the v2 preset will be tested against the current fixture outputs byte for byte. I added the point to the plan document.

summary: Wrote the codemod that moves the flat overlap and table options into the grouped shape and tested it on the repository's own examples and three user configs.
body:
The codemod uses jscodeshift and handles object literals passed to splitMarkdown and streamChunks, as well as options kept in a variable in the same file. It moves overlapSize, overlapUnit and segmenterLocale into overlap: { size, unit, locale }.

It does not follow options across files, which would need type information. In that case it leaves the code alone and prints a warning with the file and line, so the user can fix it by hand.

I tested it on the README examples, the docs snippets and the examples folder, and then on three config files that users had posted in issues. Two converted cleanly. The third spread an options object from another module, which got the warning.

The output is formatted with the project's Prettier config so that the diff stays small. Table options are next, then the CLI flags, which keep their old names as aliases.

summary: Ran the codemod for the grouped options on a copy of the docs examples and found it dropped comments next to moved keys, so it now keeps leading comments.
body:
After the codemod of this morning worked on the repository examples, I ran it on every code sample in the docs folder. Most samples came out right. In six of them a comment above a flat option such as overlapSize disappeared when the key moved into the overlap group.

The cause was that the codemod rebuilt the property from the value and the key and ignored the leading comments of the old node. I changed it to copy the comments to the new property. A trailing comment on the same line is kept too.

I added two fixtures to the codemod tests, one with a leading comment and one with a trailing comment. Both pass now. The codemod also leaves an already grouped config untouched, and a test covers that.

Still open: configs that spread a variable into the options object. The codemod cannot see inside the variable, so it should print a warning with the file and line instead of staying silent. I will do that next.

summary: Built the lossless mode switch for the next major version and verified on 40 real documents that it reproduces the 2.x chunk boundaries byte for byte.
body:
The design from the lossless-mode draft said two defaults must stay frozen: the way overlap is counted and the order in which split levels are tried. Today I implemented the switch. It is the option legacy: true, and it pins those two behaviours to the 2.x code paths.

I kept the old overlap counting in its own file, legacyOverlap.ts, instead of adding branches to the new code. The new splitter calls it only when legacy is on. This keeps the new code clean and makes the old code easy to delete in a later major version.

To check the claim I took 40 documents from the test corpus, including the long wiki export and the table heavy ones. I chunked them with the 2.6.1 package and with the new build in legacy mode, then compared the output as JSON. 38 documents matched exactly. Two differed.

Both differences came from the sentence split level. In 2.6.1 a sentence longer than maxSize fell through to word splitting twice, a bug fixed after the sentence pull request was merged. The fix changes the boundaries in rare cases. I decided the legacy mode must reproduce the bug for the default config, because stored embeddings depend on the exact boundaries, but only when sentence splitting is on, which is not the default.

With the bug reproduced, all 40 documents match. I added a snapshot test that stores the chunk hashes of the 40 documents, so a later change cannot break the promise silently. The README section about legacy mode is not written yet. That comes tomorrow, together with a note in the migration guide.

summary: Wrote the migration guide for the new major version, with the codemod command, the option mapping table and a section for users with stored embeddings.
body:
Today was documentation. The migration guide now has four parts: why the major version exists, the codemod command, a table that maps every old option to its new place, and a section for users with stored embeddings.

The mapping table is generated from the codemod rules instead of written by hand, so the two cannot disagree. A small script reads the rules and writes a Markdown file that the docs site includes. I checked the output against the old options list and found two options that were missing from the rules, tableRepeatHeader and the old maxTokens alias. Both are mapped now.

The embeddings section explains legacy: true in plain words. It says what stays the same, what does not get bug fixes, and that the flag will be removed one major version later. I asked the same question I expect from users: can I switch halfway? The answer is no, since the boundaries would mix, so the guide says to re-embed everything or stay on legacy.

I rendered the docs site locally and the guide builds. The translation freshness check now lists the guide as missing in all locales, which is the right result. Next is the changelog text for the first release candidate.

summary: Published the first release candidate of 3.0.0 under the next tag and found that the CLI bin path was wrong in the built package.
body:
I prepared 3.0.0-rc.0 with changesets in pre mode and published it under the next tag, so the normal install still gets 2.6.1. Before publishing I ran the tarball test as usual.

The tarball test installed the package in an empty folder and ran npx chunkdown --help. It failed with a missing file error. The bin field in package.json still pointed to dist/cli.js, but tsdown now writes dist/cli.mjs because the package switched to ESM only output in this major version.

I fixed the bin path and added a check to the tarball script that reads package.json, takes every path in bin, main, module and types, and asserts that the file exists in the packed list. This would have caught the problem without running the CLI at all.

After the fix I packed again. The install worked, the CLI printed help, and a chunking run on the README gave the expected 14 chunks. The types resolve under both node16 and bundler module resolution in a small test project.

I published rc.0 and wrote a short comment in the major version discussion asking for feedback, with the install command. I will wait a few days for reports.

summary: A user reported that the rc fails under CommonJS require, so I documented the ESM-only decision and added a clear error message for require.
body:
The first report on the release candidate came in the discussion: require('chunkdown') throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM on Node 18. This is a consequence of dropping the CommonJS build, which the plan for 3.0 had decided on.

I looked at whether the decision still holds. Node 20.19 and later can require ESM, but Node 18 is still used by several people who wrote in. Bringing back a dual build would double the test matrix for a small library, so I kept the decision.

What I changed is the experience of the failure. The README and the migration guide now have a box about ESM only, with the dynamic import form as a workaround for CommonJS code. I also answered the user with that snippet.

I left the package exports as they are. If more reports come, I will reconsider a thin CJS wrapper that only does a dynamic import.

summary: Fixed a rc bug where the grouped overlap option accepted a negative size and produced an endless loop in the splitter.
body:
While trying odd configs against the rc, I set overlap: { size: -5 } and the process never ended. The overlap code moves the start of the next chunk back by the overlap size, and with a negative size it moved forward, then looped on the same text.

The old flat option had the same hole, but nobody hit it. With the grouped shape I now validate options once at the start in a function called resolveOptions. It throws a RangeError with the option path in the message, for example overlap.size must be a non-negative integer.

I also added a guard in the splitter itself: if a step does not advance the position, it throws an internal error instead of looping. This is a safety net for bugs I have not found yet.

Tests cover negative size, a size larger than maxSize, NaN and a string. The larger-than-maxSize case was undefined before. I decided it is an error too, because the overlap would be bigger than the chunk. The legacy mode keeps the old behaviour of clamping, to stay frozen.

All tests pass, and I will include this in rc.1.

summary: Reviewed a pull request that adds a Vietnamese translation and asked the contributor to run the glossary check and fix the heading ids.
body:
A new pull request adds the Vietnamese docs. The contributor followed the locale folder structure from the contributing note, which is good, and did not touch the English pages this time.

The CI check for heading ids failed on three pages. The translator had translated the explicit ids in curly braces, for example the id for the overlap section, so the links from other pages broke. I commented with the three file names and explained that ids stay in English.

The glossary file has no entries for Vietnamese yet. I asked for at least the terms chunk, token and overlap, so that the next translators stay consistent.

The search plugin knew the locale code already, so there was no build failure like the one with Korean. I built the site locally on the branch of the contributor and the search index for the new locale is separate as it should be.

I did not merge. I will look again when the contributor pushes the fixes.

summary: Measured the new major version against 2.6.1 on large files and found it 11 percent faster on lists but 6 percent slower on tables, caused by the options validation inside the loop.
body:
Before more release candidates I ran the benchmark suite on both versions. The corpus has a 12 MB wiki export, a long list file with thousands of short items, and a table heavy report.

Results in median time of five runs: the wiki export went from 4.1 s to 3.9 s, the list file from 2.7 s to 2.4 s, and the table report from 1.8 s to 1.9 s. The list gain is the fix from the 2.6.1 release plus the new size cache. The table result is slower by about 6 percent, which I did not expect.

I profiled the table report with the node inspector. The top item that was new was resolveOptions, called for every table split. The table splitter calls the public split function recursively on cells with long text, and that function validates options every time.

I split the code into a public entry that validates once and an internal function that takes already resolved options. The recursive calls use the internal one. After this the table report ran in 1.7 s, faster than before.

I added the numbers to the benchmark notes file and a test that fails if resolveOptions is called more than once per top level call, using a spy. That protects the change from a later refactor.

The streaming splitter has the same structure and I checked it too. It was already using resolved options.

summary: Investigated a report that the token counter option silently ignored a custom tokenizer in the streaming splitter, found a missing pass-through in the grouped options, and fixed it.
body:
A user wrote that with the rc, chunks from splitStream were measured in characters even though they passed a tokenizer. In the normal splitter the same config worked. This sounded like a regression from the grouped options, so I started with a failing test.

The test creates a fake tokenizer that counts every word as ten tokens and expects that a chunk with maxSize 30 holds at most three words. The normal splitter passed. The streaming splitter produced chunks with many more words.

I followed the options through resolveOptions. The new shape puts the tokenizer under size: { unit, tokenizer }. The streaming splitter built its own counter from the old flat field options.tokenizer, which no longer exists after resolving. It got undefined and fell back to the character counter without any warning.

The type checker did not catch it because the streaming code read the field through an index access on a loosely typed object. That was a leftover from the prototype.

Fix steps:
- the streaming splitter now takes the counter from the resolved options, the same function the normal splitter uses
- the loosely typed access is replaced with the real type
- if size.unit is tokens and no tokenizer is given, resolveOptions throws instead of falling back

The last item is a behaviour change. In 2.x the fallback was a rough estimate of characters divided by four. I kept that estimate for legacy mode only and documented it.

The test now passes in both splitters, and I added the same fake tokenizer test to the shared suite that runs against both implementations. That suite is the reason the problem could be found fast, so I also added a case with a tokenizer that throws, to make sure the error surfaces.

I replied to the reporter and will ship the fix in rc.1 with the negative overlap fix.

summary: Published 3.0.0-rc.1 with the overlap validation, the tokenizer pass-through fix and the codemod warning for spread options.
body:
I collected the three fixes since rc.0 and published rc.1 under the next tag. The changeset text lists the overlap validation, the streaming tokenizer fix and the codemod change.

The codemod warning for spread options was the last item from the earlier session. When it meets a spread of a variable inside the options object, it now prints the file and line and says the config must be moved by hand. It does not change the file in that case.

The tarball test passed, including the new path check. I also installed rc.1 in the small test project that uses node16 resolution, and the types were fine.

I posted a note in the discussion and told the user with the tokenizer problem to try rc.1.

summary: The user with the tokenizer problem confirmed rc.1 works, and also asked why the error for a missing tokenizer does not suggest a fix, so the message was improved.
body:
The reporter tried rc.1 and confirmed that token chunks are right in the streaming splitter now. The second point was about the new error. When size.unit is tokens and no tokenizer is given, the message said only that a tokenizer is required.

I agree it is not enough. The message now says which option to set, size.tokenizer, and shows a one line example with the gpt-tokenizer package, since that is what most users pair it with. It also mentions that in legacy mode the character estimate is still used.

I added a test that checks the message contains the option path. Tests that match whole error strings break often, so the test only checks the path and the word tokenizer.

No release for this alone. It goes into rc.2 when there is more to ship.

summary: Went through the Vietnamese pull request again, merged it after the fixes, and added a CI hint that prints which heading ids are missing.
body:
The contributor pushed the fixes for the heading ids and added a glossary with eleven terms. I rebuilt the site on the branch and ran the freshness script. All pages are marked current except two that were added in the meantime, and those were the new migration guide pages, which no locale has.

The CI check for ids only said that a page failed. The contributor needed two rounds to find the problem. I changed the check to print the page, the missing id and the line in the English source where it is defined.

I tested the new output by removing an id from a copy of a translated page. The message was the following form: missing id overlap-size in vi/guide/overlap.md, defined in guide/overlap.md line 41. That is enough to fix it without reading the script.

Then I merged the translation. The search index for the locale builds on its own. One small thing is left, the language switcher shows the native name only, and the contributor wrote it correctly with the accents.

I thanked the contributor in the pull request and pointed to the glossary for the next page updates. Translations of the migration guide will wait until the guide is final, which is after the last release candidate.

summary: Started the work on front matter in the new major version by writing down how YAML, TOML and JSON front matter should be detected and kept out of the chunks.
body:
Front matter support was listed in the plan, and I began with the design, since remark does not parse it by default. The goal is that a document starting with front matter does not produce a chunk full of metadata, but the metadata is still available.

First I collected cases from real files in the corpus and from the issues. YAML between three dashes is the usual one. Hugo files use TOML between three plus signs. A few users have JSON front matter in curly braces on the first lines. Some documents have a horizontal rule of three dashes at the top that is not front matter, which is the dangerous case.

Rules I decided on:
- front matter is only recognised at the very first byte of the file, after an optional byte order mark
- for YAML the closing line is three dashes or three dots, on its own line
- if there is no closing line, the text is treated as normal Markdown, never as an endless front matter block
- the content is not parsed by chunkdown; it is returned as a raw string in the result under frontMatter, with a format field

I chose not to parse YAML because that would add a dependency, and users who need it already have one. The option frontMatter can be 'strip', 'keep' or 'chunk'. Strip is the default in 3.0. The keep value leaves the block as the first chunk, and chunk puts the raw string in meta.frontMatter of every chunk of the document, which several RAG users asked for.

The size accounting is the open question for the chunk value. If every chunk carries the front matter in its meta, it does not count toward maxSize because meta is not text. I decided that it does not count, and wrote this in the design note so no one is surprised.

I used the unified ecosystem as a check. remark-frontmatter exists and could do the detection, but it creates a node type that I would have to handle in the streaming splitter as well. I decided to write the detection myself, about forty lines, working on the raw string before parsing. This also works for the streaming splitter, which reads the first block of the stream.

Next step: failing tests with ten fixtures, including the horizontal rule case and an unclosed block.

summary: Implemented front matter detection for YAML, TOML and JSON in both splitters, and found that Windows line endings broke the closing line match.
body:
I wrote the tests first with ten fixtures: YAML, TOML, JSON, a BOM at the start, an unclosed block, a horizontal rule at the top, front matter that is not at the start, an empty block, a block with dots as closing line, and one with Windows line endings.

The detection is a function detectFrontMatter(text) that returns the format, the raw content, and the offset where the body starts, or null. It does not allocate a copy of the document; it only scans line by line from the start until it finds the closing line.

Nine fixtures passed at once. The Windows one failed because the closing line was compared with three dashes exactly, while the line was three dashes followed by a carriage return. I now split lines on \n and trim a trailing \r before the comparison. The raw content keeps the original line endings, since I do not want to change user text.

The offset matters for meta. The offsets of chunks must refer to the original document including the front matter, otherwise users cannot map a chunk back to the file. I added the body offset to every position at the end of the splitter, and a test checks that text.slice(chunk.start, chunk.end) equals the chunk text for each fixture.

The streaming splitter was harder. It reads in blocks and the front matter may be split across two reads. The first block is held back until either a closing line is found, or 64 KB have been read. After 64 KB without a closing line, the text is treated as a normal document. The limit is an option, frontMatterMaxSize, but I did not document it; it is internal for now.

I tested the stream with a reader that returns one byte at a time, which found one more problem. A closing line that arrives in two pieces, as two dashes and then one dash, was missed because the check ran on each piece. The scan now works on the buffer of all text so far.

The three values strip, keep and chunk work in both splitters, and the shared test suite runs each fixture through both. The chunk value copies the raw string by reference, so memory use is not multiplied for large documents.

Open: the CLI needs a flag, and the docs need a page. I also want to check what happens with a document that is only front matter.

summary: Added the CLI flag and docs for front matter, and fixed the case of a document made only of front matter, which returned one empty chunk.
body:
I started with the odd case from yesterday. A file with only front matter, and nothing after it, gave one chunk with empty text in strip mode. Users who index a folder would then store empty vectors. The splitter should return an empty array in this case.

The cause was a rule that every document gives at least one chunk. That rule is used to avoid empty results for whitespace documents, but it was wrong here. I changed it so that the minimum of one chunk applies only if the document has text before stripping, and the result of an empty body is an empty array. A whitespace only file is also an empty array now. This is a behaviour change, so it is listed in the migration guide, and legacy mode keeps the old single empty chunk.

Then the CLI. The flag is --front-matter with the values strip, keep and chunk, the same as the option. In the JSON output of the CLI each chunk has the meta.frontMatter field in the chunk mode. I also added a line to the text output in the verbose mode that says the format of the front matter that was found, for example front matter: yaml, 212 chars.

The CLI tests run the built binary against a folder of fixtures and compare the output to stored files. I added three new stored files and checked that the diff is only the new field.

Docs steps:
- a new page for front matter with the rules from the design note
- an example for a blog folder where the title from the YAML is used to prefix each chunk
- a note about the 64 KB limit in the stream mode, which I decided to document after all because users who stream large files will wonder

The example in the docs is real code. I ran it against a sample blog post to be sure that the parsing of the title with a small regex does what the page says. It works for simple titles. For quoted titles it leaves the quotes, so the page says a YAML parser should be used in real projects.

The translation freshness script now lists the front matter page as missing in the two locales, which is expected. Next is rc.2 with the front matter, the empty document change and the error message.

summary: Published 3.0.0-rc.2 and found with a test project that the new exports map hid the package.json file, which broke a popular version checking tool.
body:
I published rc.2 with front matter support, the empty document change and the better tokenizer error. The tarball test passed again, so this was the normal flow until I did the extra check I now do with a test project that mimics what users do.

One of the steps in that project reads the version with require('chunkdown/package.json') in an ESM-friendly way through createRequire. It failed with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED. The reason is that the new exports map lists only the entry point and the types. In 2.x there was no exports map, so every file could be imported.

Some tools read package.json of dependencies, for example bundle analysers and a version check that a user mentioned in the discussion. Adding './package.json' to the exports map is the standard solution and costs nothing.

I also looked at the other paths people might have imported from 2.x, like chunkdown/dist/cli.js. Those were never public, and the migration guide already says deep imports stop working. I added one sentence with the example of the error message so that people can search for it.

After the fix I packed again and ran the test project. The version read works now. The exports map is checked by a new test that imports each listed subpath from the packed tarball and fails if one cannot be resolved.

I will publish rc.3 when there is another change, and not for a single line. The discussion has two new comments about naming of the legacy flag, which I will read tomorrow.

summary: Replied to two discussion comments about the name of the legacy flag and decided to keep legacy: true but to also accept a version string like '2' for the future.
body:
The comments asked whether legacy: true is a good name, because in the next major version there may be a different legacy to preserve. One person proposed compat: '2'.

I thought about it. A boolean is simple, and nearly all users will want exactly the 2.x behaviour. But the point about the future is right. If 4.0 changes boundaries again, legacy: true would be ambiguous.

Decision: legacy accepts true or a string. True means the previous major version, which is 2 in this release. The string '2' means the same thing, and is the form the docs recommend, because it will not silently change meaning later. Unknown strings throw an error that lists the supported values.

I changed resolveOptions and its tests, and updated the guide and the embeddings section. I replied in the discussion with the reasoning and thanked both people. The change is small enough to land in rc.3.

summary: Triaged a new issue saying chunks split inside an inline math span, and confirmed it is a real gap because the parser treats dollar signs as plain text.
body:
The issue shows a physics paper in Markdown where a formula such as $a + b = c$ sometimes ends up half in one chunk and half in the next. The reporter asks if math can be kept together.

I reproduced it with their example file. The cut happens at the word level, which is the last resort split level, and a formula with spaces looks like several words to it. The parser we use has no math support unless the remark-math plugin is added, so the tree has plain text there.

I checked whether adding remark-math is reasonable. It would add a dependency, and block math with double dollar signs would become its own node type that the splitters must know. For the stream splitter it also changes the first scan.

A smaller approach is to treat a span between single dollar signs on one line as unbreakable at the word level, like the rule that already protects inline code. The risk is a text with two prices like $5 and $10, which would look like a formula. The pandoc rule helps here: the opening dollar must be followed by a non-space and the closing dollar must be preceded by a non-space and not followed by a digit.

I answered in the issue with these two options and asked the reporter to try the pandoc style rule on the real documents once it exists. I labelled the issue as an enhancement for 3.1, not for the major version.

summary: Prototyped the unbreakable inline math rule with the pandoc dollar sign test and measured its false positives on a corpus of 300 documents with prices.
body:
Since the issue could be solved with a small rule, I wrote the prototype to see how bad the false positives are. The rule lives in the word level splitter, next to the inline code protection, and it is behind an option, math: 'inline', off by default.

The matching function takes a line and returns the spans to protect. It applies the pandoc rule: the opening dollar is followed by a non-space, the closing dollar is preceded by a non-space and not followed by a digit, and an escaped dollar is skipped.

To measure false positives I used 300 documents that I had from earlier work, many of them product pages and finance notes with prices. I ran the matcher and listed every span it found. In total it found 41 spans. Looking through them by hand, 29 were real formulas from the three math documents of the corpus, and 12 were false positives.

The 12 false positives came from texts like a range written as $5-$10, where the closing dollar sign is preceded by a dash, which is a non-space. I added a rule that a span must not contain another dollar sign immediately after a digit or a dash. With this rule 3 false positives remained, all of them in one document that uses dollar signs as currency in a table cell.

A false positive here is not harmful in most cases. It means that a short span is not cut at word level, which only matters if the span is longer than maxSize. So I added a limit: spans longer than 200 characters are ignored, so a stray dollar sign cannot turn a whole paragraph into an unbreakable block.

Tests cover the formula examples from the issue, the price examples, an escaped dollar and the long span limit. Everything passes in both splitters.

I did not write docs yet because the reporter should test the prototype first. I pushed it to the issue as a comment with the tarball instructions, since there are no branches in this project and the change is only in my working copy until the release.

summary: Released 3.0.0-rc.3 with the legacy version string and the math prototype held back, then fixed a docs build break caused by the new front matter page.
body:
I prepared rc.3 with the legacy: '2' form and a small fix to the CLI help text. The math prototype is not in it, since the reporter has not answered, and I do not want an unfinished option in a release candidate. I moved the code behind an uncommitted stash, which is easy to forget, so I wrote a line about it in the issue.

The tarball test passed and I published. Then the docs build in CI failed. The error came from the new front matter page: it contains a code block with an example of YAML front matter, and the docs site itself reads front matter at the top of the page. My example started with three dashes at the very start of a fenced block inside an outer block, and the markdown processor of the docs site took a pair of three dash lines as the page's own metadata.

I looked at the file. The page began with an example, before the first heading, instead of text. The site tool saw the first three dashes of the example as the start of its metadata. I moved a paragraph of text to the beginning of the page and also used a fence with four backticks for the nested example.

The build worked after this. It was an amusing case of the problem the feature addresses.

I also checked the translations. The two locales that have the front matter page missing are flagged as expected, and the freshness check hashes the full file, so the move of the paragraph is detected as a change in English for any later translation.

Remaining before the final release:
- wait for feedback on rc.3 for a week
- decide about the math option for 3.0 or 3.1
- finish the changelog with the full list of breaking changes

I wrote the list of breaking changes now, while it is fresh. It has nine items: ESM only, the grouped options, the empty array for empty documents, the tokenizer error, the exports map, the removed deep imports, the sentence level default, the front matter default of strip, and the meta field names. For each item there is a link to the guide section. Some of these were small, but a user who upgrades should find them in one place.

summary: The math issue reporter tested the prototype on a paper corpus and found it protects formulas well, but asked for block math with double dollar signs too.
body:
The reporter ran the tarball with the prototype on about 60 papers. They said no formula was cut any more in the inline case, and the three false positives I had expected did not show up in their data.

The new request is block math between double dollar signs on separate lines. Today these blocks are treated as paragraph text, and a long derivation is split in the middle. That is more serious than the inline case, because a half derivation is useless for retrieval.

I thought about how to do it in the same rule set. A line that is only two dollar signs opens a block, and the next such line closes it. The block can then be treated as one unit like a code block, which the splitter already knows: if it fits, it is kept whole, and if it is larger than maxSize, it is cut at line breaks with a warning.

I will do it as part of the same option, math: 'inline' becomes math: true with both forms, and 'inline' remains as a value. The work goes into 3.1, so the major version is not delayed.

summary: Decided to ship 3.0.0 final after a week without new rc reports, ran the full release checklist and found the changelog still pointed to the old option names in two places.
body:
There were no new reports on rc.3 for a week, only two thumbs up on the discussion. I decided that the next step is the final release, and I went through the checklist I keep in the release notes file.

First the code. I ran the whole test suite on the three supported Node versions in CI, and all passed. The snapshot test with the chunk hashes of the 40 documents in legacy mode still matches, which is the most important promise of this release. I also ran the benchmark again and the numbers are the same as before, with the table report at 1.7 s.

Then the documentation. I read the migration guide from the top as if I were a user with a config from 2.x. The codemod command worked on a copy of three configs from the issues. In the guide, the mapping table is generated and correct.

The changelog is where I found the problem. The text from the early changesets still used the flat names overlapSize and tableRepeatHeader in two entries, because I wrote them before the options were grouped. A user who reads the changelog would look for options that no longer exist. I corrected both entries and searched the whole repository for the old names. They remain only in the codemod rules, the legacy file and the migration table, which is right.

I also checked the package metadata: the version field, the engines field with Node 18 as the minimum, the repository link, and the files list. The packed tarball has 41 files and no test fixtures, which I checked by listing it.

The translation status is that Spanish, Korean and Vietnamese lack the migration guide and the front matter page. I wrote this in the release notes so that translators know what to do, and I opened an issue with a checklist of pages, labelled for contributors.

I did not publish yet. The plan is to leave the final step for a clear head tomorrow: exit the pre mode in changesets, version, run the tarball test once more, publish with the latest tag, and then post in the discussion.

summary: Fixed the two stale option names in the changelog and added a check that fails the release script when a removed 2.x option name appears in the changelog or README.
body:
The release checklist from this morning found the changelog still using the flat option names in two places: overlapSize in the breaking changes list and tableHeader in the upgrade example. I replaced them with the grouped shape, overlap.size and table.repeatHeader, and read the whole 3.0.0 section again against the migration guide. The guide and the changelog now use the same names everywhere.

To keep this from happening again I added a small script, scripts/check-names.ts, that reads a list of removed option names and greps CHANGELOG.md, README.md and the docs folder for them. Old names are allowed only inside fenced blocks marked as 'before' in the migration guide, so the script skips those. It fails with the file and line of each hit.

The first run found one more hit in the docs page for the CLI, where the flag table still described --overlap-size as a config key. I fixed that too. I wired the script into the prepublish step and into the CI workflow after the lint job. It runs in under a second.

I also ran the rest of the checklist: the packed tarball lists the expected files, the exports map resolves for import and for types, and the bin path works after a fresh install in a temp project. Nothing else was wrong. Still open: the math work for block dollar signs, which I do not want in the final release, and the final version bump with changesets.

summary: Published 3.0.0 final to npm after the checklist passed, then confirmed a clean install and the codemod command work from the registry package.
body:
After the name fixes and the new check script passed in CI, I ran the changeset version step and reviewed the generated changelog once more. The rc entries were folded into one 3.0.0 section, which reads better than the five rc blocks.

I published 3.0.0 with the latest tag and then installed it in an empty directory. The import, the CLI and the types all resolved. I ran the codemod through npx on the repository's own example configs and it produced the same output as the local build did.

The GitHub release was created with the migration guide linked at the top, and the pinned discussion got a short post saying the final is out. I told the user with stored embeddings that legacy: true reproduces the 2.x boundaries. The math prototype stays on its own branch of ideas and is not in this release. Next I will watch the issue tracker for a few days and then pick up block math.

summary: First post-release issue was a user whose build broke because a 2.x deep import path no longer exists; added a clear note to the migration guide and a helpful runtime error.
body:
A user opened an issue two days after the release: their build failed with 'Package subpath ./dist/splitters is not defined by exports'. They had been importing from a deep path that was never documented but worked in 2.x. The exports map in 3.0 only exposes the root and the cli entry.

I did not want to reopen the deep paths, since hiding them was a deliberate part of the cleaner API. What I checked was whether everything they needed is available from the root. The splitter they used is exported there as splitMarkdown, so the fix on their side is a one-line import change.

I added a section 'Deep imports' to the migration guide with a table mapping the three most common old paths to the root exports. I also grepped the issues of the last year for deep paths and found two more mentions, which both fit the table.

The codemod can handle this case as well, so I extended it to rewrite imports from the old dist paths to the root. I added three fixtures: a named import, a default import and a require call, which the codemod leaves alone but prints a warning for. All fixtures pass.

I replied on the issue with the mapping and the codemod command, and the user confirmed it worked within the hour. I left the issue open until the guide change is released in a docs deploy. The docs deploy went out in the evening.

summary: Implemented unbreakable block math with double dollar signs, sharing the span rule from the inline prototype, and tested it on the paper corpus and on a set of shell and template documents.
body:
The issue reporter had asked for block math, so I started from the inline prototype and generalized it. Block math is easier to detect than inline math because $$ must sit at the start of a line or at the end of one, and a closing $$ must follow. The parser still sees the content as plain paragraph text, so the rule works on the text of paragraph nodes and on the raw lines between them.

The first version treated any paragraph that contains an opening $$ line and a later closing $$ line as one unit, even when a blank line separates the formula lines. In LaTeX that is allowed in some flavors, but the parser had already split such text into several paragraph nodes. I added a merge step that joins the nodes between the two markers into one atomic block before the size logic runs.

The edge cases took most of the time. An unclosed $$ would swallow the rest of the document, so I added a limit: if no closing marker is found within 200 lines the opening is treated as plain text. Escaped dollar signs are ignored. A $$ inside a fenced code block is never touched, because code blocks are already atomic.

I measured on three sets. The paper corpus has 120 documents with formulas, and all 1,480 block formulas stayed whole in the chunks. The 300 price documents produced no new false positives. A third set of 60 shell and template docs, where $$ means the process id, produced 4 false positives, all from lines that contained only $$ in an example. I added a rule that the marker line may not be followed by a shell prompt style line, which cut them to 1.

When a formula is larger than maxSize it is still emitted whole, with meta.oversized set to true, the same behavior as for code blocks. I wrote 18 new tests for it. The inline and block rules now live in one file, src/math.ts. Left to do: the docs page and the option name, which is currently math: true.

summary: Wrote the docs page for math protection, decided it is on by default in 3.x with an opt-out, and noted the one remaining false positive.
body:
I wrote the docs page for protected math spans, with examples for inline and block formulas and a section on how the dollar sign test works. The page says plainly that prices like $5 and $10 are not treated as math when the closing sign has a digit or a space next to it.

The main decision was the default. Turning it on by default changes chunk boundaries for users with formulas, so it is a behavior change in a minor release. I decided on on-by-default anyway for new users but off under legacy mode, so the lossless 2.x reproduction stays exact. The option is math: false to opt out. I put this into the changelog as a changed behavior with the reason.

I re-ran the 40 document lossless check from before, with legacy on, and the output was still identical byte for byte. With legacy off, 3 of the 40 documents changed, and all three contain real formulas.

The one remaining false positive is the shell case with $$ on its own line. I documented it with a workaround, which is to put the example in a code block. Next I will open the pull request for review by the issue reporter.

summary: The math reporter tested the pull request on their corpus and found a bug with formulas inside list items, which lost their indentation when merged; fixed it.
body:
The reporter ran the math branch on their paper collection and found that formulas inside list items came out with the indentation removed. For block math in a list item the merge step joined the paragraph nodes and used the node text, which has no indent.

I reproduced it with a small fixture of a numbered list with a $$ block inside the second item. The chunk text was correct for the splitter, but the output no longer matched the source slice. Chunks in chunkdown are meant to be slices of the original text, so this broke an invariant.

The fix was to build merged math blocks from the source offsets of the first and last node instead of joining node text. That keeps the original whitespace and also fixes a smaller issue with blank lines inside the formula, which had been collapsed.

I added a property style test that checks for every document in the fixtures folder that each chunk is a substring of the source. It found one more case, a formula in a blockquote where the quote markers were dropped. I fixed that the same way. All 1,900 tests pass, and the reporter's corpus now round-trips fully.

summary: Released 3.1.0 with math protection, and investigated a regression report where chunks of documents with Windows line endings contained mixed newlines, which turned out to be in the new math merge.
body:
I prepared 3.1.0 with the math protection as the headline. The changeset text, the docs page and the legacy behavior were all checked. The release went out in the early morning, and I installed it into a temp project to check it.

Within a few hours a user reported that chunks from files with CRLF endings now had mixed newlines, with some lines ending in LF only. The user feeds chunks into a diff tool and the mixed endings caused noise.

I reproduced it with a fixture made from a paper with CRLF endings. The cause was in the merge step of block math: when I joined the pieces between the two $$ markers, I inserted a single '\n' between nodes where the source had a blank line between them. The source slice fix from last week handled the offsets but one code path for the fallback, when offsets are missing, still joined with '\n'.

That fallback should not be needed, since the offsets are always there for parsed nodes. But nodes created by the front matter handling carry no position, and a document with front matter followed by block math went down that path. I removed the fallback and made the front matter nodes carry synthetic positions.

I then wrote a test that converts every fixture to CRLF and asserts that the chunks contain no bare LF, and that the chunks equal the source slices. It found no other cases. I also added the line ending check to the property test from last week.

I released 3.1.1 in the evening with the fix and answered the user. The commit message and changelog describe the cause. A lesson for later: the first release of a feature that touches text assembly needs a CRLF fixture from the start.

summary: Answered a user question on whether chunk overlap can be counted in sentences, and concluded it is possible with the shared segmenter but needs a new option shape.
body:
A user asked in the discussions whether overlap can be measured in sentences instead of characters, because their documents have very uneven sentence lengths. Today overlap.size is in characters or tokens, following the size unit.

I checked the overlap code. Since the sentence split change, the overlap code already uses the shared segmenter to avoid cutting a sentence in half, so the pieces are there. A sentence-count overlap would take the last N segments of the previous chunk.

The open question is the shape of the option. I leaned towards overlap: { unit: 'sentences', size: 2 } as an extra value of an existing unit field. That fits the grouped options without a new key. I wrote this in the discussion and asked the user whether two sentences would be enough, and noted that it would come in a minor release, not before the next bugfix batch.

summary: Implemented sentence-based overlap behind overlap.unit, with the rule that the overlap never pushes a chunk above maxSize, and covered it with tests on real documents.
body:
I started the sentence overlap from yesterday's discussion. The overlap.unit field now accepts 'chars', 'tokens' and 'sentences', where chars is the default as before.

In the sentence mode the splitter takes the last N segments of the previous chunk and puts them in front of the next one. The problem is the size limit. A chunk plus its overlap can be above maxSize, and in character mode the overlap budget is carved out of the chunk budget. For sentences I did the same: the splitter first measures the overlap segments, then reduces the budget for the new content by that amount.

If the overlap itself is larger than half of maxSize, I drop the oldest overlap sentences until it fits. In that case meta.overlapTrimmed is set so users can see what happened. Before that rule, a test document with a 900 character sentence and maxSize 1000 produced chunks that were almost only overlap.

Tables and code blocks are not given sentence overlap, because their chunks are not made of sentences. They keep the existing behavior, which is the header repeat for tables and no overlap for code. I wrote this into the docs.

I tested on 25 real documents with N = 1, 2 and 3. All chunks stay under maxSize, and no chunk begins in the middle of a sentence. I added 14 tests. The streaming splitter shares the code, so it works there as well, which I checked with a test.

summary: Profiled the splitter on a 40 MB generated Markdown file after a user said memory climbs past 2 GB, and found the syntax tree was kept alive for the whole run.
body:
A user reported that splitting a very large Markdown file, about 40 MB, used more than 2 GB of memory and sometimes crashed Node with an out of memory error. They use the normal splitter, not the streaming one, and asked if the memory use is expected.

I generated a similar file by repeating a mix of real documents, then ran the splitter with --heap-prof. The peak was 2.3 GB. Most of it was the remark syntax tree with position data for every node, which is expected, but a second large part was the array of node text slices that I build once up front for the size measurement.

The slices are strings that point into the source in V8, but after concatenation in the merge step they became flat copies. About 600 MB came from that. I changed the measurement to work on offsets and only materialize text for the chunk that is being emitted.

The peak went from 2.3 GB to 1.5 GB. The tree itself is the rest, and the real fix for this size is the streaming splitter, which parses in sections. I wrote a docs note recommending it for files over 10 MB.

The time did not change in any measurable way, 9.8 seconds before and 9.6 after. I will check whether the streaming splitter keeps flat memory on the same file in the next session.

summary: Checked the streaming splitter on the 40 MB file and found its memory stays at 180 MB, but only if the input is a stream and not a string read from disk first.
body:
I ran the streaming splitter on the same generated 40 MB file. With a file stream as input, the peak memory was 180 MB and it finished in 7.4 seconds, so it is both faster and much lighter.

When I passed the whole file as a string, the peak was 700 MB, since the string itself and the sections copy each other. That is what the reporter most likely did, because the README example reads the file with readFile first.

I changed the README and docs examples to use createReadStream for the streaming splitter and added a sentence that a string input defeats the purpose. I also added a runtime hint: when the streaming splitter gets a string larger than 20 MB it prints a one-time warning that suggests a stream.

I replied to the reporter with the numbers and the changed example. The memory fix from this morning goes into the next patch release.

summary: Released 3.2.0 with sentence overlap and the lower memory use, and updated the benchmark table in the docs with the new numbers.
body:
I released 3.2.0 this morning. It has the sentence overlap unit, the offset based size measurement that cut peak memory by about a third, and the large string warning for the streaming splitter.

Before publishing I re-ran the benchmark suite against 2.6.1 and 3.1.1. On lists 3.2.0 stays about 11 percent faster than 2.6.1. The table slowdown from the options validation inside the loop, which was 6 percent in the rc, is now gone, because I moved the validation out of the loop in an earlier fix and the offset change added a little more.

I updated the benchmark table in the docs, with the file sizes and the machine description, so the numbers are reproducible. The memory column is new.

The changeset check and the check-names script passed. I installed the published package in a temp project and ran the CLI on a sample. All fine. The next topic is a pull request that someone announced for a Python style docstring mode, which I have not seen yet.

summary: Investigated a report of links breaking at a chunk border when a link reference definition sits far from its use, and built a fix that appends the needed definitions to each chunk.
body:
The report came from a user who stores chunks separately: a chunk contained [the setup guide][setup] but the definition [setup]: https://... sat at the end of the document, so the chunk alone had a dead link. We solved the inline link break earlier, but reference style links were never handled.

I first checked how footnotes are done, since the duplicate footnote fix of a while ago had the same situation. Footnote definitions are appended to the chunk that uses them, under meta.appended. I decided that link reference definitions should follow the same model, so users have one concept to understand.

The implementation has three steps. First, a pass over the tree collects all definition nodes into a map by normalized label. Markdown labels are case-insensitive and whitespace-collapsed, so the normalization follows the CommonMark rule, which I checked with the spec examples. Second, for each chunk the splitter finds reference nodes, both linkReference and imageReference, and looks the labels up. Third, the needed definitions are appended after the chunk body, separated by a blank line, once per label.

The size rule was the tricky part. The appended definitions count against maxSize, because users care about the final chunk size. I measure them before the chunk is closed, the same as for footnotes. If a chunk has so many references that the definitions alone would exceed 30 percent of maxSize, the definitions are still appended but meta.appendedOverflow is set.

A second problem was the definitions themselves: they are separate nodes in the tree and sat in the normal flow of chunks. Without a change, the definition lines at the end of the document would have formed a chunk of their own, with only link lines. I now remove definitions that were appended elsewhere from the flow. When a definition is never referenced, it stays where it is, so nothing is lost from the output.

I tested with 30 real documents, among them two large READMEs with 80 reference links each. In every one, each chunk resolves all its links on its own, which I check with a test that parses each chunk alone and counts unresolved reference nodes. The count was zero in all of them. The size limit held. The types for meta.appended got a new field, links. The docs page and the option are still to do, because I want a flag to turn the appending off.

summary: Added the appendLinks option and docs for the link reference fix, and put it on by default but off in legacy mode.
body:
I added the option links.append, which is true by default, so that users with a pipeline that already resolves definitions themselves can switch it off. In legacy mode it is false, which keeps the 2.x boundaries exactly.

The option sits in the grouped options next to footnotes, and I made the docs page for footnotes and links a single page, since they work in the same way. The page has one example with a document before and after, and the meta fields.

I extended the codemod check for unknown keys, so a user who wrote the old name in a config gets a warning. There was no old name, so it is only the usual unknown key message.

The lossless check on the 40 documents still passes with legacy on. With legacy off, 9 of 40 changed, which are the documents with reference links. I wrote the changeset as a minor. The pull request is ready for the next review.

summary: Replied to the reporter of the link issue after they tested the branch and asked whether definitions with titles are kept exactly, which they are, with one whitespace exception.
body:
The reporter tested the branch on their wiki export and wrote back with a question about definitions that have titles, like [id]: http://x.com "Title". They wanted to know if the appended text is identical to the source.

I checked. The appended definition is the exact source slice of the definition node, so the title and its quotes are kept as written. The exception I found is a definition that spans two lines, with the url on the first and the title on the second. I had been trimming each appended slice and joining them with a newline, which kept the inner newline, so that case was fine too.

The one difference is the trailing whitespace of the line, which is trimmed. I wrote a test with a title on a second line and trailing spaces to pin that behavior.

The reporter also found that an image reference to a definition used by a link in another chunk was appended twice across chunks, which is intended, because each chunk must stand alone. I explained that in the reply. I will merge the pull request after one more run of the property test.

summary: Merged the link definitions work and released 3.2.1 with it, after the property test caught a chunk that lost an unreferenced definition inside a list.
body:
Before the merge I ran the property test over all fixtures and one failed: a definition inside a list item was not in the output at all. I had removed definitions from the flow when they were appended elsewhere, but I used the label to decide, and the same label was defined twice in the document. Markdown uses the first one, so the second is dead, yet it was removed from the flow although never appended.

The fix was to remove from the flow only the node that was actually used for the append, which is the first by document order. Dead duplicates stay where they are. I added a fixture with a duplicate label and a test that the full text of all chunks, minus appended parts, equals the source.

After that the property test passed on all 60 fixtures. I merged the pull request and released 3.2.1 with a changeset that describes the behavior as a fix for broken reference links.

I installed the published package, split the reporter's sample and checked the result. I closed the issue with a link to the release. The contributor who announced the docstring mode has not sent the pull request yet.

summary: Reviewed the pull request for a docstring splitting mode, which parses Python docstrings as Markdown, and asked for it to be moved out of core into a separate helper.
body:
The pull request from the new contributor adds a docstring mode: it takes a Python file, extracts the docstrings with a regular expression and splits each as Markdown. The idea is useful, since people index code documentation, and the code is tidy with good tests.

I have three concerns. The first is scope. chunkdown is a Markdown splitter, and a Python parser in core is a new area to maintain, with all its edge cases like raw strings, nested quotes and docstrings in f-strings. A regular expression will fail on these in ways that are hard to see.

The second is the option shape. The PR adds a top-level mode: 'docstring' to the options, which does not fit the grouped options of 3.x. The third is the size of the change, 600 lines in core, plus a new dependency for dedenting.

I tested the branch on five real Python files. Three worked, but one lost a docstring that used single quotes and one produced a chunk from a string that was not a docstring at all, a long message in a function call. That confirms the regex risk.

My proposal in the review was to publish the extraction as a separate small package or as an example in the docs folder, which would pass text to the normal splitter. I offered to link it from the README and to expose an hook for a custom text source if that is missing. I wrote the comments politely and with the examples of the failing files, so they can be turned into tests.

I am not sure the contributor will agree, so I also wrote down what I would accept in core: nothing that parses another language. I will wait for their answer.

summary: Landed a splitText export and a smaller API surface for the docstring helper after the pull request review, then fixed a test that depended on the order of exported names.
body:
The docstring pull request from the review a few days ago needed one thing from core: a way to split a string without going through the file based entry point. I started by reading how the helper called the splitter and found it wrote each docstring to a temporary file only to pass a path, which was slow and broke on read-only systems.

I added a splitText export that takes a string and the same grouped options as the main function. It shares the code path with the file reader, so the chunk boundaries are identical. I checked this by running both on 25 real documents and comparing the output byte for byte; all 25 matched, including three with Windows line endings.

The type for splitText reuses the existing options type, so nothing new had to be documented for the option shape. I wrote a short docs section with one example and added it to the API page. The legacy mode also works with splitText, because the switch lives in the options and not in the entry point.

While adding the export I found that an API snapshot test compared the list of exported names in file order. Adding one name in the middle changed the snapshot for no real reason. I changed the test to sort the names before comparing and added a second check that every export has a docs entry.

The build with tsdown produced the types file with the new export on the first try. I packed the tarball and installed it in a scratch project to confirm that both the ESM import and the types resolve. The exports map still exposes package.json, which was a problem in an earlier release candidate.

I wrote a changeset marked as a minor change. Still open: the docstring author wants a way to pass a base heading level, so that docstring headings nest under the function name. I think that belongs in their helper and not in core, and I will say so in the reply. Next step is to ask them to build against the branch before the release.

summary: Investigated why some tables with merged-looking empty header cells were repeated wrongly when split by rows, and fixed the header detection for tables whose first row is empty.
body:
A user sent a sample document where the header row of a table repeated in every chunk as a row of empty cells, and the real column names, which sit in the second row, were never repeated. The table came from a tool that exports with an empty first line, like | | | | and then the names.

In GitHub flavored Markdown the first row is the header and the second line is the separator row with dashes, so in the sample the header was truly the empty row, and the names were body data. Technically the splitter did what the spec says. But the result is useless for retrieval, and the user's other tools show the same table in the same way.

I considered what a good rule is. If a header row has only empty cells, and the first body row has text in at least one cell, the first body row is likely the real header. I did not want to change the table in the output, because chunks should be slices of the source. So the rule only changes what is repeated at the top of the follow-up chunks: the empty header line and the separator stay as the table needs them, and the names row is repeated after them.

That means each follow-up chunk starts with the empty header, the separator and the names row. That is still a valid table, and the names show up in every chunk. I implemented it in the table splitter with a function isEmptyRow that treats cells with only whitespace or a non-breaking space as empty.

I looked for false positives. In 200 tables from the test documents, 3 had an empty header, and all of them were of this export type. No table with a real header was changed. I also tested a table with only an empty header and no body rows, which stays untouched.

The option is table.promoteFirstRow, set to 'auto' by default, with false to turn it off. In legacy mode it is false. I considered making it a bugfix without an option, but the legacy mode promise to reproduce 2.x chunks makes the option necessary, and users who disagree can switch it off.

I wrote 9 tests, including the case with a non-breaking space and a table in a blockquote. The meta field table.headerRows tells how many rows were repeated, which is now 2 in these cases, and the docs say so. I did not yet check the CLI output, since it prints the meta only with a flag. I will do that tomorrow, together with the release notes.

summary: Released 3.3.0 with the splitText export and the table header promotion, after the docstring package author confirmed their package builds against it.
body:
The docstring package author tested the branch and wrote that their package now builds against splitText and maps offsets correctly on their 40 file sample. They found one thing: the returned type did not export the Chunk interface by name, so they had to use ReturnType. I added the export of Chunk and ChunkMeta to the root entry.

I checked the CLI as planned yesterday. With the --meta flag the table.headerRows value is printed in the JSON output, and the new value 2 for promoted headers shows up correctly. The human readable output does not print meta, so nothing changed there.

I went through the release checklist. The changelog had the right grouped option names, so the check-names script passed. The packed tarball includes the types for splitText and Chunk. The exports map resolves both the import path and the types path, and package.json is still visible, as fixed in the release candidate.

I ran the lossless check again on the 40 documents with legacy on, and the chunks are identical byte for byte. With legacy off, 2 documents changed because of tables, which is the expected number. I ran the benchmark suite too. Tables are the same speed as in 3.2.1, within noise, and the promotion check adds almost nothing.

The release went out around noon. I installed the package in a temp project, called splitText and checked the types in an editor. I posted in the discussions about the new export and linked the docs page, and I linked the docstring package in the README under 'Related projects' after asking its author.

The user with the empty header table confirmed that their sample now repeats the names. They also asked if the same could be done for tables with two header rows. That is a different problem, because GFM has no such thing, so I opened a discussion rather than an issue, and I explained that I would want a clear rule first.
